Experiments show that SAE feature-based redundancy strongly correlates with performance-based redundancy across 17 benchmarks, while SAE-guided subset selection produces more stable and representative subsets than random sampling. SAE feature overlap also predicts inter-benchmark performance similarity across 8 benchmarks. These results show that SAE features can turn benchmark analysis from a costly performance-matrix problem into a feature-footprint problem, enabling evaluation-free benchmark compression and suite curation.

t: How Far Are AI Scientists from Changing the World? A Survey of Autonomous Scientific Discovery
a: Guangzhou Institute of Tropical and Marine Meteorology, China Meteorological Administration
Southern University of Science and Technology
ab: This survey asks how far AI Scientist systems are from changing the world, and argues that their impact should be evaluated not by whether they produce plausible papers, but by whether they produce auditable research trajectories that can be inspected, reproduced, and challenged. We first provide a definition of AI Scientists, distinguish them from adjacent scientific AI systems, and organize the field around four core capabilities: knowledge acquisition, hypothesis generation, experimental validation, and evolution. We further synthesize representative systems by autonomy, execution grounding, auditability, human control, and evidence level. The resulting picture shows a field moving from prompt-to-paper automation toward auditable research laboratories, where executable grounding, provenance, and human-governed autonomy become central. We conclude by identifying open challenges toward trustworthy AI-driven science and providing a roadmap for integrating AI Scientists into the future landscape of scientific discovery.

t: MENTOR: Reinforcement Learning via Flexible Teacher-Optimized Rewards for Tool-Use Distillation
a: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
ab: Distilling the tool-use capabilities of large language models (LLMs) into small language models (SLMs) is essential for their practical application. The predominant approach, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), is an off-policy distillation method that suffers from poor out-of-domain (OOD) generalization because it rigidly aligns with static teacher trajectories. While reinforcement learning (RL) offers an alternative, the capacity limitations of SLMs pose a severe dilemma: sparse outcome rewards provide insufficient guidance, whereas strict trajectory matching imposes overly restrictive constraints. To bridge this capacity-driven gap, we propose MENTOR, an on-policy distillation framework that introduces a flexible yet process-aware reward structure. Instead of enforcing rigid replication, MENTOR uses the teacher’s reference to guide tool-use behavior, balancing behavioral alignment with downstream performance. Extensive experiments on controlled executable-tool benchmarks demonstrate that MENTOR improves OOD tool-use performance compared to SFT and strict RL baselines. Our findings suggest that within verifiable tool-use environments, flexible tool-use alignment offers a more effective approach than strict trajectory replication for developing adaptable small models.

t: AP-GRPO: Anchor-Gated Phonetic Alignment with Policy Optimization for Pathological Speech Reconstruction
ab: Pathological speech from patients with neurodegenerative and neuromotor disorders is often acoustically distorted and linguistically fragmented, making pathological speech reconstruction necessary to recover intended textual content from distorted and incomplete speech recordings. Crucially, such recordings are rarely uniformly degraded: some words or short phrases remain reliable and can serve as audible anchors for reconstructing the corrupted surrounding content. We introduce **Anchor-gated Phonetic Group Relative Policy Optimization (AP-GRPO)**, a GRPO framework with phonetic reward that aligns speech language models (SLMs) through audible-anchor preservation and inter-anchor phonetic compatibility to the original speech signal. AP-GRPO consists of: (i) an **anchor-gated reward** that matches reliable audible anchors in clear regions; and (ii) an **inter-anchor phonetic alignment reward** that evaluates whether recovered contents are phonetically supported by the corresponding corrupted inter-anchor speech span. Across four disease conditions, AP-GRPO improves faithful speech reconstruction, and the learned anchor constraint automatically adapts to each condition and thus reveals interpretable disease-specific profiles: conditions with severe articulatory degradation require stronger anchor enforcement, whereas milder impairment or linguistically impaired conditions rely more on phonetic alignment for inter-anchor recovery.

t: Towards AI-Assisted Research Writing: Benchmarking LLMs for AI/ML Introduction Generation
ab: As researchers increasingly adopt LLMs as writing assistants, generating high-quality research paper introductions remains both challenging and essential. In this work, we benchmark Scientific Introduction Generation (SciIG), evaluating how well LLMs can produce coherent introductions from titles, abstracts, and related works in the machine learning domain. Curating new datasets from NAACL 2025 and ICLR 2025 papers, we assess five state-of-the-art models, including both open-source (DeepSeek-v3, Gemma-3-12B, LLaMA-4 Maverick, MistralAI Small 3.1) and closed-source GPT-4o systems across multiple dimensions: lexical overlap, semantic similarity, content coverage, faithfulness, consistency, citation correctness, and narrative quality. Our comprehensive framework combines automated metrics with LLM-as-a-judge evaluations. Results demonstrate LLaMA-4 Maverick’s superior performance on most metrics, particularly in lexical overlap, content coverage, citation quality, and perplexity. Moreover, three-shot prompting outperforms fewer-shot approaches more than 50% of the time on formula-based automated metrics and performs consistently better on all human evaluation metrics. These findings provide practical insights into developing effective research writing assistants and set realistic expectations for LLM-assisted academic writing. To foster reproducibility and future research, we publicly release all code and datasets.[Project page, code, and datasets: <https://kgarg8.github.io/emnlp26-sciig/>]

t: DVD: A Robust Method for Detecting Variant Contamination in Large Language Model Evaluation
a: Alibaba Group and Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
ab: Large language model (LLM) evaluation is increasingly confounded by *variant contamination*: training corpora contain semantically equivalent but lexically or syntactically altered test items. These variants can evade detectors based on sampling consistency or perplexity, inflating benchmark scores through memorization rather than reasoning. We formalize this problem and introduce **DVD** (**D**etection via **V**ariance of generation **D**istribution), a detector requiring only the test item, without external reference corpora or paired contaminated/clean sets. DVD models the local output distribution through repeated temperature sampling. Our key insight is that contaminated items alternate between *memory-adherence* and *perturbation-drift* states, producing unusually high variance in the synthetic difficulty of low-probability tokens, whereas uncontaminated items remain in drift with comparatively stable difficulty values. We construct the first dedicated variant-contamination benchmark across Omni-MATH and SuperGPQA by generating and filtering semantically equivalent variants, and simulate contamination by fine-tuning Qwen2.5 and Llama3.1 models of different scales. In most evaluated settings across datasets, model scales, architectures, and training configurations, **DVD** outperforms perplexity-based, Min-*k*%++, edit-distance (CDD), and embedding-similarity baselines, while showing strong robustness to hyperparameters. These results support generation-distribution variance as a principled and practical signal for detecting variant contamination, helping improve the reliability of LLM evaluation.

t: Want Better Synthetic Data? Steer It: Activation Steering for Low-Resource Language Generation
a: German Research Center for AI and Universität des Saarlandes
ab: Large language models (LLMs) have become an effective tool for synthetic data generation, including for low-resource languages, where generated data can improve downstream task performance. Current best-performing approaches typically rely on few-shot prompting with target-language examples, which increases inference costs and may reduce diversity through lexical anchoring. In this work, we investigate activation steering as an alternative for low-resource synthetic data generation. We study two steering strategies: Language Steering, which targets the linguistic identity of a language, and Quality Steering, which captures well-formedness by contrasting human-written and backtranslated text representations. We evaluate these methods across four open-source LLMs, multiple layers, and 11 typologically diverse languages by generating sentiment and topic classification data and fine-tuning smaller classifiers. Steering is applied in both zero-shot and few-shot prompting settings and compared against non-steered counterparts. Our results show that steering on early layers consistently improves the diversity of generated data while often yielding stronger downstream model performance, particularly for low-resource languages.

t: Canonical Color as a Lens into Concept Decodability in Vision Encoders and VLMs
a: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
ab: Vision encoders construct the image representations used by vision-language models. How much conceptual information, rather than immediately visible image evidence, do these representations contain? We use canonical color as a controlled test case: can a vision encoder represent the typical color of an object concept, such as yellow for bananas, when visible color is removed from the input image? We construct a dataset of objects with canonical color labels and probe vision encoders for both color and object identity using RGB and grayscale inputs. We find that canonical color remains decodable from grayscale images and is tied to predicted object identity, suggesting a conceptual link between object and color information. Extending this analysis to full VLMs, we find that VLM post-training can have a surprisingly large effect on color decodability in the vision encoder. Overall, canonical color provides a controllable lens for tracing object-level semantic information in vision encoders and VLMs.

t: How to Attack Stealthily? A Letter Frequency-based Backdoor Attack Against LLMs Bounded by Logit Fluctuation
ab: Trigger stealthiness is crucial to the effectiveness of backdoor attacks in Large Language Models (LLMs). Current attacks construct triggers at word level, leading to poor stealthiness since removing critical words can drastically alter model output logits, as we observed. This significant fluctuation is different from the stable output on normal data, and thus may expose backdoor attacks. To achieve greater stealthiness, we formalize this observation as a new stealthiness metric, termed Logit Fluctuation (LF), and derive a sufficient condition for stealthy backdoor attack bounded by LF. We then introduce a simple yet effective backdoor attack method, termed BadFreq, which satisfies the stealthiness bound. BadFreq launches an attack at a fine-grained letter level, which is activated when the frequency of letter ‘z’ in the input exceeds a predefined threshold. This method distributes triggers across letters rather than specific words, thereby avoiding reliance on critical words and enhancing stealthiness. We test three LLMs, evaluating five attackers against three defenders across three pattern recognition tasks under seven metrics. BadFreq achieves superior attack performance and the best stealthiness in all metrics, outperforming the second-best attacker by 49% in LF-averaged stealth[Code in <https://anonymous.4open.science/r/BadFreq-5836>.].

t: LoMaR: Local Margin Preservation via Residual Subspace Adaptation for Noisy Prompt Robustness in Small Language Models
ab: SLMs are increasingly deployed on devices, yet real-world prompts often contain textual or ASR noise that can destabilize model predictions. We analyze this problem from a token-level perspective and find that SLMs exhibit narrow logit margins between the gold token and the top-ranked non-gold token, making noisy prompts more likely to induce local rank flips. To address this issue, we propose LoMaR, a two-stage parameter-efficient framework for robust fine-tuning. In Stage I, LoMaR trains the model on clean prompts with a local logit margin expansion objective to expand the local decision boundary. In Stage II, LoMaR performs residual-subspace adaptation with local logit margin alignment on noisy prompts. After training, the main and residual updates are merged into a standard LoRA adapter, introducing no additional inference cost. Experimental results show that LoMaR outperforms baselines in most noisy settings and achieves lower Performance Drop Rate and Rank Flip Rate. Code and datasets are available at https://github.com/HongJin2828/LoMaR.

t: HEAL: Anchored Hyperspherical Equilibrium for Multilingual Safety Alignment
ab: Safety alignment in large language models is markedly uneven across languages: behaviors learned from English preference data fail to transfer reliably into lower-resource languages, and existing remedies based on per-language preference data or pairwise translation pivots do not scale. We propose Hyperspherical Equilibrium for Aligned Languages (HEAL), a lightweight auxiliary objective that augments any DPO-style alignment pipeline without altering its supervised pairs. HEAL applies two opposing forces to the multilingual representations of the same prompt: a shrink term draws each non-English representation toward a stop-gradient English anchor, while a dilation term repels same-prompt language representations through a pairwise hinge. At equilibrium, representations occupy an English-centered shell-like region that supports cross-lingual transfer while preserving per-language distinctness. Across multiple backbones, HEAL substantially strengthens multilingual safety with the largest gains on the weakest languages, while preserving general capability and showing favorable out-of-distribution behavior on jailbreak evaluation.

t: SaFeR-Steer: Evolving Multi-Turn MLLMs via Synthetic Bootstrapping and Feedback Dynamics
a: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
ab: MLLMs are increasingly deployed in multi-turn settings, where attackers can escalate unsafe intent through the evolving visual-text history and exploit long-context safety decay. Yet safety alignment is still dominated by single-turn data and fixed-template dialogues, leaving a mismatch between training and deployment.To bridge this gap, we propose SaFeR-Steer, a progressive multi-turn alignment framework that combines staged synthetic bootstrapping with tutor-in-the-loop GRPO to train a single student under adaptive, on-policy attacks. We also introduce Trajectory-Consistent Summative Reward (TCSR), which aggregates the historical minimum and average of turn rewards so that any low-quality turn affects the trajectory-level return.I. Dataset. We release STEER, a multi-turn multimodal safety dataset with STEER-SFT (12,934), STEER-RL (2,000), and STEER-Bench (3,227) dialogues spanning 1–10 turns. II. Experiment. Starting from Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B, SaFeR-Steer substantially improves Safety/Helpfulness on both single-turn (48.30/45.86 → 81.84/70.77 for 3B; 56.21/60.32 → 87.89/77.40 for 7B) and multi-turn benchmarks (12.55/27.13 → 55.58/70.27 for 3B; 24.66/46.48 → 64.89/72.35 for 7B), shifting failures to later turns and yielding robustness beyond scaling alone.Code is available at https://github.com/Ed-Bg/SaFeR-Steer-full

t: From AI Reviewers to Evidence Assistants: Quantifying the Human-AI Responsibility Boundary in Peer Review
ab: The rapid growth of AI conference submissions is putting new pressure on peer review. AI reviewer systems are increasingly proposed as support, but prior work leaves unresolved what responsibility their outputs should carry when they can surface useful critiques yet remain risky as independent judgments. We frame this as a responsibility-boundary problem. Using 600 ICLR 2026 submissions, 2,231 human reviews, and 3,600 AI reviews, we operationalize this boundary through usable feedback, rating calibration, panel breadth, and grounded synthesis. AI can prepare critiques and organize evidence, while scoring, independent panel judgment, high-level synthesis, and final responsibility remain human-led. A GLM-5.2 validation on 100 NeurIPS 2022 papers with pre-ChatGPT reviews reproduces the workflow and calibration patterns. Motivated by this boundary, we develop Review Copilot, a workflow in which AI suggestions are inspected, edited, or rejected by human reviewers. In an initial controlled reviewer-in-the-loop study, Human+AI reviews improve actionability, evidence support, and professionalism relative to standalone baselines, while scores and recommendations remain human-authored. A user study of 275 reviewers across 411 papers further supports its practical usefulness. Together, these results support a review paradigm in which AI expands evidence-grounded critique while humans retain judgment, synthesis, and accountability.

t: Size Sound Symbolism Survives Genealogy Across 27 Languages
a: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
ab: Sound symbolism, the non-arbitrary mapping between word sounds and meanings, is well known from effects like Bouba–Kiki. But its cross-linguistic scope is difficult to assess because phonological similarity can also arise from shared ancestry, contact, or language-specific inventories. We propose a genealogy-aware stress test for size sound symbolism across 27 languages spanning 13 language families, using 810 phonemically transcribed size adjectives validated with native-speaker audio. We treat cross-family iconicity as a hard generalization task: train on languages grouped by lexical distance to a held-out target, test transfer from increasingly distant languages, and apply adversarial pressure against similarity-bin and source-language cues. Interpretable bag-of-phoneme classifiers predict size above chance, with clear patterns involving /i/ for smallness and /o,a/ for largeness, while consonants add more language-specific cues. Adversarial training prevents the jointly trained model from exploiting genealogy while held-out size prediction stays above chance, though post-hoc probing shows language identity is still recoverable. The residual signal is small but consistent, indicating cross-family size cues.

t: REINS: Refusal-Enhanced Inhibitory Steering with Sparse Autoencoder Features
a: University of Science and Technology of China
ab: Steering with Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) offers a lightweight inference-time path for adapting the behavior of large language models without retraining. By exposing sparse and interpretable features, SAE steering provides a promising interface for safety control that guides harmful continuations toward refusal. However, we observe that complex wrappers can still undermine existing SAE steering methods on harmful prompts. To evaluate this failure mode systematically, we construct Generalized Undercover Instruction Safety Evaluation (GUISE), a dataset of harmful prompts with complex wrappers. Existing single direction SAE steering methods do not reliably produce refusals on harmful prompts, suggesting that refusal enhancement alone can be too weak when the harmful continuation path remains active. This motivates us to propose Refusal-Enhanced INhibitory Steering (REINS), which suppresses harmful continuation features and enhances safe refusal features in the same SAE feature space. Experiments on GUISE and other datasets show that prior methods either intervene too weakly or achieve only apparent safety through collapse, while REINS substantially reduces harmful responses, markedly improves safe refusals and largely preserves general capabilities.

t: Learning to Remember: End-to-End Training of Memory Agents for Long-Context Reasoning
a: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: Long-context LLMs and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems expand accessible context, but still defer state tracking and evidence consolidation to query time. This passive paradigm is brittle in streaming settings where facts are updated and answers depend on latent states rather than explicit spans. We introduce Unified Memory Agent (UMA), an end-to-end reinforcement-learning framework that trains a single policy to maintain external memory and answer questions. UMA updates a structured memory bank via CRUD operations and combines it with raw-context retrieval for QA. To jointly optimize memory maintenance and question answering, we propose Task-Stratified GRPO, which normalizes heterogeneous trajectories separately for more effective credit assignment. We also introduce Ledger-QA, a controlled benchmark for long-horizon state tracking over accumulated updates. Experiments on Ledger-QA and 13 TTL/AR benchmarks show that UMA improves long-horizon tracking, achieves the best average TTL/AR score among compared methods, and remains competitive on retrieval-centric benchmarks. Our results highlight learned proactive memory management as a complement to longer context windows and query-time retrieval.

t: Debias-SparseGPT: Bias-Aware Pruning for Large Language Models
ab: Model compression techniques such as pruning and quantization facilitate the efficient deployment and acceleration of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, recent studies show that weight sparsification methods, such as SparseGPT, can amplify existing biases in models, with outputs varying significantly depending on persona cues in the prompt. In this paper, we introduce Debias-SparseGPT, a post-training pruning method incorporating representational debiasing using a second-order term defined over demographically contrasting inputs. We perform empirical validation of our method over a wide range of generative LLMs. Across models and sparsity regimes (25%, 50%, and structured 2:4 sparsity), Debias-SparseGPT consistently reduces pruning-induced bias compared to SparseGPT while preserving model perplexity and zero-shot accuracy. Under the most restrictive 2:4 structured sparsity pattern, which most aggressively degrades model quality, augmenting the calibration set with long-context, content-rich examples further improves both downstream performance and fairness. Overall, Debias-SparseGPT advances the bias-performance trade-off while preserving the computational efficiency of sparse models.

t: 3D-MoE: Towards Spatial Intelligence with Mixture-of-Experts for 3D Reasoning and Action Generation
a: Shanghai Academy of AI for Science and Fudan University
ab: Spatial intelligence, encompassing 3D perception and reasoning, is the essential next frontier of AI. Scaling current 3D vision-language models (VLMs) that rely on dense Transformers for spatial tasks incurs prohibitive computational costs. In this paper, we introduce 3D-MoE, a 3D VLM leveraging an efficient mixture-of-experts architecture with a modality- and spatial-context-aware probabilistic routing scheme, stably cultivated by a novel routing curriculum. To seamlessly extend 3D-MoE to embodied AI, we integrate a diffusion-based action head, Pose-DiT, transforming 3D-MoE into a 3D vision-language-action (VLA) model. By employing a rectified flow framework, Pose-DiT generates precise 6D pose actions in a single sampling step. Extensive experiments demonstrate that 3D-MoE achieves superior performance on diverse 3D vision-language benchmarks with drastically fewer activated parameters and yields higher success rates while enabling real-time inference for robot manipulation tasks.

t: LLM Reasoning for Machine Translation: Synthetic Data Generation over Thinking Tokens
ab: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have led to new possibilities in terms of problem-solving, through the devising of a natural language thought process prior to answering a query. While their capabilities are well known across mathematics and coding tasks, their impact on the task of machine translation (MT) remains underexplored. In this work, we explore the benefits of the generation of intermediate tokens when performing MT across multiple language pairs of different levels of resourcedness and multiple setups. We first show that the "thinking tokens" of general-purpose LRMs do not help them better perform MT, motivating the question of what kind of intermediate tokens could help when building a dedicated thinking MT model via fine-tuning. We then show that distilling chains of thought (CoT) from a teacher model using CoT templates inspired by human translators’ step-by-step practices fails to outperform standard input-output fine-tuning. In contrast, constructing CoT traces with prompting strategies specifically designed for MT does yield improvements. A closer analysis reveals that these gains stem from the teacher’s translation attempts embedded in the traces, rather than from the surrounding reasoning. More broadly, our results suggest that leveraging a teacher to refine target translations or expand parallel corpora is more impactful than distilling its CoT explanations into "thinking" MT models.

t: RATF: Robust Adaptive Tri-Encoder Framework for Fake News Detection against Style-Confusion Attacks from LLMs
ab: The rise of Large Language Models (LLMs) enables a new challenge for fake news detection: style-confusion attacks, where attackers rewrite news to mimic trusted styles, challenging detectors that rely on stylistic features. Current defenses like style-invariance training ignore stylistic features, but this is suboptimal for style-confusion attack datasets as it discards valuable cues in clean (non-attacked) articles. To defend against style-confusion attacks, we propose the Robust Adaptive Tri-Encoder Framework (RATF). Our framework uses an LLM to decouple news into content features and style features, and leverages conditional probability curvature to compute a “rewritten score” estimating the likelihood that the article has been rewritten by an LLM. RATF injects this score into a score-conditioned cross-attention fusion module and a learnable parametric gating module. The former uses the content representation as a reliable query to retrieve relevant semantic and stylistic evidence, while the latter continuously calibrates the contributions of original semantics, content features, and style features. We simulate these attacks by creating an equal mixture of original articles from the PolitiFact and GossipCop datasets and their four corresponding style-rewritten versions generated by an LLM. Our experiments show RATF achieves state-of-the-art performance with superior robustness against style-confusion attacks, while also proving highly adaptable across various backbones.

t: GUI-PRA: Process Reward Agents for GUI Tasks
ab: Long-horizon GUI automation remains challenging due to error accumulation over extended interaction sequences. Process Reward Models (PRMs) provide dense step-level supervision for mitigating error accumulation, yet standard PRMs are poorly suited to GUI verification. Standard PRM judgments often rely on superficial visual alignment rather than functional correctness, reflecting an evaluative knowledge gap caused by missing domain-specific adjudication logic. Standard PRMs also perform passive, single-pass visual assessment, which creates Visual Ambiguity when reliable judgment requires actively locating, parsing, or inspecting task-relevant UI evidence. We introduce GUI-PRA, a Process Reward Agent that transforms GUI process evaluation from passive scoring into active investigation. GUI-PRA couples Experience-Injected Criterion Synthesis, which distills generalized verification principles into state-specific criteria, with Criterion-Guided Autoregressive Perception, which uses these criteria to navigate multi-granularity visual tools and gather grounded evidence. On AndroidWorld and Mobile-MiniWoB++, GUI-PRA achieves improvements of 5.0% and 6.5% over standard PRMs on the Qwen-VL series, with Qwen3-VL attaining 54.74% success rate on AndroidWorld. On the offline OS-Critic Bench, GUI-PRA demonstrates strong competitiveness against fully trained critic models.

t: Peeling the Matryoshka: Extracting Ontological Structure from Retrieval Embeddings
ab: Taxonomy construction is essential for knowledge-intensive NLP yet remains costly: clustering-based methods (i) need careful per-corpus tuning and yield unstable hierarchies, while LLM-based pipelines (ii) depend on expensive task-specific training that does not transfer across domains. We report an empirical finding that bears on both: in Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) embeddings, where each leading prefix is itself a usable, coarser vector, prefix length aligns with the coarse-to-fine granularity of gold taxonomies; shuffled- and reverse-dimension controls isolate the alignment to the learned early prefix dimensions. The pattern holds across three architecturally distinct MRL models (full statistics in §3). To test whether this regularity is usable, we introduce PEEL (Peeling Embeddings to Extract Latent ontologies): a minimal probe over these frozen embeddings, trained once with an order-embedding objective that represents hierarchy as vector containment; a minimum spanning arborescence then decodes taxonomic DAGs. Using only a concept vocabulary (no documents), PEEL recovers taxonomic DAGs with high structural fidelity on two OLLM benchmarks, transferring to a new domain with no target-edge supervision. The end-to-end OLLM pipeline—which jointly discovers concepts and induces structure from document corpora—is reported as a cross-task reference (§5.3). Pre-trained retrieval embeddings encode a decodable granularity gradient; a minimal probe renders it as explicit parent–child (is-a) structure.

t: Not All Evidence Is Equal: Source-Sensitive Calibration in Large Language Models
ab: Large language models are increasingly used in settings where information must be evaluated not only for content, but also for reliability. This paper introduces a human-grounded evaluation[All data and code used in this paper will be made available with the camera-ready version.] of source-sensitive calibration in Turkish and English. Across hearer-side uptake tasks, we manipulate source reliability while holding propositional content constant, and test whether humans and LLMs adjust action-readiness judgments according to source trustworthiness. Turkish human participants show robust source sensitivity: they are substantially more willing to act on information attributed to high-trust sources than to low-trust sources, while Turkish evidential morphology itself does not independently affect uptake once the source is overtly specified. LLMs show weaker calibration. In Turkish, models partially register explicit source reliability, but the effect is much smaller than in humans and there is no reliable effect of the -DI/-mIş contrast. In English, models show small effects of both source reliability and the lexical marker apparently, but no robust interaction between them. These results suggest that current LLMs encode source cues only partially and often fail to convert them into human-like judgments about when information is reliable enough to guide action.

t: KnowSim: Evaluating Information Calibration in LLM Assistants with User Simulators that Learn
a: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
ab: To effectively collaborate with users on knowledge-intensive tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) must perform information calibration: matching content to a user’s evolving understanding and cognitive capacity. Yet user simulators used to evaluate and train LLMs do not explicitly model user knowledge, so they neither produce realistic interactions across knowledge levels nor reflect how interactions unfold as that knowledge evolves. To close this gap, we introduce KnowSim, an evaluation framework built around a user simulator that maintains explicit knowledge states—a graph of Information Units with prerequisite relationships—that evolves under update rules grounded in learning theory. KnowSim computes three metrics (Knowledge Gain, Delivery Calibration, Cognitive Overload) directly from the knowledge state trajectory, reflecting key mechanistic aspects of information calibration. We validate KnowSim against 705 human–AI sessions across two domains, stratified by knowledge level: its rankings align significantly with human judgments (73–74% sign agreement), outperforming three baseline simulators. Applied to 8 frontier LLMs, KnowSim reveals that the best model shifts by user knowledge level—aptitude–treatment interactions invisible to standard evaluation.

t: HoliTok: A Continuous Holistic Tokenization with Robust Dual Capabilities of Speech Generation and Understanding
ab: Unified speech foundation models require a holistic tokenization space that is both learnable by language models and decodable into high-quality waveforms. Existing speech tokenizers, however, often fail to satisfy these requirements simultaneously, leading to increased architectural complexity and more involved training designs. We propose HoliTok, a continuous Holistic speech Tokenization model designed for unified generation-understanding modeling. HoliTok encodes 48kHz speech into a compact 25Hz sequence of 128-dimensional latents. It is trained with a progressive strategy that jointly preserves signal-level fidelity, incorporates semantic information, and maintains strong latent learnability. Based on this tokenization, we build a unified AR+DiT model for speech synthesis and recognition, where the same latent sequence supports both generation-specific and unified generation-understanding tasks. Experiments show that HoliTok achieves competitive reconstruction fidelity, improves generative learnability for high-quality and controllable synthesis, and, among the evaluated representations, is the only one that operates robustly in our unified generation-understanding architecture without additional optimization tricks. These results suggest that HoliTok serves as an effective speech tokenizer and a foundational representation interface for unified spoken language modeling. The code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/HoliTok-2852.

t: MaS-VQA: A Mask-and-Select Framework for Knowledge-Based Visual Question Answering
ab: Knowledge-based Visual Question Answering (KB-VQA) requires models to answer questions by integrating visual information with external knowledge. However, retrieved knowledge is often noisy, partially irrelevant, or misaligned with the visual content, while internal model knowledge is difficult to control and interpret. Naïve aggregation of these sources limits reasoning effectiveness and reduces answer accuracy. To address this, we propose MaS-VQA, a selection-driven framework that tightly couples explicit knowledge filtering with implicit knowledge reasoning. MaS-VQA first retrieves candidate passages and applies a Mask-and-Select mechanism to jointly prune irrelevant image regions and weakly relevant knowledge fragments, producing compact, high-signal multimodal knowledge . This filtered knowledge then guides the activation of internal knowledge in a constrained semantic space, enabling complementary co-modeling of explicit and implicit knowledge for robust answer prediction. Experiments on Encyclopedic-VQA and InfoSeek demonstrate consistent performance gains across multiple MLLM backbones, and ablations verify that the selection mechanism effectively reduces noise and enhances knowledge utilization.

t: LLM Fine-tuning with an Unconstrained Fine-tuned Teacher
ab: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on a single target task requires balancing task adaptation with retention of prior capabilities. Existing teachers mainly guide preservation or transfer, but do not identify which target-task samples should be emphasized when fine-tuning must retain prior capabilities. We propose the **U**nconstrained **F**ine-tuned **T**eacher (**UFT**), shifting the teacher role from ”knowledge transfer” to ”value discovery”. UFT is obtained by unconstrained fine-tuning on the target task and then compared with the source model to identify high-value samples. These samples are upweighted during student fine-tuning and receive value-weighted UFT-guided distillation, allowing the student to prioritize task-critical signals while preserving prior capabilities. Experiments on Magicoder and MetaMathQA show that UFT improves the trade-off between target-task performance and prior-capability retention, while converging faster and more stably. By turning teacher behavior into sample-value discovery, UFT establishes a new teacher role for data-efficient fine-tuning.

t: Benchmarking Patent Drafting from Inventor-Style Disclosures
a: University of Cambridge and Duke University
ab: While recent large language models (LLMs) have achieved promising results on individual patent drafting tasks, they fundamentally fail to investigate the core challenge of real-world patent drafting: generating a complete and legally coherent patent application directly from early-stage invention materials. Prior work predominantly assumes later-stage, highly structured, or already legalistic inputs. However, real patenting workflows begin with informal, de-legalized disclosures authored by inventors. To bridge the gap, we introduce Dis2Pat, a disclosure-to-patent dataset that reflects realistic patenting workflows by requiring the generation of complete patent applications directly from inventor-style, de-legalized disclosures. Given the inherent difficulty of long-form, legally constrained patent drafting and the strong privacy requirements, we further propose a strong baseline named Patent-MAF. It is a multi-agent framework for locally deployable patent drafting. Benchmark results reveal that current LLMs exhibit limitations in patent drafting, while Patent-MAF provides a strong baseline that consistently outperforms evaluated open-source models and remains competitive with large closed-source models.

t: SWE-MEM: Learning Adaptive Memory Management for Long-Horizon Coding Agents
a: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
ab: Long-horizon software engineering agents often need to manage lengthy and noisy interaction histories under limited context budgets. Existing memory management methods rely on static compression workflows or rigid compression schedules, and often decouple memory decisions from task-solving performance. We present SWE-MeM, a training framework for proactive and on-demand memory management in software engineering agents. SWE-MeM provides a flexible memory tool that lets agents decide when, what, and how to compress based on trajectory state, task progress, and remaining context budget. We train agents with synthesized proactive memory-management trajectories and Memory-aware GRPO, which jointly optimizes memory management and issue resolution through memory-aware trajectory splitting and step-level credit assignment. On SWE-Bench Verified, SWE-MeM achieves 43.4% and 60.2% resolve rate with 4B and 30B models, respectively, outperforming existing memory management baselines in both performance and efficiency.

t: Self-Corrected Speech Reasoning: Diagnosing and Improving Condition Updating via PACER
ab: Speech large language models (Speech LLMs) are increasingly expected to reason in everyday spoken interactions, where users often revise task conditions through self-correction. Unlike ordinary disfluencies, self-corrections alter the premise structure of a problem: obsolete conditions must be discarded, while final corrected conditions must guide reasoning. We formulate this setting as self-corrected speech reasoning and study it as a condition-update problem. We construct SCUR-Bench (Spoken Condition-Update Reasoning Benchmark), a controlled Chinese benchmark of 13,295 instances organized by reasoning difficulty and self-correction difficulty, and introduce a three-path diagnostic protocol to analyze speech-side recovery, condition use, and reasoning. Our analysis reveals a recurrent failure pattern in current Speech LLMs: corrected conditions may be perceived, transcribed, or even mentioned, yet still fail to serve as active premises in reasoning. We term this final-condition adoption failure. A controlled English parallel evaluation exhibits the same recovery–adoption gap, providing preliminary evidence that this failure is not unique to Chinese. To mitigate it, we propose PACER, a perception-aware condition-enhanced reinforcement framework based on GRPO. On Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, PACER reduces end-to-end error and condition-related errors by 39.8% and 67.5%, respectively, relative to the untrained baseline.

t: I Am Multitudes: A Survey and Roadmap for Rethinking Identity in NLP
a: IT University of Copenhagen and Bocconi University
ab: Natural Language Processing (NLP) systems engage with identity across datasets, models, tasks, and evaluation frameworks, yet they often do so by reducing people to fixed categories (e.g., race, gender, age). This reduction is particularly consequential in identity-sensitive applications: for example, it affects how systems classify harm or generate tailored responses to user needs. But individuals contain multitudes: they are not a homogeneous group, but are situated, context-dependent selves whose differences exceed fixed categories. To examine how identity is addressed in NLP, we survey ACL Anthology papers that mention "identity". Our study investigates how the term is operationalized, where it enters the NLP pipeline, which tasks incorporate identity-related information, and whether its use is explicit or implicit. Our analysis shows that identity is most often operationalized through explicit sociodemographic categories, especially those referring to protected groups by law. Moreover, it is primarily used during the evaluation stage to audit systems for bias and harm. We synthesize these patterns into a taxonomy of identity operationalizations in NLP. Finally, we propose a roadmap to treat identity as relational, contextual, intersectional, and linguistically indexed, with the broader scope of achieving socially aware NLP.

t: Bridging Text and Structure via Latent Query Refinement for Knowledge Graph Completion
a: Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: Knowledge graph completion(KGC) aims to infer missing facts from observed relational triples, which demands jointly modeling textual semantics and relational structure. Existing structure-based methods capture graph topology but often struggle with sparse entities and long-tail relations, while text-based methods exploit entity and relation descriptions but weakly model relational neighborhoods. In this paper, we propose LQ-KGC, a latent-query refinement framework that enables iterative interaction between semantic inference and structural reasoning for KGC. Instead of treating all missing triples as latent variables, LQ-KGC constructs a restricted set of semantically plausible latent queries and alternates between two refinement steps: the language model predicts latent tail distributions from textual descriptions, while the graph model incorporates high-confidence pseudo tails as pseudo edges for relation-aware message passing. Meanwhile, structure-aware graph predictions are distilled back into the language model to refine semantic representations. Experiments on WN18RR and FB15k-237 demonstrate that LQ-KGC consistently improves over text-based and graph-based baselines, with additional analyses highlighting the effectiveness of pseudo-edge augmentation and latent-query construction.

t: OptiSkill: A Hierarchical and Evolving SkillBank for LLM-Based Optimization Modeling
a: Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
ab: Automated operations research (OR) modeling requires LLMs to translate natural-language decision problems into correct mathematical programs. Existing methods can improve individual formulations, but they often solve problems in isolation, retaining little reusable experience and repeating similar formulation errors. Prior memory-based approaches store examples, thoughts, or insights as references, while OR modeling requires reusable formulation skills that transfer across problem narratives and guide concrete modeling decisions. We propose **OptiSkill**, a skill-augmented framework that builds a hierarchical and evolving SkillBank for LLM-based OR modeling. SkillBank stores solver-verified experience as reusable skills, with *Global Strategies* for problem-level formulation skeletons and *Step Experiences* for local error-prevention rules. It is further refined through stable batch-level test-time evolution, where candidate skills are incorporated only after validation. Experiments on eight OR modeling benchmarks show that OptiSkill improves formulation accuracy across LLM backbones, outperforms strong agentic baselines, and gains further by expanding SkillBank coverage and reliability. Code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/OptiSkill-E16F/.

t: Reviewing the Reviewer : LLM-Assisted Reviewer Feedback Generation for Guideline Compliance
a: Institute for Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence and Technology, Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and Technische Universität Darmstadt
ab: Peer review is central to scientific quality, yet reliance on simple heuristics, namely *lazy thinking* and non-*specific* critiques, has threatened review quality. Prior work frames *lazy thinking* detection as single-label classification and stops at detection, yet review segments often exhibit multiple co-occurring issues, and reviewers benefit more from actionable, guideline-aware feedback than from labels alone. We further show that off-the-shelf LLMs prompted for feedback frequently rewrite the entire review or address the authors rather than the reviewer, motivating an inference-time approach. We introduce an LLM-driven framework that decomposes reviews into argumentative segments, identifies issues violating ACL Rolling Review (ARR) guidelines, and generates targeted feedback using issue-specific templates refined by a novel iterative, reranking-based generation algorithm. In a controlled rewriting study, our feedback reduces guideline violations by up to 92.4%. We also release LazyReviewPlus, the *first* multi-label dataset of 1,309 sentences annotated for detecting *lazy thinking* and lack of *specificity*.¹¹ Code and Data: https://github.com/UKPLab/emnlp2026-reviewfeedbackagent

t: Can Humans Dream of Electric Sheep? Human-Written Samples for Fine-Grained Vision-and-Language Hallucination Benchmarking
ab: In an age of rapid model turnover, how do we make hallucination evaluation more perennial? We explore whether human-written hallucination samples could take the place of model-generated hallucinations, in order to make benchmarking detection independent of particular models. To this end, we construct SHEEP, a dataset of 1,600 human-written samples, spanning four languages (Chinese, English, French, Italian), and 18,400 samples from five vision-and-language models, all annotated for hallucinations using a fine-grained span-level labeling scheme. We find that human-written samples result in higher agreement and allow greater control of dataset contents, while remaining distributionally similar to samples derived from vision-and-language samples and providing a reasonable portrayal of detection capabilities — suggesting that human data is a viable substitute for model-based hallucination benchmarks.

t: TriggerBench: Investigating Prospective Memory for Large Language Models
a: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
The Chinese University of Hong Kong
The Chinese University of Hong Kong
ab: While Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in long interactions, existing evaluations focus predominantly on retrospective memory (RM) via explicit queries. Prospective memory (PM), the ability to spontaneously recall and act on latent constraints without direct requests, remains largely unevaluated. We introduce **TriggerBench**, a five-dimensional PM benchmark across daily assistants and professional workflows. TriggerBench pairs scenarios with matched RM controls, contrastive positive/negative variants, and overloaded triggers, enabling fine-grained measurement of proactive recall, false-alarm rate, and attentional robustness. We find: (i) PM shows a precision-recall trade-off and attentional fragility. Though enhanced reasoning improves proactive recall, models can overfit to always-remind heuristics. Furthermore, PM accuracy degrades substantially under implicit constraints or triggers overloaded by concurrent requests, indicating that robust PM remains an open challenge. (ii) PM is notably harder than RM: on identical contexts, RM remains near-saturated up to 100K tokens, while PM decays sharply as context length increases. (iii) PM may serve as a behavioral probe of spare reasoning capacity. Pairing PM with AIME-2025 math problems reveals that successful trajectories yield higher PM accuracy than failed ones at the same context length, showing PM is a behavioral correlate of spare reasoning budget that token count obscures. Project page: https://github.com/KristenZHANG/TriggerBench-Official.

t: TORe: Rehearsal-Free Continual Learning for Table QA via Operation Recipe Reconstruction
ab: Continual learning for Table Question Answering (TableQA-CL) aims to train models on sequential tasks with limited supervision per task. Existing methods either rely on replaying historical data or assume ideal conditions like gold task boundaries, limiting real-world applicability. We propose TORe (Table Operation Recipe Reconstruction), a rehearsal-free framework that reconstructs historical knowledge through schema-aware reasoning patterns. TORe extracts abstract Operation Recipes from table reasoning processes, identifies fine-grained knowledge deviations between current and past tasks, and employs execution-verified LLM synthesis to generate pseudo-examples reflecting both current and historical reasoning patterns. Experiments on two TableQA-CL benchmarks and multiple backbone models show that TORe consistently improves average accuracy over strong rehearsal-free baselines, remains competitive with replay-based methods, and maintains robust performance under different task orders.

t: Revisiting Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards from a Contrastive Perspective
ab: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is one of the most widely adopted RLVR algorithms for post-training large language models on reasoning tasks. We first show that GRPO admits an equivalent discriminative reformulation, in which policy optimization maximizes the expected score gap between verified positive and negative rollouts. This reformulation reveals two objective-level limitations: likelihood-misaligned surrogate scores, in which clipped ratio-based scores are optimized rather than the sequence likelihoods that govern generation, and score-insensitive credit assignment, in which rollout-level credit does not reflect the current score gaps between positive and negative rollouts. To address these limitations, we propose ConSPO, a Contrastive Sequence-level Policy Optimization method that uses length-normalized sequence log-probabilities as rollout scores and contrasts verified positive rollouts against negative distractors within the same group. ConSPO optimizes a group-wise InfoNCE-style objective to adaptively strengthen updates for poorly separated positives and high-scoring negatives, together with a curriculum-scheduled margin that preserves separation pressure as training progresses. Experiments across diverse settings show that ConSPO outperforms strong baselines on challenging reasoning benchmarks.

t: RePro: Proof-Verified Benchmark Rewriting for Reliable Evaluation of LLM Mathematical Problem Solving
a: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
Institute for Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence and Technology
ab: Data contamination undermines the reliable evaluation of large language models (LLMs) on mathematical problem solving. While rewriting-based evaluation mitigates memorization, existing methods lack guarantees of problem validity and answer correctness. We propose Proof-Verified Benchmark Rewriting (RePro), the first framework to integrate Lean-oriented neural automated theorem provers (ATPs) into benchmark rewriting, which rewrites problems and regenerates answers with correctness ensured by Lean-verified proofs. Experiments on GSM8K and MATH show that RePro’s retained rewritten instances achieve 100% well-definedness, feasibility, and answer correctness, while existing methods still produce invalid or incorrect instances. Moreover, several models exhibit accuracy drops on proof-verified rewritten benchmarks, suggesting that their performance is sensitive to surface-level and structural variations and may partly reflect memorization effects. Our source code and data are available at https://github.com/AI4Engi/RePro.

t: How Much is a Human Right Worth? ECtHR-NPD: A Benchmark for Predicting Non-Pecuniary Damage Awards
a: University of Sheffield and University of Sheffield
ab: Existing legal benchmarks cover diverse tasks, while continuous monetary remedies remain comparatively underexplored. We introduce ECtHR-NPD, to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark for predicting non-pecuniary damage (NPD) awards at the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) from case information when no statutory formula or explicit calculation rule determines the amount. ECtHR-NPD contains 14,575 cases with case-level awards in nominal euros, chronological splits, and a protocol separating target construction from model input. We evaluate a battery of methods, including constant predictors, gradient-boosted trees, retrieval methods, fine-tuned encoder language models (LMs), prompted decoder LMs, and knowledge-augmented agents. Our results show that more sophisticated LM and agentic approaches do not consistently outperform the strongest feature-based baseline. All model families struggle to identify zero awards and to calibrate high-award predictions, with further degradation on the Challenging test view, making ECtHR-NPD a challenging testbed for current state-of-the-art open-weight and proprietary LMs.

t: Diagnosing LLM Fragility: An Empirical Study on Reasoning Entropy and Malicious Outputs
ab: Chain-of-Thought prompting is increasingly relied upon as a safety monitoring surface: if a model reasons before acting, its trace can be inspected before harm occurs. Yet reasoning is a stochastic branching process rather than a deterministic, auditable path. We introduce Bifurcation Entropy (H_{BE}), a step-level diagnostic metric that extends Kernel Language Entropy to intermediate reasoning steps, measuring the semantic breadth of a model’s next-step distribution at each point in the Chain-of-Thought. We deploy H_{BE} via In-Distribution Attacks, a controlled probing instrument that injects the model’s own high-entropy continuations to test whether H_{BE} predicts exploitability. Across five reasoning models in high-stakes blackmail scenarios, phrases in the top H_{BE} quartile are exploited 6.2\times more often than the lowest, with H_{BE}-targeted probing inducing significantly more alignment failures than random selection. These results establish H_{BE} as a principled probing signal that concentrates safety monitoring effort on the minority of reasoning steps that carry the majority of alignment risk.

t: Phrase-Localized Language-Contrastive Guidance: Training-Free Localized Accent Control for Code-Switching Text-to-Speech
ab: Current speech synthesis struggles with code-switching, which mixes a foreign language phrase into a primary language utterance, causing the phrase to be spoken with the primary language’s accent rather than its native one. We propose Phrase-Localized Language-Contrastive Guidance (LCG), a training-free inference framework that restores a native accent to code-switched phrases in cross-lingual text-to-speech. LCG replaces the single language guidance applied across the whole utterance with a separate guidance for each region, so each part is guided by its own language. To choose where to apply this localized guidance, we propose a self-attention probing technique that finds the phrase boundaries without external alignments. Together, these components generate speech in which each region carries the accent of its own language, requiring no fine-tuning or auxiliary models. Across diverse language pairs, LCG robustly increases the nativeness of the code-switched phrase while suppressing accent leakage, and preserving overall speaker identity and naturalness.

t: Refuse without Refusal: A Structural Analysis of Safety-Tuning Responses for Reducing False Refusals in Language Models
a: Pohang University of Science and Technology
ab: Striking a balance between helpfulness and safety remains a fundamental challenge in aligning large language models. To achieve this balance, models should refuse harmful queries (e.g., "How do I shoot someone?") while remaining responsive to benign inputs, even those superficially resembling harmful queries (e.g., "Where can I shoot a good photo?"). However, models often struggle to distinguish genuinely harmful queries from benign queries that contain superficially risky language, resulting in false refusals. In this paper, we address the issue by decomposing a response in the safety-tuning dataset into two distinct components: (i) a boilerplate refusal statement and (ii) a rationale explaining the refusal. Our experiments and analyses show that refusal statements impede accurate discrimination between harmful and benign queries by inducing reliance on superficial cues. In contrast, training solely on rationales reduces false refusals while maintaining a comparable level of safety performance. Rationale-Only benefits also appear in our ICL configuration and remain compatible with the evaluated inference-time mitigation methods. The results emphasize the necessity of precisely curated, fine-grained safety supervision datasets and outline directions for constructing aligned agents that better reconcile helpfulness with safety.

t: Forgetting Across Modalities: Unlearning in Multimodal Large Language Models
a: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Institute of High Performance Computing, Singapore, A*STAR
Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Southern University of Science and Technology
ab: Gradient conflict between forgetting and retaining objectives is a well-known obstacle in machine unlearning, where opposing gradients on shared parameters cause destructive interference. In Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), cross-modal coupling entangles visual and textual representations within the same parameters, making this conflict considerably more severe. We propose EASE (Efficient Alignment-aware Selective Erasing), which explicitly balances the conflicting gradient directions. EASE first dynamically locates the conflicting parameters at each step by detecting opposite-sign gradients, then performs a manifold-constrained optimization within the two-dimensional subspace spanned by the task gradients to find the linear combination that maximally aligns them, yielding a valid descent direction for both objectives without any manually tuned trade-off coefficient. Nonconflicting parameters keep their standard updates, keeping the method lightweight. Experiments across multiple MLLM architectures and unlearning benchmarks show that EASE achieves superior unlearning efficiency and faster convergence while matching or surpassing existing methods in multimodal quality.

t: Knowing What Not to Answer: Selective Non-Compliance in Vision-Language Models
a: Pohang University of Science and Technology
Pohang University of Science and Technology
ab: Vision-language models (VLMs) are expected to respond helpfully to appropriate requests while withholding compliance with requests that are incorrect, unsafe, infeasible, or unanswerable. However, existing benchmarks predominantly evaluate non-compliance at the level of the query as a whole, assuming that each request either warrants compliance or requires withholding compliance. In practice, real-world queries can contain a mixture of answerable content and components for which compliance should be withheld. In this paper, we introduce KoNA, a benchmark for evaluating selective non-compliance in VLMs across five categories: False Premise, Visual Inaccessibility, Universal Unknown, Task Feasibility, and Safety. Each task evaluates two capabilities: query-level non-compliance and component-level non-compliance under paired single and compound queries. Our evaluation across diverse VLMs shows that models often fail to refuse, correct, or abstain appropriately, and these failures become more pronounced when queries require selective non-compliance. To address this challenge, we fine-tune VLMs using KoNA examples that require selective non-compliance, together with a fully answerable set that should receive direct answers. Our fine-tuned models achieve substantial improvements in non-compliance accuracy while largely maintaining performance on fully answerable tasks. These results suggest that the fine-tuned models can distinguish between answerable components and those requiring non-compliance and respond in a task-appropriate manner.

t: CAME: Company-Aware Evidence-Memory Experts for Interpretable Quarter-Ahead Revenue Forecasting
a: National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
ab: Quarter-ahead revenue forecasting requires company-scale numerical accuracy, strict temporal validity, and company-specific interpretation of narrative disclosures. LLMs can distill textual evidence but can produce scale-misaligned forecasts, whereas history-based anchors are stable but miss forecast-time signals such as product transitions, supply constraints, and management guidance. We introduce **CAME** (**C**ompany-**A**ware Evidence-**M**emory **E**xperts), a residual-forecasting framework that refines a no-leakage statistical anchor when current semantic evidence and prior error patterns justify an adjustment. On a development-inclusive rolling backtest of 336 company-quarters from 12 large public technology and platform firms, CAME achieves the lowest aggregate point-estimate error among the reported methods, with statistically supported macro-sMAPE gains over the matched Statistical Anchor, and outperforms History + Guidance on all six aggregate metrics. CAME also links adjustments to source-linked evidence cards and guarded memory traces, supporting forecast inspection, provenance, and failure localization.

t: Where Does an LLM Decide What’s Right? Sparse Normative Circuits Across Languages and Model Families
ab: Where does an LLM decide what’s right? We study whether normative judgment is implemented by a sparse, identifiable substrate or distributed across the model. Conventional circuit analysis can conflate normative computation with the multiple-choice format machinery that surrounds it. We pair four normative datasets (legal and moral, Chinese and English) with a non-normative MMLU control and apply a locate–disentangle–intervene pipeline that sets aside format-processing heads. Across Qwen3-8B, Llama3.1-8B, and Mistral-7B-v0.1, this isolates 5–10 normative-specific (NS) heads per model (under 1% of total) in MCQA settings. Targeted knockout and amplification reveal bidirectional causal effects across legal and moral tasks. The resulting heads form a sparse, late-layer intervention substrate for normative MCQA. Their coordinates differ across model families, so cross-model agreement is structural and circuit findings require functional re-identification in each family.

t: Auditing Chinese Web-scale Corpora via Sampled BPE Token Statistics
a: Beijing University of Post and Telecommunications
ab: Chinese web pollution has surfaced in LLMs, motivating audits of upstream Chinese corpora. However, auditing such corpora faces three challenges: (1) their web-scale size makes full scan costly; (2) prior analyses are often too coarse to expose token-level pollution; (3) Chinese web pollution is implicit and rapidly changing. We propose Sampled-BPE, a lightweight token-level auditing pipeline that sample a small subset and train BPE tokenizer to surface polluted tokens. Experiments show that Sampled-BPE preserves usable estimates while substantially reducing runtime and memory: a 148.4 \times speedup and a 35.8 \times memory reduction induce only 4.25% relative error for pollution categories. We apply the pipeline to 11 open Chinese corpora and 6 Chinese Common Crawl snapshots from 2021 to 2026. The audit reveals widespread but uneven pollution across open corpora, as well as highly polluted and temporally shifting Chinese web content. We further release a hierarchical Chinese web token dataset with 660k+ token records, each with web context, category, and explanation fields, organized as trees to support review and tracing of pollution.

t: Cross-Version \Delta-Transfer of QLoRA-Trained Adapters
ab: To investigate whether QLoRA-trained adapters transfer across model versions like LoRA-trained adapters, we train LoRA and QLoRA adapters on Llama-3-8B-Instruct and transfer them to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with a task-specific merge scale λ. Both methods are evaluated on a BF16 target base, isolating the training-time precision difference; NF4 deployment is evaluated separately. Across 20 main tasks, the absolute evaluation-score gap between QLoRA Transfer and LoRA Transfer is at most 0.054 on all tasks and at most 0.03 on 18/20 tasks, so training the adapter on a quantized base does not compromise its cross-version transferability. In a two-task deployment case study, serving QLoRA adapters with an NF4 base uses 5.7–10.0 GB peak allocated inference VRAM, compared with 15.1–19.6 GB for LoRA-merged BF16. Across 44 settings (22 tasks × 2 methods), the task-optimal λ consistently exceeds the Frobenius-distance optimum (we call this discrepancy the λ gap), suggesting that weight-space proximity alone is insufficient for identifying it. Replicating the pipeline on two further families (Mistral v0.1→v0.3, Qwen2→2.5) reproduces these findings. We also report a negative case: on CommonsenseQA, QLoRA Transfer falls significantly below direct adaptation.

t: DEPPO: Dual Experience Pool Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon Reinforcement Learning
a: China Telecom Corporation Ltd. Data&AI Technology Company
ab: Reinforcement learning for long-horizon agents and multi-step reasoning models typically relies on outcome-level rewards, which provide only trajectory-level supervision and make it difficult to identify the contribution of individual intermediate actions. As a result, redundant actions in successful trajectories may be over-reinforced, while useful actions in failed trajectories may be undesirably penalized. To address this issue, we propose **Dual Experience Pool Policy Optimization (DEPPO)**, a critic-free and experience-driven framework for adaptive step-level credit assignment. DEPPO maintains two structured experience pools for successful and failed trajectories, and estimates the relative quality of each action by comparing its state-conditional likelihood under the two pools. The resulting success–failure preference signal is used to adaptively rescale the advantage, amplifying actions aligned with successful patterns while suppressing those associated with failure modes. Furthermore, DEPPO introduces an asymmetric and dynamically evolving update mechanism: the success pool emphasizes both correctness and novelty through freshness-aware insertion, while the failure pool focuses on consistently risky behaviors, with decay and pruning to keep the memory compact and up-to-date. Without additional value models or process-level supervision, DEPPO provides a lightweight, interpretable, and effective solution for fine-grained credit assignment in long-horizon reinforcement learning. Code available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DEPPO-1051/

t: When Fairness Evolves: Value Orientation and Evolution in Multi-Agent Resource Allocation
ab: This study employs LLM-based multi-agent simulation to investigate how fairness-related behavior evolves in repeated resource allocation. Thirty agents with five idealized value orientations participate in a survival-production cycle under equal, needs-based, contribution-based, and negotiation-based allocation mechanisms. Results show that negotiation achieves the highest productive return and subjective satisfaction with the strongest consensus in our main setting, and its subjective advantage holds across eight LLMs, suggesting that deliberative allocation can help navigate the fairness–efficiency tradeoff. Agents also exhibit systematic misalignment between subjective satisfaction and objective resource outcomes, shaped by value orientations and interaction conditions. Over repeated interaction, agents’ reflection-derived fairness positions shift away from their initial orientations toward more hybrid combinations of equality-, merit-, and needs-related reasoning. To provide human-grounded structural comparison, we further benchmark GPT-4o against published human choice distributions in 16 controlled allocation scenarios, finding moderate rank-level correspondence but substantially more concentrated LLM choices. These findings characterize value-conditioned reasoning and semantic change in LLM societies while remaining computational hypotheses rather than direct evidence of human fairness behavior.

t: Ask, Answer, or Act: Learning Interaction Modes for Tool-Use Agents
a: Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München and Siemens Corporate Research
ab: Robust tool-use agents must navigate mixed-intent interactions, deciding whether to ask for missing information, answer directly, or invoke tools. We tackle this challenge by introducing a novel task formulation that structures the planner’s action space into explicit interaction instructions over an explicit Ask/Answer/Act space, thereby making these behavioral boundaries an explicit target of optimization. In this framework, a planner predicts the interaction mode and semantic payload, while a frozen executor realizes the instruction into an observable behavior. Coupled with this structured decision process, we propose Executor-Grounded Failure-Routed Planner Learning (EFPL). EFPL optimizes the planner via executor-observed outcomes and strategically leverages privileged feedback for targeted correction when outcome rewards provide insufficient guidance, further refining these behavioral boundaries. Experiments on BFCL and When2Call across three backbone sizes show that EFPL consistently improves clarification, abstention, when-to-call decisions, and robustness to irrelevant tools, while fully preserving strong multi-turn tool-calling performance.

t: Efficient Listwise Reranking with Compressed Document Representations
ab: Reranking, the second stage of modern retrieval pipelines, is computationally expensive when performed by Large Language Models (LLMs). Existing efficiency-oriented approaches either rely on smaller models or restrict input length, both at the cost of effectiveness. Inspired by recent advances in soft document compression for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), we introduce **RRK**, an efficient and effective listwise reranker that operates directly on multi-token compressed document representations rather than raw text. Trained via simple distillation from a strong teacher, RRK combines rich compressed representations with listwise reranking to deliver a highly efficient yet competitive system: despite its 7B-parameter backbone, it runs 5-20 faster than smaller rerankers (0.6-4B parameters) while matching or outperforming them in effectiveness. The advantage widens further on long-document benchmarks, where input compression yields the largest speedups.

t: Colla-Q: Toward Collaborative Experts in MoE Quantization via Minimax Precision Balancing
ab: In this paper, we present a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) quantization method based on activation entropy. Although quantization reduces memory and computational costs, it can substantially degrade performance. In particular, performance decline is pronounced in quantized MoE models, where individual experts have a small number of parameters that are sensitive to low-bit representation. Considering that MoE operates as an ensemble model with collaborative contributions from routed experts, a significant performance decline of a particular expert due to quantization can harm model performance. Therefore, we propose **Colla-Q**, a bit-allocation framework to maintain balanced performance across experts through an activation-entropy-based bit-width allocation algorithm. This approach encourages each expert to operate collaboratively in the quantized model, thereby 1) improving the overall MoE performance and 2) reducing the dependence on the calibration dataset. Since uniformly adjusting each expert’s performance facilitates robustness and stability of the MoE model, the proposed MoE quantization method can generalize more consistently across different calibration datasets. Our code is available at: https://github.com/mmai-laboratory/Colla_Q

t: In-Place Feedback: Reliable Refinement for Multi-Turn Expert-LLM Collaboration
a: Pohang University of Science and Technology
Pohang University of Science and Technology
Pohang University of Science and Technology
Pohang University of Science and Technology
Pohang University of Science and Technology
ab: LLM-generated drafts often contain subtle factual or logical errors, yet prior work shows that models struggle to reliably integrate multi-turn feedback aimed at fixing them. We propose *in-place feedback*, an interaction paradigm in which the user directly edits the model’s previous response and the model continues generation from the edited context. In-place feedback consistently outperforms standard multi-turn feedback across five reasoning-intensive benchmarks while requiring fewer tokens, and our fine-grained analysis shows that it applies corrections more reliably and propagates them to subsequent reasoning. A user study with domain experts refining LLM-generated summaries corroborates these findings: participants report higher final-output satisfaction and substantially lower fatigue with in-place feedback, and a mixed strategy combining in-place and multi-turn feedback improves every dimension we measure. These results suggest that editing errors in place is a more reliable way to incorporate expert corrections than multi-turn feedback, while combining the two acts complementarily to form a more effective collaboration than either mechanism alone.

t: AdaPLD: Adaptive Retrieval and Reuse for Efficient Model-Free Speculative Decoding
ab: Speculative decoding accelerates generation by verifying multiple drafted tokens in a single target-model forward pass, reducing sequential decoding iterations. Model-free variants avoid auxiliary draft models by reusing text and model states already available during generation, but their speedup depends on the reliability of the constructed drafts. We identify two limitations of existing reuse-based methods: lexically anchored retrieval has limited recall under surface-form variation, and deterministic span copying can be brittle when the retrieved context does not uniquely determine the continuation. We propose AdaPLD, a training-free method that adaptively improves both retrieval and draft construction. AdaPLD preserves high-precision lexical reuse while using semantic similarity to recover additional reuse opportunities when lexical matching fails. It further constructs branched reuse hypotheses to account for continuation uncertainty, rather than relying on a single copied span. Across diverse benchmarks, AdaPLD reduces target-model forward passes and achieves up to 3.10\times decoding speedup.

t: SpecTr-GBV: Multi-Draft Block Verification Accelerating Speculative Decoding
ab: Autoregressive language models suffer from high inference latency due to their sequential decoding nature. Speculative decoding (SD) mitigates this by employing a lightweight draft model to propose candidate tokens, which are selectively verified by a larger target model. While existing methods either adopt multi-draft strategies to increase acceptance rates or block verification techniques to jointly verify multiple tokens, they remain limited by treating these improvements in isolation. In this work, we propose SpecTr-GBV, a novel SD method that unifies multi-draft and greedy block verification (GBV) into a single framework. By formulating the verification step as an optimal transport problem over draft and target token blocks, SpecTr-GBV improves both theoretical efficiency and empirical performance. We theoretically prove that SpecTr-GBV achieves the optimal expected acceptance length within the class of conditionally independent couplings (CIC) induced by our multi-draft verification design, and show that this optimal value increases with the number of drafts. Empirically, we evaluate SpecTr-GBV across five datasets and four baselines. Our method achieves superior speedup and significantly higher block efficiency while preserving output quality. In addition, we perform comprehensive ablation studies to evaluate the impact of various hyperparameters in the model. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/junemily/SpecTr-GBV.git.

t: I^3CL: Restoring Interactive Capabilities to Implicit In-Context Learning
ab: To address the limitations of conventional ICL, recent task-vector-based methods, such as Implicit ICL (I^2CL), encode demonstrations into a unified task vector that is injected during inference, yielding promising improvements in efficiency and stability. However, existing methods encode each demonstration in isolation, neglecting the rich interactions between demonstrations and between demonstrations and queries—a core capability of standard ICL. This results in task vectors with limited expressiveness. To bridge this gap, we propose Interactive Implicit In-Context Learning (I^3CL), a simple yet effective framework that restores these essential interactive capabilities. I^3CL introduces only two lightweight attention-based modules, preserving the efficiency advantages of I^2CL while delivering significant performance improvements. Experiments across nine diverse tasks using four LLMs show that I^3CL achieves an average performance improvement of 3.54% over prior task-vector-based baselines.
