On mathematical and code reasoning benchmarks, -8B achieves results competitive with leading open autoregressive models such as Qwen3-8B. This work establishes a practical foundation for efficient, reasoning-capable diffusion language models. We release our model at https://github.com/DreamLM/DreamReasoner.

t: Seeing the Unseen: Visual Similarity for Pixel Language Model Adaptation
ab: Pixel-based language models (LMs) replace traditional tokenizers by processing rendered images of text, making cross-lingual transfer heavily dependent on the visual and structural properties of writing systems. However, the dynamics of adapting these models to low-resource languages with complex morphology and written in unique scripts are not yet explored. Using Tibetan as a case study, we analyze how continued pre-training of pixel-based LMs is influenced by data scale, initial script exposure, and cross-lingual transfer from languages written in other Brahmic scripts. We introduce four rendering-level metrics to quantify visual script similarity. We evaluate downstream performance across three tasks. Our results show that higher orthographic proximity enhances semantic transfer, even under severe data constraints. Additionally, we find a performance asymmetry based on the pre-training starting point: while multilingual pre-training (PIXEL-M4) has stronger initial performance, its capacity for subsequent adaptation seems to be constrained, whereas adapting a monolingual model (PIXEL) with mixed scripts yields more gains on sentence-level tasks. Our metrics and case study offer empirical observations that could help inform data selection and script adaptation choices when working with pixel-based models in similar low-resource settings.

t: Length and Meaning for Language Model Maps
ab: Various studies have proposed methods to quantify and compare the rapidly growing number of large language models (LLMs). However, when constructing a macroscopic map of LLMs, there is a trade-off between estimation accuracy and computational cost, making the selection of evaluation texts critical. In this work, we propose Predictive Importance Sampling (PredIS), which selects informative texts by predicting likelihood variance from text-level features. Experiments on 100 LLMs across 25 domains demonstrate that our predictor generalizes robustly. Furthermore, we reveal that text importance cannot be explained by text length alone, as it is also closely tied to meaning reflected in the embedding space.

t: Intrinsic Temporal Adaptation of CLIP for Partially Relevant Video Retrieval
a: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
ab: Partially Relevant Video Retrieval (PRVR) aims to retrieve untrimmed videos that contain moments relevant to a text query. Since the target moment occupies only a portion of the video, PRVR requires retrieval based on fine-grained understanding beyond coarse video-level matching. However, existing methods often rely on frozen CLIP frame features, which lack temporal understanding. Even with recent progress in parameter-efficient CLIP adaptation, video-level predictions can still be supported by imprecise frame-level evidence. In this paper, we propose an Intrinsic Temporal Adaptation (ITA) framework for PRVR. First, our Backbone-Internal Temporal Adaptation allows the last few visual transformer layers to attend over groups of neighboring frames. This provides temporally aware frame embeddings while keeping CLIP frozen and training only adaptation parameters. Second, we introduce Affinity-Weighted Gradient Propagation to address the weakly supervised nature of PRVR, softly aggregating top-k frames based on text-frame affinities and propagating learning signals to multiple query-relevant frames. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on PRVR benchmarks, demonstrates robust cross-dataset transfer, and retrieves substantially more accurate frame-level evidence within ground-truth query-relevant moments. Our code is available at github.com/hynnsk/ITA.

t: Seeing is Believing: Benchmarking and Mitigating the Interference of Language Priors on Visual Perception in MLLMs
a: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
ab: Language priors in MLLMs can override visual evidence, impairing visual perception. Existing benchmarks assume shared priors across models and rely solely on accuracy. However, cross-model prior agreement falls below 80%, and over 15% of items can be answered correctly without any image, causing accuracy to overestimate prior resistance. To address these limitations, we introduce ViSiP-Bench, a benchmark grounded in rare-but-real scenarios across six prior categories, with a model-aware dynamic prior induction protocol and three metrics that more precisely and continuously measure prior resistance than accuracy alone. Evaluating 24 models reveals that prior adherence is pervasive, does not improve with scale, and larger models tend to either strongly override their priors or firmly adhere to them. We therefore propose MAPS, which identifies each model’s strongest priors and fine-tunes on factually grounded knowledge to soften excessive prior reliance without disrupting general capabilities.

t: Enhancing Long-Context Reasoning via Verifiable Atomic Skills
ab: Long-context reasoning remains a critical challenge for Large Language Models (LLMs). Current research typically focuses on curating specialized training data by treating long-context reasoning as a monolithic task, yet it is challenging to verify its quality due to its internal cognitive complexity. In this paper, we propose a paradigm shift: viewing long-context reasoning as a hierarchical spectrum of core atomic skills. To operationalize this, we present an Anchor-based Reasoning (AbR) pipeline that automatically synthesizes strictly verifiable training data for each skill, thereby enabling reliable quality. Diagnostic analyses confirm that proficiency in these atomic skills strongly predicts general long-context reasoning performance. By training exclusively on a highly compact set of merely four thousand synthesized samples with Reinforcement Learning (RL), we explicitly sharpen these foundational capabilities. Extensive experiments across six challenging benchmarks demonstrate that this targeted RL causally delivers robust and generalizable performance gains, outperforming DeepSeek-R1-distill-32B by an average margin of 7.7% (improving from 46.3% to 54.0%). Furthermore, in-depth ablations reveal that these skills operate synergistically, establishing a scalable, data-efficient, and verifiable path to advancing long-context reasoning.

t: Language Model Maps for Prompt-Response Distributions via Log-Likelihood Vectors
ab: We propose a method that represents language models by log-likelihood vectors over prompt-response pairs and constructs model maps for comparing their conditional distributions. In this space, squared Euclidean distances between models are approximately proportional to the KL divergence between the corresponding conditional distributions. Experiments on a large collection of publicly available language models show that the maps capture meaningful global structure, including relationships to model attributes and task performance. The representation also captures systematic shifts induced by prompt modifications and their approximate additive compositionality; we use the vectors to predict downstream task scores and leverage their additive structure to approximate the effects of composite prompt operations without directly observing the corresponding log-likelihood vectors. We further introduce PMI vectors to reduce the influence of unconditional distributions; in some cases, PMI-based model maps better reflect training-data-related differences. Overall, the framework supports the analysis and prediction of input-dependent model behavior.

t: Tournament-GRPO: Group-Wise Tournament Rewards for Reinforcement Learning in Open-Ended Long-Form Generation
ab: Reinforcement learning in open-ended long-form generation is challenging because reliable reference answers and automatic metrics are often unavailable. Existing rubric-based methods typically rely on pointwise LLM-as-a-judge scoring, but absolute scores are difficult to calibrate across complex responses, may provide weak discrimination among same-query rollouts, and can become saturated during optimization. We propose Tournament-GRPO, a group-wise reward framework that converts rubric-guided LLM judgments into relative rewards through repeated multi-round tournaments among same-query rollouts. Tournament-GRPO compares candidates within groups, accumulates tournament outcomes, and normalizes them into group-wise rewards for GRPO training. Experiments on Deep Research Bench show that Tournament-GRPO consistently outperforms existing reward-design baselines, achieving a 4.52-point overall-score improvement over the strongest baseline. Further analyses show that tournament rewards provide a favorable effectiveness–efficiency trade-off and that tournament design affects training dynamics. These results suggest that rubric-guided tournament comparison provides an effective reward signal for reinforcement learning in open-ended long-form generation.

t: Stop Training Against Soft Users: Mentalized Adversarial Self Play for Proactive Dialogue
a: ByteDance Inc. and Beijing Institute of Technology
ab: Proactive dialogue agents must guide multi-turn interactions toward task goals while adapting to users whose intentions and attitudes evolve. Existing planners improve system side action selection through search, learned policies, or user aware planning, but are often trained and evaluated against fixed or overly compliant simulators; as a result, high simulated success can reflect soft user bias rather than robust dialogue ability. We introduce MASP, a Mentalized Adversarial Self Play framework that treats proactive dialogue as a partially observable game between a system and a rationally resisting user. MASP represents the user’s evolving mental state with a BDI based latent state, separates reward side teacher mentalization from policy side student mentalization, and alternates self play updates for the system and user policies. This turns robustness to rational resistance into a training objective rather than only an evaluation condition. Across diverse proactive dialogue benchmarks, compared with the widely used SFT and Planner-only approaches, MASP substantially improves success rate (SR) and rationality constrained success (RCSR), reduces average turns (AT), and performs better against hard users who make the task goal more difficult to achieve.

t: Measuring Affinity between Attention-Head Weight Subspaces via the Projection Kernel
ab: Understanding relationships between attention heads is essential for interpreting the internal structure of Transformers, yet existing metrics do not capture this structure well. We focus on the subspaces spanned by attention-head weight matrices and quantify head-to-head relationships using the Projection Kernel (PK), a principal-angle-based measure of subspace similarity. Experiments on GPT2-small, BLOOM-560M, and Qwen2-0.5B-Instruct show that PK reproduces known head-to-head interactions on the IOI task more clearly than prior metrics such as the Composition Score. We further introduce a framework to quantify the informativeness of PK distributions by comparing them with a reference distribution derived from random orthogonal subspaces. As an application, we analyze a directed graph constructed from PK and show that, in GPT2-small, L4H7 acts as a hub by functioning as an Identity Head.

t: Inter-3D VQA: A Roadside Multimodal Benchmark for 3D Spatiotemporally Grounded Visual Question Answering
ab: Recent advances in visual question answering (VQA) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have enabled natural-language reasoning over traffic scenes. However, existing benchmarks are largely built from ego-vehicle views or 2D roadside videos, limiting their ability to evaluate 3D-grounded reasoning over real-world distances, trajectories, infrastructure topology, and safety-critical interactions. We introduce Inter-3D VQA, a large-scale roadside multimodal benchmark for 3D spatiotemporally grounded VQA at intersections. Built from synchronized point clouds and multi-view images, Inter-3D VQA contains 407K QA pairs covering lane-level positions, object relationships, motion patterns, and near-miss-oriented interaction reasoning. We further propose Inter-Geo, an MLLM baseline that integrates object- and scene-level aligned LiDAR representations, and Inter-Metrics, a unified evaluation framework for textual consistency, numerical accuracy, and semantic correctness. Experiments show that Inter-Geo outperforms image-based VLMs, especially on grounded spatial and temporal reasoning tasks.

t: SHICD: Self-Hallucination-Inducing Contrastive Decoding for Efficient LLM Hallucination Mitigation
ab: Hallucinations undermine the reliability of Large Language Models (LLMs) in real-world settings. Current contrastive decoding methods mitigate hallucinations by generating multiple responses based on an amateur model and an expert model or using the logit distribution across all layers, leading to considerable redundancy and computational inefficiency during inference. To address these limitations, we propose SHICD (Self-Hallucination-Inducing Contrastive Decoding), a novel training-free decoding framework that requires a single response from an individual model and leverages information from a subset of all layers, without any external intervention on activations. Specifically, SHICD first identifies the inducing layer of the LLM when an initial semantic representation emerges in the model. The hallucination direction is then extracted to induce hallucinations by itself while preserving the initial semantic information encoded before the inducing layer. Finally, we employ an adaptive contrastive decoding mechanism to determine when to apply contrastive decoding during generation. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmark datasets demonstrate that SHICD significantly improves factual accuracy over baseline methods while achieving lower inference latency.

t: HachiWare: One-Shot Selective SVD in a Dual-Branch Framework for KV Cache Compression
a: National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
ab: Long-context inference is increasingly limited by the memory and access cost of the key-value (KV) cache. Existing KV cache compression methods face a fundamental trade-off between efficiency and information preservation. Eviction-based methods are efficient but may discard critical tokens, whereas low-rank-based methods preserve all tokens at the cost of substantial computational overhead. We propose HachiWare, a dual-branch framework that applies one-shot selective SVD to semantic-critical cache states while handling less critical states with lightweight eviction. It stores these states in a Semantic-Critical Branch (SCB) using low-rank factors, while assigning the remaining states to an Eviction Branch (EB) for cheaper eviction. During decoding, bounded active-cache refresh selectively reconstructs only active SCB entries, avoiding reconstruction of the full SCB cache. On the RULER benchmark with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, HachiWare incurs only a 3% accuracy drop compared with the full KV cache baseline at a KV cache compression ratio of up to 16x, while improving accuracy by 5% over existing compression methods. For decoding efficiency, HachiWare achieves up to 9.44x and 16.50x throughput speedups over Full KV at 64K and 128K context lengths. These results highlight selective allocation of reconstructability as an effective way to improve the accuracy-efficiency trade-off of KV cache compression.

t: One Instruction Is a Benchmark: End-to-End Instruction-Following Evaluation with FlexBench
ab: Real-world deployments of large language models (LLMs) increasingly rely on user-provided instructions that are long, precise, and tailored to specific workflows. In such settings, aggregate leaderboard performance is often a weak proxy for a model’s ability to faithfully execute the particular instruction that a practitioner intends to deploy. To address this gap, we introduce FlexBench/FlexEval, an instruction-conditioned evaluation framework that instantiates a specialized test suite from a user-provided target instruction. Given a target instruction, FlexBench (i) derives a set of verifiable evaluation dimensions and (ii) generates an instruction-conditioned conversation corpus. FlexEval then aggregates dimension-level judgments into two complementary metrics: Coverage, which measures workflow progress, and Achievement, which measures conditional correctness. We evaluate the framework on nine multi-turn target instructions spanning diverse scenario categories and workflow topologies, across nine contemporary LLMs over 3,888 generated dialogues. The results show that model rankings and failure modes vary substantially across target instructions, highlighting the need for instruction-conditioned evaluation beyond fixed aggregate benchmarks. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Coryyy/FlexBench.

t: TRACE-GRPO: Teacher-Refined Advantage Credit Estimation for Long-Horizon Agentic RL
a: Shanghai Academy of Artificial Intelligence for Science
Shanghai Innovation Institute and Fudan University
ab: Group-Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is widely used to post-train LLM agents, but its trajectory-level advantage is ill-suited to long-horizon credit assignment. Reward-homogeneous rollout groups yield zero advantage; otherwise, one scalar uniformly scales every token, obscuring which decisions determine the outcome. We propose **TRACE-GRPO** (**T**eacher-**R**efined **A**dvantage **C**redit **E**stimation for GRPO), which converts teacher-LLM feedback into hierarchical credit. Teacher scores provide a sample-level fallback for zero-variance groups, reweight trajectory advantage at the turn level, and redistribute turn credit at the token level using the policy’s log-probability shift under a teacher critique. This yields dense training-time credit without token-level annotations or learned critics. We also introduce **CAPA** (Critique-Aware Paged Attention), which reuses trajectory KV caches and reduces the isolated critique-conditioned forward from roughly 2\times a vanilla GRPO step to approximately 5% of a training step. On ALFWorld and ScienceWorld with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, TRACE-GRPO achieves 96.3% and 73.4% success, respectively, outperforming strong agent RL baselines. Ablations show cumulative gains from the three credit levels, and comparison with supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated successes confirms that critique-guided policy optimization provides benefits beyond imitation. Code is available at [https://github.com/Lau-Jonathan/TRACE-GRPO](https://github.com/Lau-Jonathan/TRACE-GRPO).

t: VIABLE: A Visually Impaired Assistance Benchmark for VLM-as-a-Judge Evaluation
ab: AI-based Visually Impaired Assistance (VIA) remains challenging, largely due to the high cost of human evaluation. The VLM-as-a-Judge paradigm may offer a promising alternative, although it has mostly been studied in general domains. We therefore ask whether such judges can be trusted for VIA tasks. To investigate this question, we introduce VIABLE (Visually Impaired Assistance Benchmark for VLM-as-a-Judge Evaluation), the first benchmark for VLM-as-a-Judge evaluation in VIA. VIABLE contains over 300K judgment samples across three scenarios and introduces an Effectiveness–Impartiality–Stability framework with a 12-mode failure taxonomy. Based on VIABLE, our systematic study of seven judges across different model scales shows that existing models are largely unreliable across all evaluation axes. The strongest judge, GPT-5.4, achieves only 52.6% single-failure diagnostic accuracy, yet exhibits the highest self-preference rate at 94.2%; while open-source judges are strongly biased and adversarially fragile. To address these issues, we propose VIA-Judge-Agent, a model-agnostic inference-time harness that augments judges with visual evidence extraction and a taxonomy-guided workflow. It enables positive improvements in diagnostic accuracy and downstream VIA responses more preferred by BLV users. Data and code are available at:https://github.com/YiyiyiZhao/VIABLE.

t: FAMPWQ: Fisher Information-based Adaptive Mixed Precision Weight Quantization for Effective LLM Inference
ab: Recent years have witnessed remarkable achievements of Large Language Models (LLMs) in multiple domains, while the excessive resource requirements of LLMs hinder the deployment on resource-constrained devices. Although model quantization stands out as an effective approach, conventional quantization approaches typically incur severe performance degradation due to uniform bit-width or simple heuristic sensitivity evaluation. In this paper, we propose a novel Fisher information-based Adaptive Mixed Precision Weight Quantization approach, i.e., , which performs layer-adaptive weight quantization for effective LLM inference on commodity GPUs. First, we propose a system model with a novel Fisher information metric to measure the layer-wise sensitivity to quantization. Second, we propose a reinforcement learning-based bit-width allocator in , which generates an adaptive bit-width allocation strategy based on the Fisher information sensitivity metric. Extensive experiments on 7 models and 5 benchmarks demonstrate that significantly outperforms 7 baseline approaches in terms of PPL (up to 3.39 smaller), accuracy (up to 6.87% higher), and LLM-as-a-judge comparison (up to 76% win rate).

t: DuraS2ST: Chain-of-Thought and Reinforcement Learning for Duration-Aligned Speech-to-Speech Translation
a: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
The Chinese University of Hong Kong
The Chinese University of Hong Kong
ab: Speech-to-speech translation (S2ST) in time-sensitive applications such as video dubbing requires not only semantic fidelity and speaker preservation, but also strict duration consistency to avoid audio-visual misalignment. However, existing S2ST systems largely generate target speech without explicit temporal planning, making duration control an unresolved challenge. We introduce DuraS2ST, a duration-aligned reasoning framework that enables a single speech language model to first generate an explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) for planning target wording and phonetic length, and then synthesize the corresponding speech tokens. To support this paradigm, we construct DuraSet-440K, a high-quality duration-aligned CoT corpus for supervised initialization. We further optimize the model with multi-modal multi-dimensional reinforcement learning, using a Duration Margin Reward to balance translation quality and duration consistency, and Modality-Aware Reward Attribution to assign rewards to appropriate token spans. Experiments on CVSS-T show that DuraS2ST achieves a strong balance between translation quality and duration consistency, outperforming competitive open-source and commercial baselines. Project page: https://github.com/Mia11939/DuraS2ST.

t: Fast-Slow Thinking RM: Efficient Integration of Scalar and Generative Reward Models
ab: Reward models (RMs) are critical for aligning Large Language Models via Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). While Generative Reward Models (GRMs) achieve superior accuracy through chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, they incur substantial computational costs. Conversely, Scalar Reward Models (SRMs) offer efficiency but suffer from limited performance and adaptability in complex scenarios. We introduce Fast-Slow Thinking Reward Models (F/S-RM), a hybrid RM architecture inspired by Dual Process Theory. It trains a single model to integrate two distinct reward paradigms: scalar-style first-token pairwise judgment (fast thinking) and CoT-based judgment (slow thinking), regulated by a dual-confidence activation mechanism that determines when to activate slow thinking. Under hybrid inference, F/S-RM achieves state-of-the-art accuracy with an average score of 84.3 across benchmarks, while reducing token consumption by 22.5%. Code and data are publicly available.

t: Representation-Aware Advantage Estimation: Your Reward Model Provides More Than A Scalar Output
ab: Current reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) methods primarily rely on scalar rewards from a trained reward model (RM). While effective, scalar rewards are often noisy and fail to capture fine-grained preference differences, whereas RM hidden states encode richer semantic and preference information. We introduce the representation-aware advantage estimation, which leverages RM hidden states and models them as auxiliary signals for better advantage estimation. Specifically, we propose the Graph-based Advantage Estimation (GraphAE), treat each sampled group as a graph, where nodes correspond to responses and edges capture their similarity in the RM hidden space. Then advantages are computed via graph propagation, enabling each sample to incorporate contextual information from its neighbors. GraphAE is lightweight and can be seamlessly integrated into existing group-based RL algorithms. We apply GraphAE to GRPO, GSPO and RLOO, and conduct extensive experiments on different models and benchmarks. Empirical results show consistent improvements across three benchmarks, with gains of up to + 6.3 on Arena-Hard-v0.1, + 8.27 on AlpacaEval 2.0, and + 0.22 on MT-Bench. These results demonstrate that leveraging RM representations leads to more sample efficient and robust RLHF.

t: SOLID: Infusing Symbolic Logic into LLMs via Dual-Verified Backward Reasoning
a: Chinese Academy of Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle with rigorous logical reasoning, suffering from hallucinations and inconsistent deduction. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting relies heavily on the frozen model’s inherent capabilities, while neuro-symbolic approaches face a "translation reliability" bottleneck in which semantic parsing errors mislead external solvers. Recent work attempts to infuse symbolic capabilities via fine-tuning, but typically mimics forward reasoning, suffering from search-space explosion and irrelevant intermediate facts that dilute attention. We propose SOLID (Symbolic Oriented Logic Infusion via Dual-verification), a framework that synthesizes high-quality supervision through a Dual-Verification Mechanism: bidirectional consistency checks filter out hallucinated translations. Crucially, instead of forward chaining, we execute validated translations to generate backward reasoning traces—verifying necessary premises from the goal. By fine-tuning on these focused, goal-oriented paths, SOLID infuses the model with the efficient deduction process of a symbolic engine. Experiments on ProntoQA, LogicNLI, and ProofWriter demonstrate state-of-the-art accuracy, significantly outperforming CoT baselines, solver-based methods, and forward-chaining variants. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/ejie22/SOLID.

t: AgentEHR: Advancing Autonomous Clinical Decision-Making via Retrospective Summarization
ab: Large Language Models have demonstrated profound utility in the medical domain. However, their application to autonomous Electronic Health Records (EHRs) navigation remains constrained by a reliance on curated inputs and simplified retrieval tasks. To bridge the gap between idealized experimental settings and realistic clinical environments, we present AgentEHR. This benchmark challenges agents to execute complex decision-making tasks, such as diagnosis and treatment planning, requiring long-range interactive reasoning directly within raw and high-noise databases. In tackling these tasks, we identify that existing summarization methods inevitably suffer from critical information loss and fractured reasoning continuity. To address this, we propose RetroSum, a novel framework that unifies a retrospective summarization mechanism with an evolving experience strategy. By dynamically re-evaluating interaction history, the retrospective mechanism prevents long-context information loss and ensures unbroken logical coherence. Additionally, the evolving strategy bridges the domain gap by retrieving accumulated experience from a memory bank. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that RetroSum achieves performance gains of up to 29.16% over competitive baselines, while significantly decreasing total interaction errors by up to 92.3%.

t: TVIR: Building Deep Research Agents Towards Text-Visual Interleaved Report Generation
a: Taobao (China) Software Co., Ltd. and Alibaba Group
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: Deep Research Agents have shown strong capability in multi-step information retrieval, reasoning, and long-form report generation, but existing benchmarks and systems remain predominantly text-centric, with limited evaluation of whether visual elements are factually reliable and well aligned with the surrounding analysis. To address this gap, we introduce TVIR (Text–Visual Interleaved Report Generation), which includes TVIR-Bench, a benchmark of 100 expert-curated multimodal deep research tasks that require visual elements to serve specific analytical sub-goals, and TVIR-Agent, a hierarchical multi-agent framework for constructing structured outlines, retrieving images, generating charts with traceable sources, and composing reports through context-aware sequential writing. We further develop a dual-path evaluation framework that combines Textual Assessment and Visual Assessment. Experiments across nine deep research systems show that TVIR-Agent achieves strong overall performance, underscoring the importance of explicit multimodal design and evaluation for evidence-driven report generation.

t: Generative Models Enhanced by Sequence Labelling and Aspect-Code Switching Improve Cross-lingual Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis
ab: Cross-lingual aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) transfers knowledge from a source language with annotated data to a target language, enabling fine-grained sentiment analysis without annotated target-language data. While monolingual ABSA has seen significant progress, cross-lingual ABSA remains underexplored, especially for complex tasks involving multiple sentiment elements like target-aspect-sentiment detection (TASD). In this paper, we propose a novel SeqLab framework that enhances cross-lingual ABSA using a sequence-to-sequence model with an auxiliary sequence-labelling task performed by the encoder, enhancing aspect term recognition and sentiment predictions. Additionally, we incorporate aspect-code switching (ACS), a translation-based technique that swaps aspect terms between source and translated sentences, generating additional training data to enhance the model’s cross-lingual understanding. We evaluate our approach across eleven languages, three domains, and two backbone models, surpassing previous state-of-the-art results for the commonly studied E2E-ABSA task. Unlike most prior work that relies solely on English as the source language, we systematically assess different source-target language pairs and extend our evaluation to the more challenging, yet underexplored TASD task in cross-lingual settings. Finally, we provide a detailed error analysis highlighting key challenges and limitations.

t: Manifold Embedding: A Point-to-Hyperplane Approach
a: Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, Tübingen and University of Trento
ab: Neural networks over non-Euclidean manifolds have attracted increasing attention across various applications. A fundamental step in these networks is to map Euclidean features onto a target manifold. Existing methods mainly use exponential maps and projections, operate through tangent or ambient Euclidean spaces, and may therefore distort intrinsic manifold geometry. On the other hand, point-to-hyperplane distances have recently shown great success in building manifold-valued networks. Based on this, we propose the Point-to-Hyperplane Distance Map (PHDM), a parameter-free mapping that extends Euclidean fully connected layers to Euclidean-to-manifold transformations. Specially, the exponential map is recovered as a pseudo-distance-based special case. We manifest PHDM on the Lorentz, Poincaré, spherical, and projected-spherical models, covering both negative and positive curvature. Experiments on arithmetic reasoning across four LLMs, image classification, graph node classification, and link prediction demonstrate consistent improvements over the corresponding baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/Longchentong/PHDM.

t: TrustRAG: Metadata-Governed RAG for Compliance-Oriented Question Answering
a: University of Science and Technology Beijing
University of Science and Technology Beijing
ab: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances large language models with external evidence, but in compliance-oriented QA, semantic relevance alone does not determine whether evidence should be used for generation. A retrieved document may be relevant and factually correct, yet inadmissible because it is inaccessible to the current user, explicitly superseded, or in unresolved conflict with other active evidence. We formalize three post-retrieval governance failures in this setting: unauthorized leakage, stale citation, and unsupported answers. To address them, we propose TrustRAG, a RAG framework that incorporates a metadata-governed routing layer between the retriever and the generator. Given correct and complete governance metadata for the retrieved candidate set, this layer filters inadmissible evidence before generation, returns a deterministic refusal when no admissible evidence remains, and preserves unresolved conflicts for conflict-reporting generation. We construct AeroTrustBench, a counterfactual compliance QA benchmark for evaluating evidence governance in RAG. Across Qwen-Max, DeepSeek-V3, and GLM-4-32B-0414, TrustRAG consistently reduces the three failures relative to unguided RAG and baselines based on prompting, filtering, routing, verification, and recency. Mechanism-matched and 50-document comparisons show benefits beyond filtering under larger candidate pools, while metadata-noise tests and human audits characterize dependencies on upstream metadata and evaluator choice.

t: From Poetry Parties to Poetry Critics: Benchmarking Classical Chinese Poetry Generation and Evaluation
ab: Classical Chinese poetry generation and evaluation with Large Language Models (LLMs) face two intertwined challenges: existing generation benchmarks rely on simplistic keyword inputs devoid of literary context, and no ground-truth benchmark exists for objectively validating poetry evaluation methods. We present a comprehensive framework addressing both challenges. On the **generation** side, we construct **Honglou-Poem**, the first narrative-driven poetry generation benchmark derived from Dream of the Red Chamber, where each entry provides rich author personas and narrative backgrounds—moving far beyond traditional keyword-to-poem paradigms. A ”Digital Poetry Party” pipeline evaluates 12 state-of-the-art LLMs in this challenging setting. On the **evaluation** side, we introduce **Poetry-Tree**, a benchmark with axiomatically ordered quality levels created through systematic merit degradation, providing objective ground truth for evaluator validation. Leveraging Poetry-Tree as a training signal, we employ **GRPO** reinforcement learning with Spearman’s correlation as the reward to train a dedicated poetry evaluation model, **Poet-4B**. Our Poet-4B achieves a Spearman’s \rho of **0.8253**, dramatically improving from the base model’s 0.2929 and closely approaching the best closed-source model GLM-4.6 (0.8764) with over 100{\times} fewer parameters—a gap of only 0.051 in Spearman’s \rho. We release all benchmarks, trained models, and a leaderboard to facilitate future research.

t: Disentangling the Interpretive and Predictive Roles of LIWC: Controlled Substitution in Depression-Related Classification
ab: Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) provides auditable psycholinguistic categories that are widely used to interpret depression-related language, but its incremental predictive role in modern multimodal systems remains unclear. We evaluate LIWC across two English and three Chinese depression-related corpora under matched participant-level cross-validation. We ask whether LIWC improves classification and what any performance change reflects. Intact LIWC is compared with three fold-local substitutes: a PCA-rotated version that removes direct access to named category coordinates, a participant-shuffled version that preserves real LIWC profiles while breaking participant alignment, and a random-marginal version that preserves feature-wise distributions. Across multiple fixed representation contexts, the results provide limited evidence for stable LIWC gains under frozen, participant-level early fusion. None of the prespecified dataset-blocked contrasts survives multiple-comparison correction. A separate SBERT calibration produces larger observed intact-versus-shuffled and intact-versus-random separations, indicating that larger participant-aligned signals can produce correspondingly larger separations under the same procedure, while not resolving the five-corpus power limitation. LIWC remains useful as an auditable, corpus-conditioned interpretive layer. These conclusions should not be generalized to fine-tuned, sequence-aware, or end-to-end architectures.

t: Tampered ML: Evaluating LLM Judgment of Machine Learning Research
ab: One approach to accelerating progress on AI alignment is to automate parts of alignment research itself. Doing so requires systems that can perform reliably on hard-to-supervise research tasks, including identifying flaws in research proposals and evaluating whether a proposed experiment supports its intended claim. To evaluate this capability, we introduce **Tampered ML**, a benchmark of 1{,}858 item-pairs, each consisting of an experiment proposal reconstructed from a published machine learning paper and a minimally edited counterfactual that introduces a targeted methodological flaw. Models must identify the more methodologically sound proposal in both presentation orders. A human validation study on a stratified sample estimates that 80{-}90% of items are valid. Frontier models perform above chance but remain far from reliable (with Opus 5 achieving 77.9% accuracy). They are highly sensitive to the order of presentation and favor flawed designs that appear more specific, transparent, or conventional.

t: SyRuP: Enhancing System-Prompt Following via Reward-Guided Prediction in LLM Decoding
ab: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly controlled through system prompts that specify roles, formats, and safety requirements. However, models follow these prompts only implicitly through in-context learning, which can be insufficient for complex or compositional prompts. Existing approaches often require model tuning or response-level reranking, limiting their practicality for lightweight inference-time control. We introduce SyRuP, a decoding-time framework for improving system-prompt adherence while keeping the base LM frozen. SyRuP trains a cross-attention reward head from system-prompt-conditioned preference pairs, treating the system prompt as a separate memory to produce token-level adherence scores. At inference, SyRuP reranks the base LM’s top-k candidates by combining base logits with both the learned reward signal and a contrastive signal that captures system-induced logit shifts. Experiments on system-prompt following benchmarks show that SyRuP consistently outperforms prompting and decoding-time baselines with moderate inference overhead. These results suggest that explicit token-level guidance is an effective and practical mechanism for reliable system-prompt following.

t: Frozen Cores Need Task Signal: Fisher-Whitened Cross-Covariance for Low-Resource LLM Adaptation
a: College of Computer Science and Technology, Zhejiang University
ab: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning is usually framed as a question of how many parameters to update. Under a severe trainable-state budget, however, where those coefficients act is equally consequential. We study this choice through frozen-core adaptation: a calibration pass fixes left and right bases for each weight matrix, and fine-tuning optimizes only an r\times r core. This removes the ability of trainable factors to repair a poor initial span and makes subspace quality directly observable. We introduce FCCA, which estimates the signed input–error cross-covariance, whitens it with diagonal Fisher moments, truncates it in the resulting local metric, maps the selected directions back, and applies thin QR to obtain stable core coordinates. Under a matched r^2 budget, we compare eight basis constructors on 11 tasks, four model settings, and three seeds. On Qwen2.5-3B, FCCA reaches an 83.0 macro-average, 2.3 points above the next-best matched-budget constructor, and exceeds its unwhitened RawGrad control on all 11 tasks. It ranks first at all three Qwen scales and finishes within 0.13 points of the best method on Llama-3.2-1B. Controlled ablations show gains of 2.7–17.2 points from whitening and identify QR as necessary for stable core optimization in the tested regime. Finally, FCCA comes within 0.32 and 0.23 average points of LoRA and DoRA while optimizing 36.9K rather than roughly 7.4M parameters. These results show that a carefully selected fixed span can recover most of the benefit of movable low-rank factors at a much smaller trainable and optimizer-state cost.

t: Unlocking Multimodal Protein Language Models at Inference Time
a: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong Polytechnic University and Hong Kong Polytechnic University Shenzhen Institute
ab: Multimodal protein language models (pLMs) learn joint protein sequence-structure distributions, and their generation performance should also depend critically on inference-time sampling strategies. Yet prior work has focused more on model training than on how inference-time strategies behave. In this paper, we establish a three-stage investigation framework to empirically study the inference design space of multimodal pLMs across three representative pLMs and four fundamental tasks. We evaluate vanilla sampling, task-specific classifier-free guidance, and reward-guided beam search on multimodal pLMs, corresponding to controls over sampling distributions, per-step logits, and parallel trajectories. Throughout the complementary advancements centered on exploration-exploitation trade-off, we (1) reveal the suboptimality of default inference protocols and identify task-oriented sampling preferences; (2) observe substantial quantitative gains across tasks, consistently boosting the upper bound performance of multimodal pLMs without updating model parameters; (3) derive conclusions about base models that differ from prior consensus. Our code is available at: https://github.com/EchoChou990919/mplm_inference.

t: GSR-LoRA:Group-Sparse Routing-aware Low-Rank Adapter Compression for Multi-Task Mixture-of-Experts Fine-Tuning
ab: In multi-task mixture-of-experts parameter-efficient fine-tuning, fixed-rank Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters often struggle to accommodate the heterogeneous representation requirements across different tasks and network layers. Existing methods mainly focus on task-level expert selection, layer-wise rank allocation, or post-training parameter compression, making it difficult to jointly characterize low-rank capacity differences across tasks, layers, and modules within a unified framework. To address this issue, we propose Group-Sparse Routing-aware Low-Rank Adaptation (GSR-LoRA), a routing-aware structured rank compression method for multi-task parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). Specifically, we model low-rank components as selectable rank groups and use a task-dependent router to allocate rank capacity across tasks. Furthermore, we introduce a Group Lasso structured sparsity constraint to suppress redundant rank groups during training, forming a prunable adapter structure. During compression, we select rank groups by jointly considering parameter importance and routing usage signals, and map the router to the compressed rank space to obtain compact LoRA adapters that remain consistent with task routing. Experiments on GLUE show that GSR-LoRA reduces the average adapter rank from 16 to 5.5, removing 65.6% of rank components with only a 0.1-point performance degradation. These results demonstrate its ability to learn compact task-adaptive LoRA adapters while preserving multi-task performance. The code is available at https://github.com/HNLP93/GSR-LoRA

t: From Global to Regional Coverage: Hyperspherical Prototype Discovery for Storage-Efficient Multimodal Retrieval
a: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
ab: Multi-vector visual document retrieval models encode pages into hundreds of patch-level embeddings, enabling fine-grained interaction but incurring substantial storage overhead. Existing train-free compression approaches rely on token pruning or heuristic merging, which often fail to preserve the broad semantic coverage of the original representations under constrained budgets. To address this, we propose CovMerge, a geometry-aware, train-free index compression framework that formulates token reduction as a budgeted semantic coverage problem on the unit hypersphere. Given frozen patch embeddings, CovMerge applies Farthest Point Sampling (FPS) for coverage-aware prototype initialization, followed by spherical K-Means refinement aligned with MaxSim retrieval. The primary variant, Global Coverage, operates directly on all page patches without external dependencies, providing the strongest simplicity–efficiency trade-off. An optional Regional Coverage extension leverages document layout structure to guide prototype allocation, offering additional gains on layout-sensitive documents when reliable detection is available. Operating purely as post-processing without retraining, CovMerge supports flexible deployment budgets. On the ViDoRe V1 benchmark, CovMerge retains up to 98.1% and 98.6% of the original nDCG@5 for ColPali and ColQwen2, respectively, while using only 10% of the original storage, establishing a new state-of-the-art for storage-efficient multimodal retrieval.

t: What and Whose Knowledge? Measuring Epistemic Diversity in Large Language Models
ab: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as primary knowledge sources, yet their epistemic diversity — defined as the diversity of real-world claims in their outputs — has never been measured. The dominant paradigm is that overall LLM diversity is low, but this is always with respect to a single point in time, with no reference baseline or consideration for variation across countries. We address this by performing the first systematic study of epistemic diversity in LLMs across time and cultural context, testing 27 LLMs on 155 topics covering 12 countries, resulting in 1.7M responses and 70M individual claims. We find that epistemic diversity has increased substantially over the past three years, a positive counter to recent diversity pessimism. However, despite progress, we find that every LLM is less diverse than a search baseline. The gap is not uniform: RAG can improve diversity, while larger models are counterintuitively less diverse than smaller ones. Moreover, LLMs systematically reflect English-language knowledge over local-language knowledge for country specific topics. Together, these results demonstrate that while progress on epistemic diversity is tangible, it is insufficient and unevenly distributed.

t: When Compression Helps and When It Hurts: Condition-Aware Analysis of Chain-of-Thought Distillation
ab: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) distillation transfers multi-step reasoning from large reasoning models to smaller students, but verbose teacher traces inflate both training and inference cost. Existing CoT compression methods fall into two families, selective pruning and generative rewriting, yet prior studies have left key factors entangled: granularity is confounded with importance criteria in pruning, restructuring level is rarely isolated in rewriting, and compression budgets are not systematically evaluated across domains or regimes. We recast CoT compression along three dimensions: importance criterion, restructuring level, and compression budget. Sweeping these across two model families, Math and General domains, and Long-/Short-CoT regimes, we find that (i) importance criterion utility is strictly governed by granularity: step-level criteria converge on a shared reasoning backbone, while token-level pruning requires symbol-aware signals to preserve the logical core; (ii) restructuring level inverts across domains: Math degrades monotonically with structural disruption, while aggressive rewriting acts as a denoiser on General tasks; (iii) training-time compression does not necessarily translate to inference-time savings: Long-CoT students retain verbose habits despite concise supervision, making the training ratio an optimistic lower bound on deployment cost. These findings yield condition-aware guidelines for matching compression to deployment context.

t: Learning What to Share and What to Personalize: Hierarchical Strategy Co-Evolution for Agent Memory
a: City University of Hong Kong and University of Science and Technology of China
City University of Hong Kong and University of Science and Technology of China
ab: Memory-augmented agents maintain compact user profiles throughout extended conversations, enabling personalized and consistent responses without the need to process the entire dialogue history. The quality of these user profiles relies on the underlying memory management strategy: at each step, the agent must determine what to retain, compress, or discard. However, existing methods typically employ a static, one-size-fits-all strategy established before training. In practice, the optimal memory decision is inherently user-specific and dynamically evolves alongside policy optimization. To address this, we propose HiPS (Hierarchical Personalized Strategy), a framework that decouples memory management into a globally shared foundation and a user-specific adaptive tier. Specifically, HiPS employs Universal Strategy to extract shared principles from cross-persona trajectories, alongside Persona Delta Distillation to generate tailored rules for users whose behaviors diverge from general patterns. Cross-Level Rule Flow dynamically calibrates their boundary by promoting broadly validated personal rules and demoting contradicted global ones. The architecture establishes a co-evolution loop where a mechanism guarantees that all strategy refinements are anchored to task outcomes. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over memory-augmented baselines.

t: HEMP: Hierarchical Entity-aligned Memory Prompting for CT Report Generation
ab: Automated CT report generation remains challenging because it requires both fine-grained grounding of pathological entities in multi-view volumetric evidence and clinically coherent language that reflects diagnostic priors from historical cases. Existing methods often rely on noisy cross-modal alignment or underutilize retrieved report knowledge during decoding. We propose HEMP, which is a Hierarchical Entity-aligned Memory Prompting framework for LLM-based CT report generation. HEMP first performs two-stage entity-visual alignment where graph-constrained entity-conditioned attention retrieves initial evidence and an optimal transport refinement enforces principled coupling between entity nodes and visual tokens under marginal constraints. To inject case-conditioned linguistic priors, we design a Conditional Dual-Hopfield Memory module that retrieves case-conditioned report priors and integrates them through both implicit feature-level fusion into entity representations and explicit memory tokens appended to the prompt. Finally, we enforce clinical consistency via hierarchical severity supervision at the entity, region, and sign-group levels. Comprehensive Experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms previous methods and achieves SoTA performance.

t: HalloMTBench: A Large-Scale Human-Verified Benchmark for Diagnosing Hallucination Triggers in LLM Translation
ab: Large Language Models (LLMs) have advanced Machine Translation (MT), yet they remain vulnerable by hallucinations. Most existing benchmarks, originally designed for neural MT models, do not effectively elicit hallucinations from multilingual LLMs, resulting in a low density of samples for LLM translation hallucination analysis. To address this, we create HalloMTBench, a human-verified hallucination benchmark derived from tens of millions of translations, for studying signals that trigger LLM translation hallucinations across 11 English-to-X directions. We curate 6,908 authentic hallucination instances through a rigorous process: frontier LLMs first translate a large source corpus, and their outputs are then validated by both an LLM-judge ensemble and human experts. Based on our analysis of these hallucination instances, we introduce a taxonomy for translation hallucination that distinguishes Instruction Detachment from Source Detachment. Our evaluation of 21 model variants on HalloMTBench reveals several observable vulnerability patterns, including model Characteristics, source length, language proximity, hallucination reproducibility, and model-dependent effects of reasoning-style decoding. HalloMTBench offers a forward-looking testbed for diagnosing LLM translation hallucination. All resources will be released.

t: New Intent Discovery: From Local Relations to Global Structure
ab: New Intent Discovery (NID) aims to uncover unseen intent categories from unlabeled user queries, with the core objective of learning an intent representation space with a clear clustering structure. However, in the absence of explicit supervision, how to reliably form a global clustering structure remains challenging. To address this issue, we start from the constituent units of the global structure, namely local relations, and introduce more accessible and more stable forms of local supervision. Based on this idea, we propose LR2GS, which directly trains the intent encoder by leveraging multiple complementary local supervision signals, allowing local constraints to continuously act on the training process and thereby progressively shaping a well-separated global intent structure. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that LR2GS achieves state-of-the-art performance in both unsupervised and semi-supervised settings.

t: Bayesian Control for Coding Agents
a: Athena Research Centre, National Technical University of Athens and PolyShape
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and Independent Researcher
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and The University of Melbourne
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
ab: Modern coding agents pair LLM generators with various tools, including cheap diagnostics and expensive verifiers. The tool-use decisions are typically governed by orchestrators that often use fixed rules and ignore uncertainty. We formulate orchestration as cost-sensitive sequential hypothesis testing: a Bayesian controller maintains a belief over candidate correctness and dynamically decides whether to gather more evidence, refine the candidate, verify it, or stop. Across six generators and nine coding benchmarks, Bayesian control proves to be most valuable when verification is costly and critics are informative but imperfect. Beyond control, the belief state yields an interpretable correctness score that outperforms token-probability and raw tool-success baselines for uncertainty quantification.

t: Reactivating Alignment: Defending LLMs from Jailbreaks via Intention-Aware Input–Output Matching
ab: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that conceal harmful intent within complex adversarial prompts. Existing defenses primarily rely on input perturbation or harmful-output suppression, but they rarely model where malicious intent resides, resulting in brittle protection and excessive over-refusal.We propose SENTINEL, a plug-and-play, generation-time jailbreak defense that reframes mitigation as an intent extraction problem. Our key insight is that instruction-tuned LLMs exhibit strong input–output semantic consistency: regardless of jailbreak complexity, generated outputs tend to align with the attacker’s true intent. SENTINEL exploits this property by matching semantically aligned input–output regions to extract intention-revealing subsequences, scores these subsequences using refusal-direction projections to estimate harmfulness, and halts generation when necessary. Experiments on HarmBench across multiple LLMs show that SENTINEL reduces jailbreak success rates to close to 5% while maintaining low over-refusal. We further demonstrate robustness to adaptive attacks and provide a mechanistic interpretation: SENTINEL re-distributes jailbreak features from alignment blind spots to aligned regions.

t: Reconstructing the Right Episode: Evaluating Interleaved Conversational Memory Beyond Long Context
ab: Conversations with chat assistants increasingly span many topics in a single long-running thread, challenging memory systems. Existing long-context and memory benchmarks often expose session or topic boundaries, or probe direct personal-memory questions. These settings understate a harder assistant-memory regime: a flat mixed-topic thread where the system must infer which earlier episode makes a later task decision valid. We introduce SCALE-QA, a constraint-grounded task QA benchmark for flat unsegmented threads targeting episode integrity failure. The dataset contains 3,000 audited questions across 10 domains, uses deterministic four-way multiple-choice grading, and includes a deterministic runtime builder; experiments use all 3,000 questions through 128k and a stratified 400-question diagnostic at 1M. SCALE-QA questions are ordinary task-oriented requests whose correct answer depends on causally related evidence introduced earlier in the conversation. We also propose Temporal-Semantic Interleaved Memory Reconstruction (TSIM), which segments the turn stream into coherent episodes and indexes them through a hierarchical multi-view memory stack with deterministic episode-level summary and cluster-routing views. Experiments show that SCALE-QA challenges strong RAG baselines and long-context LLMs alike; across three open-source and proprietary LLM backends, TSIM achieves the highest accuracy in every backend setting, gaining 5.6–17.6 accuracy points over the strongest corresponding baseline.

t: SPRInG: Continual LLM Personalization via Selective Parametric Adaptation and Retrieval-Interpolated Generation
ab: Personalizing Large Language Models typically relies on static retrieval or one-time adaptation, assuming user preferences remain invariant over time. However, real-world interactions are dynamic, where user interests continuously evolve, posing a challenge for models to adapt to preference drift without catastrophic forgetting. Standard continual learning approaches often struggle in this context, as they indiscriminately update on noisy interaction streams, failing to distinguish genuine preference shifts from transient contexts. To address this, we introduce SPRInG, a novel semi-parametric framework designed for effective continual personalization. During training, SPRInG employs drift-driven selective adaptation, which utilizes a likelihood-based scoring function to identify high-novelty interactions, selectively updating the user-specific adapter on drift signals while preserving hard-to-learn residuals in a replay buffer. During inference, we apply strict relevance gating and fuse parametric knowledge with retrieved history via probability interpolation. Experiments on the long-form personalized generation benchmark demonstrate that SPRInG significantly outperforms existing baselines, validating its robustness for real-world continual personalization.

t: Beyond the Illusion of Consensus: From Surface Heuristics to Knowledge-Grounded Evaluation in LLM-as-a-Judge
ab: Agreement among LLM judges is widely used as evidence that automated evaluation is reliable. Yet consensus may be stable without reflecting a shared understanding of quality. We call this Evaluation Illusion: judges can produce detailed critiques while relying on overlapping surface cues or a common evaluation instrument. In a fully crossed baseline study, three frontier judges conduct 105,600 evaluations of 32 models. First, for the two highest-scoring models, moving from a shared five-dimension rubric package to independently generated rubrics reduces agreement by 62%, a joint contrast we term the Rubric Commensurability Problem. Second, nearly identical model-level rankings coexist with substantially weaker criterion-level agreement under non-equivalent metrics and sample sets, yielding the Resolution Paradox. We further introduce MERG, a four-stage protocol that elicits task knowledge and potential biases before scoring. In a controlled comparison on the same models at t{=}0.0, agreement decreases under independently generated MERG rubrics. These results do not establish that MERG scores are more accurate; they show that consensus depends on the evaluation instrument and analytical resolution at which it is measured.

t: The Persona-Switch Jailbreak Backdoor in LLMs: From Payload Retrieval to Trigger-Gated Persona-State Selection
a: University of Science and Technology of China
University of Science and Technology of China
University of Science and Technology of China
ab: Jailbreak backdoors typically pair a trigger with non-refusing responses, but under capability-based evaluation such payload-retrieval attacks often suppress refusal without producing actionable harm. We propose the persona-switch backdoor, where the trigger selects a persona-conditioned behavioral state rather than retrieving a fixed harmful response: style-consistent fine-tuning installs a persona, trigger training converts it into a dormant, trigger-addressable state, and persona-aligned framing amplifies harmful generation after activation. Across two model families and three personas, our attack substantially outperforms payload-retrieval baselines under capability-based evaluation while preserving high refusal rates on non-triggered inputs. The effect holds even for personas whose fine-tuning data contain no explicit harmful instructions, although they encode misaligned dispositions. Applying the same framing to clean and untriggered backdoored models yields near-zero harmful generation, showing that framing alone does not account for the attack and that harm depends on trigger activation of the poisoned persona-conditioned state. Activation steering supports a causal role for the persona-associated direction, pointing to representation-level intervention as a defense.

t: MoralSteer: Safety-Preserving Fidelity Gains in Morally Complex Role-Playing via Theory-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation
ab: Aligned LLMs systematically fail at morally complex role-playing: villains collapse into prosocial defaults due to a structural safety and fidelity tension. We present MoralSteer, a theory-guided on-policy self-distillation framework that improves morally complex role-play fidelity while preserving the safety behavior of aligned base models. MoralSteer treats Moral Foundations Theory (MFT) reasoning chains as privileged information for a frozen teacher, introduces a moral-complexity-adaptive KL interpolation \alpha(c){=}\sigma(M(c){-}\tau) to prevent prosocial collapse, and couples this with M(c)-adaptive trajectory mixing to mitigate rollout degeneration. Across four base models, MoralSteer improves Moral RolePlay L3+L4 scores by +5.8\sim+9.9\%; across five safety benchmarks, the observed rate differences remain within \pm1pp of the aligned bases. We find that villain failure concentrates in Care/Fairness foundations (67% of the L4 gap) and that aligned models perform trait substitution rather than deletion. Our code is available at https://github.com/Sii-yuning/MoralSteer.

t: Seeing Before Synthesizing: VLM-Guided Transition Event Discovery for Weakly-Supervised Dense Video Captioning
ab: Weakly-Supervised Dense Video Captioning aims to localize and describe multiple events in untrimmed videos given only an ordered set of event-level captions per video. Recent work synthesizes auxiliary transition captions via LLM to provide additional vision-language alignment, but these captions lack visual grounding and are rigidly assigned to every inter-event gap at a fixed location and duration. To address these, we propose Seeing Before Synthesizing (SBS), a framework that adaptively provides visually grounded linguistic guidance only where warranted. Leveraging a VLM, we generate frame-level narratives for the inter-event gap and detect transitions from the semantic variation across them. For identified transitions, we then refine inter-event temporal masks by blending the temporal midpoint with the semantic change point and selecting the width that maximizes vision-language alignment. Experiments on ActivityNet Captions and YouCook2 demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both captioning and localization.

t: ClueTracer: Question-to-Vision Clue Tracing for Training-Free Hallucination Suppression in Multimodal Reasoning
a: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications
Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications
Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications
ab: Large multimodal reasoning models solve challenging visual problems via explicit long-chain inference: they gather visual clues from images and decode clues into textual tokens. Yet this capability also increases hallucinations, where the model generates content that is not supported by the input image or the question. To understand this failure mode, we identify reasoning drift: during clue gathering, the model over-focuses on question-irrelevant entities, diluting focus on task-relevant cues and gradually decoupling the reasoning trace from visual grounding. As a consequence, many inference-time localization or intervention methods developed for non-reasoning models fail to pinpoint the true clues in reasoning settings. Motivated by these insights, we introduce ClueRecall, a metric for assessing visual clue retrieval, and present ClueTracer, a training-free, parameter-free, and architecture-agnostic plugin for hallucination suppression. ClueTracer starts from the question and traces how key clues propagate along the model’s reasoning pathway (question \rightarrow outputs \rightarrow visual tokens), thereby localizing task-relevant patches while suppressing spurious attention to irrelevant regions. Remarkably, without any additional training, ClueTracer improves all reasoning architectures (including R1-OneVision, Ocean-R1, MM-Eureka, .) by 1.21 on reasoning benchmarks.

t: Structured Claim-Level Discourse Representations for Dense Health Narratives
ab: Health discourse in social media videos often contains densely entangled claims spanning multiple thematic aspects, stances, evidential frames, and rhetorical functions within short conversational spans. Existing approaches largely rely on coarse topic-level, sentiment-based, or stance-oriented representations that do not adequately capture this structure. Our analysis identifies an average of 13.22 atomic claims per minute, motivating richer claim-level discourse representations. We introduce a structured framework for claim-level discourse analysis in dense health narratives. Our framework models discourse through tuples linking atomic claims with thematic aspects, stance, and multidimensional pragmatic discourse attributes. To support this setting, we construct a benchmark spanning four health domains with 1,191 manually annotated claims from 60 videos. Using this framework, we evaluate automated structured discourse analysis under different discourse context settings. Results show that current LLMs achieve strong performance on thematic categorization and stance prediction, but struggle with high-dimensional pragmatic profiling. We also find that different discourse tasks benefit from different forms of contextual reasoning, suggesting that future systems may require task decomposition and specialized inference strategies.

t: V-Rubrics: Visual Faithfulness via Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
ab: Vision-language models can produce fluent answers that are insufficiently grounded in the visual evidence: a single unsupported object, chart value, or intermediate inference can undermine an otherwise plausible response. We argue that this is a credit-assignment failure in multimodal post-training. Scalar outcome rewards indicate whether an answer is acceptable, but do not identify which visual facts are grounded, which reasoning steps are valid, or which instruction constraints are missed. We introduce Visual Rubrics-Based Reinforcement Learning, which decomposes reference responses into atomic propositions and scores generated answers along Visual Faithfulness (VF), Reasoning Consistency (RC), and Instruction Following (IF). The resulting rubric items provide structured partial credit and localize rubric credit when supporting evidence spans are available. We first obtain an SFT checkpoint by fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct on the public OpenMMReasoner-SFT-874K corpus, adapting OpenMMReasoner’s cold-start data recipe. We construct V-Rubrics 50K, a 50,248-example training set from 17 visually grounded sources, by applying rule-based filters before deriving example difficulty from rejection-sampling scores and then annotating every example with Gemini-3-Pro under the same structured prompt and protocol. We train our model based on the same SFT checkpoint using component-wise, prefix-localized rubric credit. Experiments show that our rubricbased GRPO improves over both the shared SFT baseline and answer-only GRPO, with the largest gains on knowledge-oriented and visually grounded reasoning benchmarks. The results show rubrics as a useful reward abstraction for visual post-training.

t: Tracing Error Propagation in Reasoning Language Models
ab: Reasoning language models (RLMs) increasingly tackle complex problems through long reasoning traces, but identifying when and where failures arise remains difficult. In this work, we study whether reasoning errors are signaled in model representations before they manifest as failed traces. We first show that step-level errors are locally predictable within a short window of neighboring steps, suggesting that models encode early warning signals. However, trace-level failures often result not from isolated errors, but from persistent ones originating earlier in the trace. To study this, we distinguish *recoverable* from *unrecoverable* traces via counterfactual resampling. We find that unrecoverable traces induce final-step representations that are clearly separable from those of recoverable traces. Moreover, the persistent error can be retrospectively decoded from the final-step representation, indicating that error signals propagate and accumulate through the reasoning trace.

t: VTC-R1: Vision-Text Compression for Efficient Long-Context Reasoning
a: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
ab: Long-context reasoning has significantly empowered large language models to tackle complex tasks, yet it introduces severe efficiency bottlenecks due to the computational complexity. Existing efficient approaches often rely on complex additional training or external models for compression, which limits scalability and discards critical fine-grained information. In this paper, we first propose VTC-R1, a new efficient reasoning paradigm that integrates vision-text compression into iterative reasoning. Instead of processing lengthy textual traces, VTC-R1 renders intermediate reasoning segments into compact images, which are iteratively fed back into vision-language models as "optical memory". We construct a training dataset based on OpenR1-Math-220K achieving 3.4\times token compression and fine-tune representative VLMs–Glyph and Qwen3-VL. Extensive experiments on benchmarks such as MATH500, AIME25, AMC23 and GPQA-D demonstrate that VTC-R1 consistently outperforms standard long-context reasoning. And VTC-R1 improves inference efficiency, achieving 2.7× speedup in end-to-end latency, highlighting its potential as a scalable solution for reasoning-intensive applications.

t: The Imitation Game: When LLMs Learn to Reason Like Programs via Code-Centric Reasoning Data Synthesis
ab: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at programming tasks but frequently fail at deterministic, fine-grained reasoning in natural language, relying heavily on semantic approximations rather than robust symbolic execution. To bridge this gap, we propose MIMIC, a framework that leverages executable code as a rigorous medium for reasoning data synthesis. MIMIC fundamentally transforms algorithms into verifiable reasoning trajectories through narrative fusion, code-guided test synthesis, and dynamic code instrumentation. Crucially, these explicit intermediate execution states naturally form a Code-Instrumented Reward (CIR), providing dense, high-fidelity process supervision for reinforcement learning without external reward models. Extensive evaluations reveal that models trained via SFT and GRPO on our synthesized dataset achieve substantial, consistent gains. Our method significantly elevates accuracy across general reasoning, complex mathematical benchmarks, and fine-grained deterministic tasks, demonstrating that the procedural rigor of executable code can effectively unlock and enhance the generalized reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/zjy1298/MIMIC.

t: On the Role of Supporting Evidence in LLM Reasoning: A Causal Analysis of Legal QA with Activation Patching
a: Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais, Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais
Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais, Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais
Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais, Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais
ab: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly considered for high-stakes legal applications, a central question for trust and auditability is whether their outputs reflect genuine reasoning over the supplied legal materials, or merely surface statistical patterns absorbed during pre-training. We address this question at the mechanistic level by applying activation patching, a causal-mediation technique, to four open-source multilingual LLMs on two bar-exam datasets: U.S. MBE and Brazilian OAB. For each multiple-choice question we contrast a gold supporting passage with an irrelevant-but-plausible counterfactual. We then surgically replace residual-stream activations across layers and token regions and measure recovery of the logit difference. Gold passages exert a measurable but model- and linguistic-dependent causal effect; integration concentrates in the upper layers (a late-binding signature); and the size of the effect is strongly mediated by the linguistic and discourse structure of the passage itself, not just its relevance. We introduce a four-cluster taxonomy that operationalises these regimes and identifies cases where retrieved evidence is causally decisive, inert, or actively harmful.

t: InfoSpec: Information-Guided Anchor Selection for Retrieval-Based Speculative Decoding
ab: Retrieval-based speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference without training an additional draft model, but its effectiveness is often limited by retrieval ambiguity. Existing future-guided methods typically rely on a fixed future-token position, such as a proxy for the next-next token, as the retrieval anchor. However, this fixed-anchor strategy may be suboptimal across different contexts. We propose InfoSpec, a training-free framework that formulates retrieval-anchor selection as an optimization problem performed at inference time. At each decoding step, InfoSpec constructs a lightweight candidate anchor pool from the target model, estimates the retrieval utility of each candidate via hash-index probing, and selects anchors based on model confidence, ambiguity reduction, locality, and continuation consistency under a fixed draft-tree budget. Experiments on generation, reasoning, code, and long-context benchmarks show that InfoSpec improves mean accepted tokens and end-to-end speedup over strong retrieval-based baselines. Further analyses show that InfoSpec reduces high-ambiguity matches and uses the verification budget more effectively while preserving plug-and-play deployment.

t: LatticeMind: A Conflict-Aware Memory Primitive for Multi-Agent Systems
a: Harbin Institute of Technology and Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory
University of Oxford and University of Oxford
AItonomy Foundation and University of Oxford
Shanghai Innovation Institute and University of Oxford
ab: Multi-agent LLM systems often fail not for lack of candidate answers, but because they have no persistent mechanism for deciding which incompatible claim should currently be trusted. Majority vote, debate, and judge-based selection choose an output without recording which claim wins, which is contested, or why a later update supersedes it. We present LatticeMind, a conflict-aware structured memory that handles contradiction at write time. It maintains explicit item status, applies cheap symbolic conflict checks, and routes the flagged cases to an LLM reconciler. On a label-blind ConflictBank evaluation that removes source-name hints, over a uniform draw of 200 examples from the full benchmark pool, LatticeMind reaches 0.965 accuracy versus 0.525 for the strongest baseline, with every gap significant at p<10^{-24} by paired McNemar test. Ablations show that removing the checker or the reconciler costs 12 to 14 points. Our claims are scoped to credibility conflicts, where one claim should defeat another: the coordination branch of the design is a safety override that we do not validate empirically, and all prompt-based comparisons are conditioned on a single backbone. On three secondary planning benchmarks and one synthetic scheduling diagnostic the picture is mixed: LatticeMind beats naive merge on three of four, but does not replace deliberation methods on tasks rewarding iterative search.

t: AdaRetouch: An Interleaved Vision-Language Agent for Adaptive Multi-Turn Image Retouching
ab: Image retouching requires sophisticated aesthetic understanding and precise parameter control, yet existing agents typically rely on fixed, open-loop execution or software-specific supervision. We introduce AdaRetouch, an interleaved vision-language agent for adaptive, multi-turn image retouching.
