Using this environment, we study reward hacking in open-weight LLMs and find that such behaviors can be unintentionally learned during supervised fine-tuning (SFT) when even a small fraction of reward-hacking trajectories leak into training data. As little as 1% contamination in distillation SFT data is sufficient for models to internalize reward hacking which resurfaces during subsequent reinforcement learning (RL). We further show that RL amplifies misalignment and drives its generalization beyond the original domain. We open-source our environment and code to facilitate future research on reward hacking in LLMs. Our results reveal a previously underexplored pathway through which reward hacking can emerge and persist in LLMs, underscoring the need for more rigorous validation of synthetic SFT data.

t: TIDE: Tree-Induced Fine-Grained Diagnostic Evaluation from Model Behaviors
ab: Benchmark performance is the dominant standard for comparing large language models (LLMs), typically summarized by a single aggregate score, such as accuracy, pass rate, or rubric score. This aggregate score provides limited information about a model’s underlying capabilities, yet understanding these capabilities is crucial for model development and evaluation. To this end, we propose Tree-Induced Diagnostic Evaluation (TIDE), which recasts diagnostic evaluation as behavior-driven decision-tree induction to perform fine-grained capability diagnosis. TIDE recursively builds a hierarchical capability tree from benchmark samples and model scores: at each node, an LLM judge proposes candidate splits and performs sample-to-group classification, and behavior-based information gain selects among them. We apply TIDE to five models across four benchmarks to demonstrate its effectiveness, and find fine-grained capability contrasts invisible at the aggregate level: Claude Opus 4.6 achieves 100% on microeconomic market reasoning where GPT-5.4 scores 83.3%, but trails GPT-5.4 on contract law reasoning with 77.8% versus 88.9%. We hope TIDE can be extended to past and future benchmarks so that the rich behavioral signal in evaluation results is fully leveraged for understanding model capabilities.

t: Learning Interaction-Centric Capability Representation for LLM Tool Calling
ab: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly serve as the backbone of agentic systems with tool-use capabilities, predicting correctness, latency, and cost for a given tool-calling query is essential for efficient model evaluation, selection, and routing. Existing approaches predominantly adopt a semantics-first perspective, without capturing the complex interaction patterns inherent in tool-calling queries and without jointly accounting for cost and latency. We observe that query-model interaction matrices in tool-calling scenarios exhibit a low-rank structure, indicating that behavioral outcomes are governed by latent factors beyond surface semantics. We leverage this observation to propose a dual-pathway framework that decomposes interaction matrices into low-dimensional latent spaces for multi-objective prediction. The **Capability-First (CF)** pathway discovers latent structure via matrix factorization and then projects natural language queries into latent space. The **Joint Capability-Semantic (JCS)** pathway concurrently optimizes the text encoder and model embeddings, implicitly shaping query embeddings through capability-semantic interactions. Experiments on 75 LLMs demonstrate strong performance in predicting correctness, latency, and cost. Further experiments show that our method enables few-shot unseen-model generalization, parameter-efficient training, and interpretable latent representations.

t: CCStories: Improving the Safety and Age-Appropriateness of LLM-Generated Chinese Children’s Stories
a: University of Liverpool and Eindhoven University of Technology
ab: Children’s stories play a crucial role in early cognitive and language development, yet existing story generation models lack the safety and age-appropriateness required for educational applications, especially in non-English languages. We introduce CCStories, a curated dataset of 22,200 high-quality Chinese children’s stories designed specifically to support safe and appropriate AI-generated content for young readers. Unlike general-purpose datasets derived from adult-oriented platforms, CCStories targets three critical dimensions of child-appropriate text: readability, syntactic complexity, and toxicity. We further propose a multi-dimensional evaluation framework that jointly assesses appropriateness and generation quality. As a validation of the dataset’s utility, we fine-tune five representative backbones: CPM, PanGu-\alpha, GLM-4, Qwen, a Chinese-adapted LLaMA-3 variant (Gigi-Llama-3-8B-zh), and additionally benchmark GPT-5-mini as a zero-shot instruction-tuned reference. Fine-tuning reduces offensive-prompt toxicity by up to 26.7 percentage points and raises readability by up to 14.3 percentage points, narrowing much of the gap to the GPT-5-mini reference. A human evaluation confirms that appropriateness rises from 53% to 86% after fine-tuning, and human validation of the toxicity classifier shows that the model ranking it induces matches the human ranking. CCStories provides a publicly available resource for building and benchmarking safer, more age-appropriate Chinese generative models for children’s education.

t: Lost at the End: Primacy Bias in Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Question Answering
ab: Knowledge-based visual question answering (KB-VQA) lets vision-language systems answer questions that exceed their parametric knowledge by conditioning a reader on passages retrieved from a Wikipedia-derived knowledge base. In pure-text long-context LLMs, retrieved-context use follows the U-shaped lost-in-the-middle effect of Liu et al. (2024): information at the start and end of context is used, the middle is lost. Whether this transfers to deployed multimodal KB-VQA is open. To close this gap, we design the first controlled probe of reader-side position dependence in multimodal KB-VQA: a gold-position protocol in which only the gold passage’s prompt slot varies within question. We run it on three open-source 7B/8B VLM readers and two KB-VQA benchmarks with up to 20 retrieved passages. The shape flips from U to primacy: gold-at-first beats gold-at-last by 16 to 26 points on all six combinations of reader and benchmark, an effect we call Lost at the End; the gap holds at every scale we test, 3B to 32B, attenuating at 32B. Three targeted ablations narrow the cause. A text-only control that removes the image and changes nothing else shows the primacy is already present in text mode and does not depend on the image. Image-position and distractor-shuffle ablations trace the effect to prompt slot 0 of the instruction-tuned reader, where a second answer-bearing passage placed later is largely wasted. On a frozen reader, three retrieval-side fixes (MMR, oracle reranking, rank-based reordering) all fail to improve on the deployment default. Our findings indicate that recall@k is the wrong metric for deployed KB-VQA and that the remaining headroom sits on the reader side; we release our protocol as a controlled instrument for evaluating reader-side interventions.

t: Debate-aware Learning Makes LLMs Genuine Debaters
a: Zhongguancun Laboratory and Harbin Institute of Technology
ab: Multi-agent debate systems are used to competitively discuss and resolve complex tasks. However, existing approaches often exhibit pseudo-debate behavior: agents either ignore opponents’ arguments or compromise too readily without critical evaluation. To address this, we propose a three-stage debate framework grounded in abstract argumentation theory. First, Debate Structuring uses principled prompts to elicit well-formed debate interactions. Second, Debate Imitation filters high-quality debates to fine-tune LLMs on proper argumentative conduct. Third, Debate Internalization employs a debate-aware reinforcement learning objective to instill adversarial reasoning patterns. To better quantify debate capability, we introduce two novel metrics: Rebuttal Engagement Score (RES), assessing how thoroughly models engage with opposing arguments, and Belief Governance Score (BGS), evaluating whether models appropriately retain or revise beliefs based on argument strength. Extensive evaluations across six benchmarks show that our framework not only improves task performance but also cultivates more authentic and robust debate behavior in LLMs. Our work contributes a theory-inspired training framework and evaluation suite for advancing multi-agent debate systems.

t: Policy of Thoughts: Scaling LLM Reasoning via Test-time Policy Evolution
a: Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München and Siemens Corporate Research
ab: Large language models (LLMs) struggle with complex, long-horizon reasoning due to instability from the frozen-policy assumption. Current test-time scaling methods treat execution feedback merely as an external signal for filtering or rewriting trajectories, without internalizing it to improve reasoning strategies. Inspired by Popper’s “conjectures and refutations,” we posit that effective reasoning requires real-time policy adaptation through learning from failures. We introduce Policy of Thoughts (PoT), a framework that recasts reasoning as a within-instance online optimization process. PoT effectively generates diverse candidates via targeted exploration, then applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to update a transient LoRA adapter using execution feedback. This closed-loop design enables dynamic, instance-specific refinement of reasoning priors. Experiments demonstrate PoT’s substantial gains across multiple benchmarks. On LiveCodeBench, a 4B model achieves 49.71% accuracy, surpassing 12 test-time scaling baselines and commercial models (e.g., GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3) despite being over 50 smaller.

t: EQUAL: Evaluating Pluralistic Alignment of LLMs Across Educational Perspectives
ab: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in education, powering tutoring systems, automated feedback, and curriculum support. Most alignment techniques optimize toward a single aggregated notion of human preference, a mismatch for education, where legitimate disagreement is the norm. Students, parents, teachers, and policymakers often hold deeply conflicting views on assessment, discipline, curriculum, and institutional authority, reflecting genuine value pluralism rather than noise. Pluralistic alignment, which seeks to represent and navigate this diversity, offers a principled path forward. Despite growing interest, no benchmark evaluates how well LLMs handle value-laden disagreement in educational contexts. To address this, we introduce EQUAL (Eliciting QUality sAmples of pLuralistic alignment in education), comprising 14,270 samples—5,824 value-laden scenarios and 8,446 multiple-choice questions, curated from six sources, including over two decades of Phi Delta Kappa polling data, via a lexical filtering pipeline and human validation. EQUAL supports evaluation across Overton, Steerable, and Distributional paradigms. We benchmark nine LLMs under four approaches and additionally evaluate three frontier reasoning-capable models. No single method consistently satisfies pluralistic objectives. These findings provide a foundation for future research on pluralistic alignment in educational AI.

t: Efficient Token-Level Policy Optimization for Masked Diffusion Models via Velocity Alignment
a: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
ab: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) successfully aligns autoregressive models in rigorous domains like mathematical reasoning and code generation. However, applying RLVR to Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) is hindered by intractable sequence-level likelihoods, forcing existing methods to rely on unstable, high-variance approximations. We propose Sequence Likelihood-Free Policy Optimization (LFPO), an efficient framework that circumvents this bottleneck by formulating policy alignment as discrete velocity alignment. Inspired by continuous flow matching, LFPO eschews trajectory-level estimation and directly optimizes denoising logits via contrastive token-level updates, providing a stable, low-variance surrogate. Furthermore, predicting terminal solutions from intermediate states implicitly straightens the generation trajectory, enabling high-quality sampling with significantly fewer denoising iterations. Extensive experiments on reasoning and coding benchmarks demonstrate that LFPO matches or exceeds the accuracy of likelihood-based baselines while substantially accelerating inference.

t: Help or Hurdle? Rethinking Model Context Protocol-Augmented Large Language Models
ab: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) enables large language models (LLMs) to access external resources on demand. While commonly assumed to enhance performance, how LLMs actually leverage this capability remains poorly understood. We introduce MCPGAUGE, the first comprehensive evaluation framework for probing LLM–MCP interactions along four key dimensions: proactivity (self-initiated tool use), compliance (adherence to tool-use instructions), effectiveness (task performance post-integration), and overhead (computational cost incurred). MCPGAUGE comprises a 160-prompt suite and 25 datasets spanning knowledge comprehension, general reasoning, and code generation. Our large-scale evaluation, spanning six commercial LLMs, 30 MCP tool suites, and both one- and two-turn interaction settings—comprises around 20,000 API calls and over USD 6,000 in computational cost. This comprehensive study reveals four key findings that challenge prevailing assumptions about the effectiveness of MCP integration. These insights highlight critical limitations in current AI–tool integration and position MCPGAUGE as a principled benchmark for advancing controllable, tool-augmented LLMs.

t: IdioLink: Retrieving Meaning Beyond Words Across Idiomatic and Literal Expressions
ab: Idioms pose a fundamental challenge for language models, as their meaning cannot be inferred from surface form alone. Understanding such expressions, therefore, requires semantic abstraction beyond lexical overlap. We introduce IdioLink, a retrieval benchmark designed to test whether models can link idiomatic expressions to conceptually equivalent meanings expressed in literal or paraphrased forms. IdioLink comprises 10,700 documents and 2,140 queries, spanning 107 idioms with both literal and figurative uses. Each document and query is annotated with spans that convey the core meaning. Evaluating strong embedding baselines (e.g., BGE, E5, Contriever, and Qwen), we show that current models struggle to retrieve equivalent meanings across divergent surface realizations, relying instead on topical and shallow semantic cues. IdioLink exposes key gaps in idiom-aware semantic retrieval and provides a challenging testbed for future models.

t: Cultural Moment Benchmark: Evaluating Video Cultural Reasoning and Grounding in Southeast Asia
ab: Cultural understanding in video means more than recognizing what is visible; it requires grasping the symbolic and temporal significance of cultural concepts. We decompose this into three abilities: naming what a concept symbolizes, visually recognizing it on video, and locating its sub-events in time. Existing video-cultural benchmarks tend to test what is seen, collapsing these three abilities into a single score that hides the bottleneck. We introduce the **Cultural Moment Benchmark** (CMB): 306 expert-curated concepts from seven countries in Southeast Asia across five categories. We evaluate each concept through three stages, one per ability. Given a description, **Stage 1** (S1) selects from four candidate concept names, **Stage 2** (S2) selects from four candidate video moments, and **Stage 3** (S3) predicts the start and end times of the moment in a video. To keep each stage focused on a distinct ability, we use three design choices: semantic-similarity distractors (S1, S2), unlabeled video moments (S2), and free-form localization on a different example video (S3). Across six vision-language models, failure modes vary by ability and modality. i) Even the strongest closed-source models score below 30% when all three stages must be correct; ii) The three abilities do not fully cascade: naming a concept correctly helps half the models recognize it on video, but recognizing it has little effect on locating the sub-event in time; iii) Audio is complementary, redundant, or distracting depending on the concept, more often distracting in non-Latin-script countries; removing both audio and subtitles hurts Games and Music the most. Our 14-rater human study shows that even **Expert** raters score below chance on concepts from a neighboring country, indicating that CMB requires country-specific cultural knowledge. CMB acts as a diagnostic harness, attributing failures to a specific ability or modality.

t: Beyond Codebook Uniformity: Triplet-Level Metrics and Triplet-Driven Semantic IDs for Generative Retrieval
ab: Generative retrieval replaces item IDs with *Semantic IDs* (SIDs) decoded autoregressively by a sequence model. Playing the role of tokenizer, the codebook largely determines the quality of generative retrieval. Existing codebook metrics, however, only characterize the global uniformity of code usage and do not reveal whether an individual SID correctly represents its item or separates it from others. We address this problem with two metrics and a matching training objective. We build a query-centered triplet dataset q, a, p, n from large-scale user behavior, and based on which we define **Overlap**, a prefix-based distance between two SIDs, and **Pairwise Overlap Ranking (POR)**, the fraction of triplets where a codebook places the positive closer to the anchor than the hard negative. Both metrics correlate strongly with downstream Hit Rate in generative retrieval. We then introduce the **Differentiable Soft Overlap Loss (DSOL)** to make these two metrics differentiable during codebook learning and optimize them directly. On a public e-commerce benchmark (ESCI-us) and a large-scale industrial video search dataset, DSOL improves HR and POR over standard SID baselines.

t: How Robust Are Automated Fact-Checking Systems? A Cross-Benchmark Evaluation
ab: Automated fact-checking (AFC) systems retrieve evidence and predict claim veracity, yet evaluations omit simple baselines, systems are developed for a single benchmark and cannot be trusted to generalise across domains. No prior work cross-evaluates the full two-stage retrieve-then-verify pipeline across diverse datasets, complementing retrieval-only studies (Thakur et al., 2021) and single-stage benchmarking studies (Calamai et al., 2025). We benchmark nine models, ranging from random and sparse baselines to fine-tuned transformers, zero-shot LLMs, and the two highest-ranked systems from the AVeriTeC 2025 shared task, across four datasets spanning scientific, open-web, and climate domains. Three findings stand out: (1) on ClimateCheck claim-only and fine-tuned models outperform zero-shot LLM and top-performing AVeriTeC 2025 systems, highlighting that noisy evidence can de- grade veracity prediction; (2) system rankings are strongly domain- and metric-dependent: the best model on SciFact (macro-F1 0.70) drops to 0.31 on ClimateCheck, while the AVeriTeC 2025 winner and runner-up swap rankings based on evaluation metrics and datasets; (3) replacing retrieved evidence with gold annotations improves veracity accuracy by 14-22 points across models, confirming retrieval remains primary bottleneck. We release code, pre-processed datasets, and all results to support reproducible AFC research.

t: Can Workflow Search Be Amortized? Demonstration-Guided Synthesis of LLM Agent Workflows
a: Arm Holdings plc, School of Computer Science, Carnegie Mellon University and CMU, Carnegie Mellon University
ab: Automated LLM workflow design often relies on expensive per-task search, which is computationally expensive and does not explicitly reuse structural knowledge across tasks. We propose SWIFT (Synthesizing Workflows via Few-shot Transfer), which reuses prior search trajectories and demonstrations to synthesize target-task workflows without iterative target-task optimization. SWIFT distills compositional heuristics and output-interface contracts from source-task trajectories, then conditions a single LLM generation pass on these priors and cross-task workflow demonstrations to produce an executable workflow. Across 5 benchmarks, SWIFT outperforms the SOTA search-based baseline while reducing marginal per-task optimization cost by three orders of magnitude given an existing source bank. It also improves performance on 4 additional held-out benchmarks and transfers from GPT-4o-mini to Grok, Qwen, and Gemma execution backbones. These results suggest that prior workflow search can expose reusable structural priors that reduce optimization cost while preserving or improving accuracy on related tasks.

t: X^3-OPD: Distilling Reasoning into Large Audio-Language Models via On-Policy Alignment
ab: While audio large language models have achieved remarkable progress in auditory perception, they still lag behind text-based large language models in deep logical reasoning capabilities. This performance disparity primarily stems from the scarcity of high-quality audio reasoning data. To bridge this modality gap, we propose a novel cross-modal on-policy distillation framework. Our approach leverages a powerful text model as a teacher to provide dynamic correction and guidance to the audio foundational model during on-policy exploration. Furthermore, we construct a three-tier symmetric dataset encompassing logical reasoning, complex audio reasoning, and speech dialogue. By dynamically aligning the student model’s reasoning trajectories within the high-noise auditory space with the teacher model’s prior knowledge in the clean text space, our method effectively distills robust reasoning capabilities into the audio domain. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our model achieves substantial improvements on the audio and speech understanding benchmarks, paving a new path for comprehensive audio-language understanding.

t: Beyond Case-Level Similarity: Multi-Defendant Legal Case Retrieval via Individual-Aware Reasoning
ab: Legal Case Retrieval (LCR) aims to identify cases that are legally similar to a given query case. Existing research has largely recast LCR as the task of modeling the textual similarity between the query case and a historical case. While this approach can handle single-defendant cases fairly easily, such surface-level matching proves insufficient for multi-defendant cases, which typically requires modeling and aligning defendants’ roles and judgment outcomes in different cases. To address the challenges associated with Multi-defendant LCR (Multi-LCR), we (1) present Multi-ELAM and Multi-LeCaRDv2, two multi-defendant datasets we create by enriching widely used benchmarks with defendant-level annotations, and (2) introduce a novel role- and judgment-aware framework for Multi-LCR. Experimental results show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, highlighting its effectiveness for Multi-LCR.

t: REFINE: LLM Refinement over Budgeted Text-Attributed Graphs for Personalized Medical Concept Representation
ab: Learning rich medical concept representations is essential for EHR prediction. Text-attributed knowledge graphs (TKGs) provide a natural foundation by organizing heterogeneous medical relations together with textual semantics. However, most existing encoders process concepts uniformly across patients, despite the fact that a code’s meaning and predictive value depend on patient-specific clinical context and trajectory. Learning patient-personalized concept representations from TKGs introduces two key challenges: (1) deciding how much KG context to incorporate for each observed code, and (2) aligning semantic information with the patient-specific relational structure. We propose REFINE, a KG-aware budgeted LLM graph refinement framework for patient-personalized medical concept encoding. Starting from a global TKG, REFINE constructs patient-specific temporal graphs. A sequential reinforcement learning policy selects a personalized KG expansion budget for each observed code. The resulting patient graph is processed by a heterogeneous GNN to capture relation-aware structural dependencies, while a frozen LLM uses graph-aware soft prompts to semantically refine concept representations. Experiments on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV show that REFINE consistently improves diverse EHR backbones, outperforms strong baselines, and demonstrates robust gains across component ablation, KG selection, and data insufficiency.

t: Beyond Append-Only Decoding: A Recursive Edit-Based Encoder for Arithmetic Length Generalization
ab: Algorithmic reasoning—internalizing a procedure from small examples and applying it at arbitrary scale—is a hallmark of human intelligence: a child who learns arithmetic on a few digits can, given time and paper, evaluate expressions of unbounded length. Modern language models cannot: Qwen3.5-27B, despite 100k-token reasoning contexts, degrades to below 10% accuracy on 30-digit multiplication. Departing from reasoning-through-scale, we introduce RACE (Recursive Arithmetic Control Encoder), a 3.6M-parameter Transformer trained from scratch that generalizes far better by recursively decomposing problems while keeping its working memory bounded. Two mechanisms drive this: token-level editing, which erases intermediate scratchwork, and self-calling, which recurses on subproblems. Within a single model, RACE improves multiplication length generalization 4.7 times over the Arithmetic Transformer and, for the first time, achieves length generalization on subtraction and division (×47.1 and ×17.6), while also solving nested, multi-operator expressions. Code is available at https://github.com/Pusheen-cat/RACE_2026.

t: How Do Document Parsers Break? Auditing Structural Vulnerability in Document Intelligence
ab: Document Layout Analysis (DLA) pipelines provide structured page representations for retrieval-augmented generation, long-document question answering, and related applications. Yet their robustness evaluation remains largely area-centric. We identify this *Footprint Bias* and propose **ProSA**, a lightweight output-level auditing framework that decouples controlled probing, policy-driven targeting, and structure-aware diagnosis. ProSA combines Block-level Structural Loss Rate (**B-SLR**), granularity-aware exposure descriptors, and pathway attribution to analyze where structural identity is lost, at what exposure granularity failures emerge, and how failures propagate. Across MinerU and PP-StructureV3 on 1,000 pages, affected area weakly tracks perturbation-induced OCR instability (R^2 = 0.384/0.110), whereas B-SLR aligns much more closely with it (R^2 = 0.727/0.916). Exposure descriptors further separate occlusion- and topology-dominant pathways, while matched-footprint structural probes cause much larger downstream QA/retrieval drops than area-matched erasure. These results shift DLA robustness evaluation from footprint-based measurement toward structure-aware vulnerability auditing.

t: RePair: Turning Retrieval Failures into Counterfactual Hard Pairs
a: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
ab: Vision-language retrieval with CLIP-style dual encoders achieves strong cross-modal performance, yet practical accuracy often hinges on localized semantic distinctions where top-ranked near misses differ from the true match by a single critical detail. Hard-sample mining can select confusable candidates but cannot construct corrected counterparts; synthetic augmentation can generate novel samples but, without conditioning on actual model failures, targets irrelevant dimensions of hardness. We observe that a top-ranked false positive is a counterfactual scaffold—sharing most of the query’s semantics while differing in a localized failure-causing residual. Minimally correcting this residual yields a hard positive of the ground truth in the same modality; the corrected and unedited versions form a hard negative pair that straddles the decision boundary, producing complementary pull–push supervision. We introduce RePair, guided by three principles—Validity, Minimality, and Locality—which mines false positives bidirectionally, applies LLM-guided counterfactual editing, and trains with a local hard-pair contrastive objective. On Flickr30K and COCO30K, RePair outperforms controlled augmentation baselines with only 107K synthetic samples—26%–75% fewer than comparable methods—confirming failure-conditioned repair is more data-efficient than error-agnostic augmentation.

t: TimeBlind: A Spatio-Temporal Compositionality Benchmark for Video LLMs
a: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill
ab: Fine-grained spatio-temporal understanding is essential for video reasoning and embodied AI. Yet, while Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) master static semantics, their grasp of temporal dynamics remains brittle. We present TimeBlind, a diagnostic benchmark for compositional spatio-temporal understanding. Inspired by cognitive science, TimeBlind categorizes fine-grained temporal understanding into three levels: recognizing atomic events, characterizing event properties, and reasoning about event interdependencies. Unlike benchmarks that conflate recognition with temporal reasoning, TimeBlind leverages a minimal-pairs paradigm: video pairs share identical static visual content but differ solely in temporal structure, utilizing complementary questions to neutralize language priors. Evaluating over 20 state-of-the-art MLLMs (e.g., GPT-5, Gemini 3 Pro) on 600 curated instances (2400 video-question pairs), reveals that the Instance Accuracy (correctly distinguishing both videos in a pair) of the best performing MLLM is only 48.2%, far below the human performance (98.2%). These results demonstrate that even frontier models exhibit significant deficiencies in temporal reasoning, positioning TimeBlind as a vital diagnostic tool for next-generation video understanding.

t: Rethinking Clustering as a Conversational Supervision Problem
a: California Institute of Technology and Harvey Mudd College
ServiceNow Inc, Servicenow and University of Trento
ab: Clustering is often a process of trial and error: we apply different algorithms (such as k-means or hdbscan), apply different embeddings, try a dimensionality reduction, explore different values of K, inspect the result with the product manager, and repeat. When the data is large, even communicating and analyzing a single clustering becomes difficult.We argue that the nature of clustering requires a fundamentally different approach. We posit that clustering is fundamentally a subjective and iterative process, and its central challenges are how to elicit the dimensions and nuances a user cares about, how to communicate a clustering effectively, and how to converge to an output of interest through efficient conversation. We reframe clustering as a conversational supervision problem. We formalize conversational clustering as a new task, derive evaluation metrics suited to it, and release an evaluation framework and reference implementation to seed further work.

t: TouchThinker: Scaling Tactile Commonsense Reasoning to the Open World with Large-scale Data and Action-aware Representation
a: Beijing Zhongguancun Academy and Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
national university of singaore, National University of Singapore
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: Touch is a key modality for embodied agents to understand the physical world. Although recent work has incorporated tactile signals into lan- guage systems for tactile Commonsense Rea- soning, scaling such systems to realistic open- world settings remains challenging due to two key bottlenecks: (1) current tactile reasoning datasets remain limited in format and scale, pro- viding insufficient supervision for reasoning from tactile observations to physical common- sense and hindering the learning of transferable tactile commonsense; (2) Tactile signals are inherently redundant and action-specific, yet existing methods often overlook these proper- ties, resulting in inefficient representations with limited semantic expressiveness. To address these limitations, we propose TouchThinker, a tactile-language framework that scales tac- tile commonsense reasoning to the open world from both data and representation perspec- tives. First, we construct TouchThinker-1M, a million-scale, multi-source tactile reasoning dataset covering 410 objects, 8 scenarios, and 7 sensor types, providing a solid data founda- tion for open-world generalization. We fur- ther introduce TouchThinker-Bench, an open- world benchmark with more realistic and di- verse tasks. Then, we further introduce action- aware tactile modeling and a two-stage training paradigm to improve tactile representation effi- ciency and enable efficient reasoning. Experi- mental results demonstrate that TouchThinker achieves competitive performance against state- of-the-art models across multiple datasets. Our code and dataset will be released.

t: SkillAttack: Automated Red Teaming of Agent Skills through Attack Path Refinement
a: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy
ab: LLM-based agent systems increasingly rely on open-registry skills, which are difficult to vet and expose agents to greater attack risks. These attacks mainly take two forms. Malicious injection attacks embed explicit harmful instructions into skills and are readily caught by auditing. Direct vulnerability attacks target latent flaws in non-malicious skills; however, directly crafted attack prompts often lead to unstable or unverified outcomes. We introduce **SkillAttack**, an automated red-teaming framework that systematically explores executable attack paths from latent vulnerabilities without modifying skill files. Evaluated across 11 target LLMs, SkillAttack substantially outperforms baselines, showing that well-intended skills can pose serious risks in realistic agent interactions. Our evaluation also yields trajectory-level attack traces with verified risk labels, providing a foundation for defense. We also release **SkillRiskBench**, a benchmark for skill risk analysis, and train a lightweight pre-execution risk guard that predicts risky invocations from the user request and skill file. The guard outperforms frontier LLM judges and existing safety guard models, highlighting the value of trajectory-grounded supervision for proactive skill defense. Code is available at https://github.com/Zhow01/SkillAttack.

t: Skim and Skip: Hierarchical Adaptive Inference for Efficient Multimodal Retrieval
ab: Universal multimodal retrieval (UMR) increasingly adopts multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as unified embedding backbones, but their strong retrieval performance comes at substantial inference cost. Existing methods typically rely on uniformly dense inference, where all input tokens are processed through the entire model and matched using the final-layer [EOS] representation. However, this paradigm overlooks two key forms of heterogeneity in multimodal retrieval: token contributions to the final retrieval embedding are highly uneven, and different queries require markedly different amounts of inference depth. To address this, we propose **Skim and Skip (SAS)**, a hierarchical adaptive inference framework for efficient multimodal retrieval. SAS first performs token-level evidence selection to preserve only the input information most relevant to the final retrieval embedding, and then performs depth-adaptive inference to determine whether the current representation is already sufficient for reliable matching. Experiments on 12 MMEB retrieval tasks show that SAS retains about 99% of the dense baseline’s average retrieval performance while reducing LLM-side FLOPs by up to **66.3%** and achieving up to **1.64×** end-to-end speedup. Our code is available at [https://github.com/GaoMengGladys/SAS](https://github.com/GaoMengGladys/SAS).

t: \text{GR}^2: Mitigating Granularity Collapse via Adaptive Query Routing in Generative Retrieval
a: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
ab: Generative Retrieval (GR) aims to directly generate document identifiers (DocIDs) without external indices. We identify granularity collapse: during training, GR models develop a preference for generating DocIDs with a specific granularity, causing retrieval failures when it differs from that of the target document’s DocID. We propose to quantify this mismatch using "isotropy" and confirm that retrieval accuracy degrades as such granularity mismatch increases. To address this, we propose Granularity Routing for Generative Retrieval (\text{GR}^2), which trains multiple expert models specialized for different granularity levels and routes each query to the appropriate expert. Experiments on NQ320k demonstrate that improves retrieval performance, with larger gains on queries that suffer more from granularity collapse.

t: CoSineVerifier: Agentic Verification for Computation-Oriented Scientific Questions
a: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
ab: While prior work focuses on treating answer verification as a general reasoning or semantic matching problem, significant challenges remain in computation-oriented scientific domains. In this paper, we introduce CoSineVerifier, an agentic verifier that actively invokes external executors to ground its judgments in precise computations and symbolic reasoning. To train this accurate agentic verifier, we propose a novel verifier training data augmentation method to increase the correctness and efficiency of tool-invoked verifications. Extensive experiments across STEM, QA, and long-form reasoning tasks demonstrate CoSineVerifier’s robust generalization abilities, achieving state-of-the-art performance on VerifyBench-Hard and SCI-Bench. Furthermore, when employed as an RLVR reward model, CoSineVerifier consistently outperforms both rubric- and model-based verifiers on AIME’24, AIME’25 and GPQA-D, highlighting its potential to advance LLM reasoning and accelerate data processing

t: Calibrating Student Models via Uncertainty-Integrated Distillation
a: University of Edinburgh, University of Edinburgh
ab: Model calibration aligns a model’s confidence with the accuracy of its predictions, directly influencing reliability and user trust. Surprisingly, existing research on knowledge distillation has paid little attention to the calibration of student models. In this paper, we evaluate calibration across diverse knowledge distillation settings and demonstrate that student models distilled from black-box teachers generally exhibit poor calibration. We attribute this to the fact that distillation fails to convey well-calibrated confidence, which serves as a crucial expression of predictive uncertainty. To address this limitation, we propose an ***U**ncertainty-**I**ntegrated **K**nowledge **D**istillation* (**UIKD**) method comprising two key components: (1) *uncertainty estimation*, which leverages the collective intelligence of multiple LLMs via a debate mechanism to quantify uncertainty in the distillation data; and (2) *uncertainty integration*, which employs an adaptive weighted loss function to integrate this data uncertainty into the student model effectively. Experiments on common-sense reasoning and natural language inference benchmarks demonstrate that UIKD consistently improves student model calibration while maintaining predictive accuracy. Our code is available at https://github.com/RuixuanZhang127/UIKD.

t: Call Neighbours Yourself: Graph Walks with Destination-Conditioned On-Policy Self-Distillation
ab: Reasoning over text-attributed graphs (TAGs) requires large language models (LLMs) to combine a node’s text with evidence distributed across its neighbourhood. Existing methods fix the set of accessible neighbours before generation, forcing reasoning to operate over a static context and preventing the model from acquiring missing evidence during inference. We argue that neighbour selection should itself be part of the reasoning process. To this end, we propose Call Neighbours Yourself (CNY), a framework that enables LLMs to proactively explore graph neighbourhoods through topology-constrained graph-walk actions. Instead of reasoning over a pre-selected neighbour set, CNY exposes lightweight neighbour previews and learns when to expand candidate neighbours for additional evidence. To address the delayed-credit challenge of neighbour exploration, we introduce destination-conditioned on-policy self-distillation, which retrospectively evaluates a selected neighbour after its content is revealed and converts the resulting change in action preference into an action-level training signal. Experiments on standard TAG reasoning benchmarks under a unified raw-text setting show that CNY consistently outperforms fixed-context post-training baselines. Furthermore, the learned exploration policy transfers to unseen graphs and to a graph-level task not encountered during training. Code is available at https://github.com/superallen13/CNY.

t: Learning to Explore the Crux in Formal Theorem Proving
a: Zhongguancun Academy and Beijing Institute of Technology
Xinjiang Future Enterprise Incubator Co., Ltd. and Xinjiang Future Enterprise Incubator Co., Ltd.
ab: Recent advancements in the application of Large Language Models (LLMs) to formal theorem proving in Lean have unveiled new prospects in complex logical reasoning scenarios. Acknowledging that the difficulty across reasoning steps in a formal theorem proof is not uniform, prior proof search algorithms have not systematically investigated which proof steps are more crucial to explore. This paper introduces \textbf{E}ntropy-Based \textbf{B}est-\textbf{F}irst \textbf{S}earch (EBFS), an entropy-inspired heuristic tree search algorithm that enhances the efficiency of proof generation models to explore proof trees, thereby increasing the probability of finding the correct proof. We also introduce a reinforcement fine-tuning approach specifically for proof tree search. Using EBFS during the generation stage further boosts the model’s performance in proof generation. Evaluations demonstrate that our fine-tuned EBFS model achieves consistent improvements over the baseline models. Under the same sample budget, it outperforms whole proof generation by 3.2% on the ProofNet testset, with further gains of 1.9% on MiniF2F and 1.5% on ProverBench.

t: Mitigating False Credit Propagation: Probabilistic Graphical Reward Aggregation for Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
a: Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
ab: Rubric-based rewards are increasingly used for open-ended language model post-training, but criterion-level scores are commonly aggregated as independent utilities. This flat scalarization ignores semantic dependencies among criteria, allowing downstream credit or penalties to be counted even when the conditions that license them are absent. We call this structural failure False Credit Propagation (FCP).We propose GEAR (Graphical Event Aggregation for Rubric rewards), a dependency-aware aggregation framework for rubric rewards. GEAR represents rubric criteria as latent events in a typed dependency graph, uses monotone retention factors to infer dependency-adjusted criterion marginals, and computes a normalized expected-utility reward.This preserves compatibility with standard rubric-based reinforcement learning while adding only linear-time aggregation over criteria and edges. Experiments on HealthBench, WritingBench, and PLawBench with two policy backbones show that GEAR consistently improves over flat aggregation and hard gating, both in controlled aggregation-only settings and as a plug-in module for existing rubric-guided RL pipelines.FCP diagnostics further show that GEAR substantially reduces invalid downstream utility while avoiding the over-suppression of deterministic gating.

t: SEA-SpeechBench: A Large-Scale Multitask Benchmark for Speech Understanding Across Southeast Asia
ab: The rapid advancement of audio and multimodal large language models has unlocked transformative speech understanding capabilities, yet evaluation frameworks remain predominantly English-centric, leaving Southeast Asian (SEA) languages critically underrepresented. We introduce SEA-SpeechBench, to the best of our knowledge, the first large-scale multitask benchmark that evaluates speech understanding in 11 SEA languages through 97,194 samples across 99 evaluation sets and 597 hours of curated audio data. Our benchmark comprises 9 diverse tasks across 3 categories: speech processing (automatic speech recognition, speech translation, spoken question answering), paralinguistic analysis (emotion, gender, age, speaker recognition), and temporal understanding, a novel dimension featuring timestamped content queries and temporal localization within extended audio sequences up to 3 minutes. We implement multilingual prompting in both native SEA languages and English to reflect user interactions with audio-language models. Evaluation of leading open-source and proprietary systems reveals marked performance gaps. Across all models, performance remains underwhelming on temporal understanding, emotion recognition, and speech translation. Prompting in low-resource languages such as Burmese and Tamil lags behind English by up to 41 percentage points. Our findings expose critical model limitations and underscore the need for inclusive model development. The SEA-SpeechBench benchmark is available at https://zwenyu.github.io/SEA-SpeechBench.

t: VIGOR: Outcome-Contrastive Visual Grounding for Multimodal Policy Optimization
a: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: While reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has advanced multimodal reasoning, coarse outcome rewards offer limited guidance for assigning credit to visual evidence. Analyzing same-prompt rollout groups, we observe that different outcomes exhibit distinct temporal patterns of measured visual dependency across reasoning segments. We therefore propose **VIGOR** (**Vi**sual **G**rounding **O**utcome-contrastive **R**einforcement), a policy optimization method that converts these group-wise contrasts into fine-grained supervision. VIGOR constructs outcome-conditioned prototypes from temporal visual fingerprints to reweight trajectories, uses segment-level contrasts to prioritize token gradients, and allocates the visual budget according to group difficulty. It requires no additional annotations or reward models and introduces no inference-time overhead. Across eight multimodal reasoning benchmarks, VIGOR achieves 57.5% average accuracy with Qwen2.5-VL-7B, improving over VPPO by 1.6 points. Controlled experiments further validate VIGOR on Qwen2.5-VL-3B and InternVL2.5-4B; on the latter, it outperforms VPPO on all eight tasks by 0.96 points on average. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/beck83879-bit/VIGOR.

t: From Saliency to Discriminability: Rank-Preserving Visual Token Pruning for VLM Rerankers
a: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
ab: Large vision-language models used as listwise rerankers must jointly process visual tokens from tens of candidates per query, making token pruning essential for practical deployment. Existing pruning methods retain tokens by attention saliency, yet we show that saliency is systematically misaligned with ranking contribution: visually prominent tokens often capture order-neutral patterns shared across candidates. This mismatch is layer-dependent: saliency becomes informative only where attention is concentrated, and normalized attention entropy diagnoses the reliability shift (Pearson r=0.87). We propose RaDiCal (Rank-Discriminative Calibration), a training-free framework that uses normalized attention entropy to decide when saliency can be trusted, fusing it with an attention-free rank discriminative prior and se-lecting pruning layers from the same trust landscape. Across three retrieval benchmarks and multiple VLM architectures, RaDiCal matches Dense MRR@10 on Flickr30K and surpasses it on MSCOCO at a 20% token budget, ranks first among all pruning methods on FashionIQ, and holds within 1.2 pp on Flickr30K and MSCOCO at 10% retention. It cuts FLOPs by 39–45% and delivers 1.28–1.45× measured speedups across two VLM architectures without dataset-specific retuning.

t: When Deep Research Agents Stagnate: Enhancing Reasoning with Retrieval-Aware Agent Control
ab: In this paper, we analyze the reasoning trajectories of a variety of DRAs and show that existing agents often suffer from reasoning stagnation: the majority of iterations contribute little or no improvement to final performance, while agents lack awareness of their trajectories and are therefore ineffective at adapting their search strategies or determining when to terminate. To address this issue, we introduce a set of unsupervised signals and a Retrieval-Aware Agent Controller (RAAC), which assists the agent in selecting optimal actions at each stage of the research process. RAAC incorporates key information retrieval principles, namely search novelty and information coverage, resulting in more effective reasoning trajectories that improve overall performance while reducing unnecessary iterations, and consequently cost and latency. Specifically on BrowseComp-Plus and across a large set of DRAs, adding RAAC reduces the number of search calls by an average of 14, significantly improves the best-performing DRA on recall and accuracy, and achieves an accuracy gain of up to 10% (3% in average).

t: SpIDER: Spatially Informed Dense Embedding Retrieval for Software Issue Localization
ab: Retrieving code functions, classes or files relevant to a user query, bug report or feature request from large codebases is a fundamental challenge for Large Language Model (LLM)-based coding agents. Agentic approaches typically employ sparse methods like BM25 or dense embedding strategies to identify semantically relevant units. While dense embedding approaches can outperform BM25 by large margins, both ignore the graph-structured characteristics of the codebase. To address this, we propose SpIDER (Spatially Informed Dense Embedding Retrieval), a dense retrieval approach that integrates LLM-based reasoning with graph-based exploration of the codebase. We further introduce SpIDER-Bench, a graph-structured benchmark curated from SWEPolyBench, SWEBench-Verified and Multi-SWE-bench, spanning Python, Java, JavaScript and TypeScript repositories. SpIDER’s graph-based candidate expansion attaches a structural reason for inclusion to each surfaced function (its seed and the edge type linking them), making the candidate set auditable while keeping the retrieval budget fixed. The graph is built from per-repository syntax trees, so it can be constructed on-demand at the start of a developer session rather than precomputed offline. Empirical results show that SpIDER consistently improves dense retrieval Recall@20 across every language and benchmark in SpIDER-Bench: by at least 13% relative (+0.05 to +0.12 absolute) along containment edges, rising to at least 27% relative (+0.11 to +0.19 absolute) once call edges are explored.

t: FigEx2: Visual-Conditioned Panel Detection and Captioning for Scientific Compound Figures
ab: Scientific compound figures combine multiple labeled panels into a single image, and downstream pretraining and retrieval require panel-aligned visual-text pairs. However, in a PubMed Central (PMC)-scale crawl of 346,567 compound figures, 16.3% have no caption and are discarded by existing caption-decomposition pipelines. We propose FigEx2, a visual-conditioned framework that takes only a compound figure as input and jointly produces labeled panel boxes and panel-wise captions. FigEx2 introduces an Entity-Attention Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularizer that aligns the detector’s cross-attention with scientific entities annotated for each panel, providing a stable conditioning signal that also improves localization, and applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a panel-level Entity-F1 reward to optimize scientific faithfulness. We curate BioSci-Fig-Cap for in-domain supervision and contribute physics and chemistry test suites for cross-disciplinary evaluation. FigEx2 achieves 0.751 mAP@0.5:0.95 on BioSci-Fig-Cap, and outperforms Qwen3-VL-8B by 6.80 Entity-F1 on MedICaT for captioning. It also transfers zero-shot to out-of-distribution domains.

t: RAD-PROTEIN: Multi-source Knowledge-enriched Retrieval-augmented Protein Structure Searching
a: Rutgers University, Rutgers University and Rutgers University
ab: The Research Collaboratory for Structural Bioinformatics Protein Data Bank (RCSB PDB) provides open access to macromolecular structures and offers an extensive structural keyword search infrastructure. However, the current RCSB PDB APIs do not support natural-language semantic search. To overcome this challenge, we propose RAD-PROTEIN, a novel multi-source knowledge-enriched Retrieval-Augmented Protein structure search system that answers user natural-language queries by jointly leveraging heterogeneous structural literature and metadata. In addition, we introduce the first benchmark for text-based protein-structure search evaluation, comprising 454 expert-verified queries. RAD-PROTEIN substantially outperforms baselines, achieving up to +19.8% Recall@1 and +16.1% in MRR with hybrid retrieval and multi-source knowledge enrichment. Comprehensive ablation studies further confirm the robustness of our proposed approach. Finally, we develop an interpretable interface to return top-ranked structures with LLM-generated explanations, enabling efficient human verification and downstream scientific analysis. Code: https://github.com/Cassie07/RAD_PROTEIN

t: DataShield: Uncovering Risky Fine-Tuning Data Across LLMs Through Consensus Subspace Alignment
a: The State Key Laboratory of Blockchain and Data Security, Zhejiang University
Shanghai Institute for Advanced Study, Zhejiang University, The State Key Laboratory of Blockchain and Data Security, Zhejiang University and Zhejiang University
ab: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on domain-specific datasets has become a standard paradigm for adapting LLMs to specialized applications. However, recent work has shown that even fine-tuning on benign task-specific data can substantially weaken the safety capabilities of LLMs. While existing efforts have made progress in identifying data responsible for safety degradation, they usually rely on a single mean vector computed over a specific model with its tokenizer to represent the safety direction, which limits both the effectiveness and transferability of their risk assessment measures. To address these limitations, we propose DataShield, a data assessment framework that identifies risky fine-tuning samples and response segments through consensus subspace alignment over joint safety-critical semantic spaces derived from multiple safety-aligned LLMs.Within these spaces, DataShield extracts consensus safe and unsafe subspaces using semantic spectral decomposition over safe and unsafe data representations. The risk of a data sample or segment is then estimated by measuring its relative alignment with the unsafe and safe subspaces, enabling both sample-level filtering and fine-grained segment-level masking. Compared with state-of-the-art filtering and masking baselines, DataShield reduces ASR by 14.6% with sample filtering and 32.3% with segment masking, while preserving downstream utility and avoiding target-model-specific risk computation.

t: Evaluating the Evaluators: A Systematic Analysis of Reference Bias in Audio Captioning Metrics
ab: Current evaluation metrics for automated audio captioning (AAC) rely on reference-based comparison, implicitly assuming that a limited reference set adequately represents valid descriptions. However, the inherent cross-modal gap between audio and language gives rise to a many-to-many correspondence: a single audio event can be accurately described by numerous semantically equivalent yet lexically diverse captions. We first demonstrate the resulting instability through ground-truth intra-evaluation on Clotho and AudioCaps, evaluating each human caption against the remaining four references using a leave-one-out protocol. To provide a controlled demonstration, we use a CVAE-based AAC model that generates diverse candidates replicating the ground-truth captions, showing that n-gram metrics reward surface-level replication. We then conduct non-word replacement, synonym replacement, and adjacent-token swapping experiments on both datasets. Overlap metrics penalize synonym replacements almost as strongly as non-word corruption, whereas embedding and CLAP-based metrics respond weakly to local word-order changes. Additional evaluation of CAF-Score and FLEUR (AF3) shows partial progress, but neither configuration clearly separates synonym replacement from adjacent swapping. No evaluated metric jointly provides acoustic grounding, tolerance to valid lexical variation, and local word-order sensitivity. We therefore contribute a reusable AAC metric diagnostic protocol for exposing these trade-offs and guiding future metric development.

t: LLMs Infer Cultural Context but Fail to Apply It When Responding
ab: Recent work has shown that LLMs overrepresent dominant cultures, particularly Western ones, while marginalizing others. We investigate whether this affects models’ ability to generate culturally adapted responses by evaluating their use of local measurement units based on the user’s perceived cultural background. We introduce Cultural and Pragmatic Response Inference (CAPRI), a dataset of conversations with varying levels of cultural cues. Experiments with state-of-the-art LLMs show that models can infer cultural background and recall relevant conventions, but often fail to utilize the information to adapt their answers to the relevant cultural conventions, unless explicitly prompted to perform the tasks sequentially. We further evaluate adaptation to the interpretation of time and quantity expressions, two subjective language grounding dimensions that are affected by culture. We find that models increasingly adapt their answers as cultural cues accumulate, but their priors are not culture-neutral, sometimes aligning with the model’s country of origin. Overall, CAPRI provides a resource for future research aimed at narrowing the gap between cultural knowledge and culturally adaptive language generation.

t: When Accuracy Aligns and Fails: Diagnosing Human–LLM Response Alignment at Population Scale
ab: We propose CAPE, a Choice-Distribution Alignment and Performance Evaluation framework for diagnosing human–LLM response alignment using population-scale human choice distributions. CAPE separates outcome-level difficulty alignment from response-distribution alignment with four metrics: OA, MAE, PA, and DA. We apply CAPE to 609 Korean CSAT items with item-level response distributions from approximately 300K examinees per item, and evaluate 16 LLMs. Results show that model capability is the strongest predictor of alignment, with accuracy closely tied to both full-choice and distractor-only alignment. However, group-level scores are affected by aggregation size and model composition, and neither reasoning augmentation nor Korean adaptation yields consistent residual advantages. Bloom-level analyses further suggest that capability-linked alignment varies across item types. CAPE thus enables evaluation beyond accuracy by diagnosing how model success and failure patterns relate to human population responses.

t: Task–Specificity Score: Measuring How Much Instructions Really Matter for Supervision
a: Soket Labs Technology and Research Private Limited and Soket Labs Technology and Research Private Limited
ab: Instruction tuning is now the default way to train and adapt large language models, but many instruction–input–output pairs are only weakly specified: for a given input, the same output can remain plausible under several alternative instructions. This raises a simple question: does the instruction uniquely determine the target output? We propose the Task–Specificity Score (TSS) to quantify how much an instruction matters for predicting the target output by contrasting the true instruction against plausible alternatives for the same input. We further introduce TSS++, which uses hard alternatives and a small quality term to mitigate easy-negative effects. Across three instruction datasets (Alpaca, Dolly-15K, NI-20) and three open LLMs (Gemma, Llama, Qwen), our strongest evidence appears in the tightest budget regime, particularly at 5% retention. In this setting, TSS and TSS++ consistently outperform existing selection baselines across most model–dataset combinations. These results show that task specificity is a useful signal for low-budget instruction-data selection and complements existing filters such as perplexity and IFD.

t: Hybrid Linear Attention Done Right: Efficient Distillation and Effective Architectures for Extremely Long Contexts
ab: Hybrid architectures that combine softmax attention blocks and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have shown a desirable performance-throughput tradeoff for long-context modeling, but their adoption and studies are hindered by the prohibitive cost of large-scale pre-training from scratch. Some recent studies have shown that pre-trained softmax attention blocks can be converted into RNN blocks through parameter transfer and knowledge distillation. However, these transfer methods require substantial amounts of training data (more than 10B tokens), and the resulting hybrid models also exhibit poor long-context performance, which is the scenario where hybrid models enjoy significant inference speedups over Transformer-based models. In this paper, we present HALO (Hybrid Attention via Layer Optimization), a pipeline for distilling Transformer models into RNN-attention hybrid models. We then present HypeNet, a hybrid architecture with superior length generalization enabled by a novel position encoding scheme (named HyPE) and various architectural modifications. We convert the Qwen3 series into HypeNet using HALO, achieving performance comparable to the original Transformer models while enjoying superior long-context performance and efficiency. The conversion requires just 2.3B tokens, less than 0.01% of their pre-training data.

t: SIP: Aligning LLM-based TableQA with Table Semantics via SQL Logic
ab: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance on Table Question Answering (TableQA), yet their reasoning processes often remain misaligned with the underlying table semantics. This misalignment can lead to decompositions and validation steps that fail to faithfully capture the table operations required by the question. In this paper, we introduce SIP, a SQL Logic-aligned framework for improving the semantic consistency of LLM-based table reasoning. SIP is built around SQL Logic, a natural-language abstraction of standard SQL operators that explicitly represents operations such as projection, filtering, ordering, and aggregation while avoiding the syntactic brittleness of executable SQL. SQL Logic serves as a shared operator-level representation that guides sub-question decomposition and supports operator-aware validation in both Direct Prompting and Python Agent settings. Experiments on three TableQA benchmarks show that SIP achieves state-of-the-art performance and consistently improves robustness across diverse LLMs, demonstrating the value of explicit semantic representations for structured table reasoning.

t: MiRD: Reliable Set-Valued Prediction for Open-Ended Question Answering via Miscoverage Risk Decomposition
a: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
ab: Reliable set-valued prediction provides a principled way to mitigate hallucinations in open-ended question answering (QA), yet existing conformal approaches typically rely on a restrictive premise: finite sampling must produce at least one admissible candidate, or calibration examples violating this condition are discarded. In this paper, we introduce MiRD, a two-stage framework that decomposes overall miscoverage into sampling failure and conditional selection failure. In Stage I, MiRD establishes an expectation-level marginal upper bound on the probability that finite sampling produces no admissible answer under a fixed sampling budget. In Stage II, conditioned on sampling success, MiRD calibrates a conformal selection threshold using admission-correlated nonconformity scores constructed from the full calibration set, thereby preserving calibration-set integrity. Across three open-ended QA datasets and eight models, MiRD controls sampling risk, conditional selection risk, and overall miscoverage, while providing tighter first-stage bounds than PAC-style alternatives and more adaptive prediction sets than successful-only calibration.

t: MSTree: Multi-Scale Evidence Tree for Training-Free Long-Form Video Question Answering
ab: Long-form video question answering hinges on locating brief, sparse evidence buried in minutes of dense action. Flattening the entire video into a single caption stream forces the LLM to sift through thousands of tokens, where decisive cues are easily drowned out by surrounding context. We present MSTree, a training-free framework that organizes captions into a Multi-Scale Evidence Tree. The tree is built by a coordinated dual-modal segmentation method that combines visual scene transitions and textual coherence under temporal contiguity, producing segments that are both visually and semantically consistent. Inference follows a mine-then-reason workflow: the LLM first scans coarse segment summaries to locate the most relevant event, then reasons over its fine-grained captions. When the first-round prediction falls below a confidence threshold, Contrastive Targeted Reflection (CTR) activates. The model articulates a discriminative gap that specifies what evidence is still missing to separate the top candidate answers, and an answer-anchoring constraint requires any newly retrieved evidence to both support the revised prediction and contradict the original. On EgoSchema, NExT-QA, and Video-MME, MSTree reaches 68.4%, 77.5%, and 55.7% accuracy, outperforming all training-free baselines.

t: Breaking Failure Cascades: Step-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Medical Multimodal Reasoning
a: Korea University and AIGEN Sciences Inc.
Samsung Research America and Korea University
ab: Recent multimodal large language models have shown great promise in clinical image reasoning, but existing post-training pipelines remain predominantly outcome-centric, relying on final answer correctness or sequence-level preferences. This approach suffers from sparse credit assignment, making it difficult to optimize the internal reasoning process essential for clinical applications. Our analysis reveals that cascading errors from early-stage reasoning failures are a leading cause of incorrect predictions in medical visual question answering (VQA) benchmarks. Motivated by this, we propose Medical Reasoning-aware Policy Optimization(MRPO), an RL algorithm that incorporates step-wise process rewards. When the final answer is incorrect, MRPO assigns exponentially larger penalties to tokens in earlier invalid reasoning steps, breaking failure cascades without compromising successful paths. Across three multimodal LLM backbones, MRPO consistently outperforms standard GRPO and a recent RL baseline, and on Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct even outperforms substantially larger medical MLLMs such as HuatuoGPT-Vision-34B by 2.79 points. Moreover, MRPO reduces early-stage reasoning failures from 64.0% to 13.0%, demonstrating that targeted mitigation of cascading failures improves both reasoning quality and final answer accuracy.

t: HiVe: Beyond Static Prompts for Multitask Learning via Hierarchy-based Vertical Mixture-of-Experts
ab: As large language models (LLMs) continue to scale, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has become a practical alternative to full-parameter adaptation. Prompt tuning is effective, but existing approaches either use flat prompt structures or hierarchical structures with fixed prompt composition, limiting adaptive prompt specialization. To address this limitation, we propose HiVe, a prompt tuning framework that models prompts at multiple levels and enables input-dependent specialization. HiVe constructs a prompt hierarchy by leveraging inter-task relationships during training, and employs a vertical mixture-of-experts (V-MoE) mechanism at inference time to compose prompts up to the level of specialization required for each input. Experiments show that HiVe consistently outperforms strong prompt tuning baselines across diverse tasks.

t: SkillShift-Bench: Benchmarking Skill Learning under Environment Evolution for Web Agents
a: Nanjing University, Nanjing University and Nanjing University
ab: Skill learning enables web agents to reuse prior experience for long-horizon interactive tasks. However, learned skills are typically evaluated in closed environments, overlooking the fact that real-world web deployment involves continuous shifts in invocation context, perceptual grounding, and execution feasibility. To this end, we introduce SkillShift-Bench, the first benchmark for evaluating skill learning with controlled open-environment shifts. SkillShift-Bench simulates Contextual Shift, Perceptual Shift, and Execution Shift across three self-hosted web systems, and evaluates agents with diagnostics covering task success, interaction cost, skill use, and skill failure. Comprehensive experiments reveal systematic robustness degradation under controlled shifts, characterized by lower success rates, higher interaction costs, and more frequent skill failures, with Execution Shift exerting the strongest pressure. We further formulate shifted skill execution as a nonstationary local executability problem and provide both a dynamic-regret analysis and a practical test-time adaptation method, demonstrating the feasibility of improving learned-skill execution without relearning the skill library. Code, tasks, environments, documentation, and the leaderboard are available at https://skillshift-bench.github.io/.

t: Semantic Flow Regularization: Teaching LLMs to Generate Diverse Yet Coherent Responses
ab: When large language models are fine-tuned to generate persona- or tone-conditioned responses, their output diversity is severely limited—a failure we term Cross-Style Collapse. We trace this collapse to the cross-entropy objective, which under shared representations tends to suppress diverse continuations. We propose Semantic Flow Regularization (SFR), a lightweight auxiliary objective that supervises the backbone with continuous sentence-encoder embeddings of future segments via conditional flow matching. The stochastic flow source preserves multi-modality by construction; the flow-matching head is discarded at inference, adding zero deployment cost. On a large-scale industrial dialogue dataset (Qwen3-32B, 9 personas), SFR improves output diversity, style fidelity, and response quality over SFT. We further validate on the public LiveCodeBench-v5 (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct), where SFR consistently improves pass@k, confirming generality beyond stylized dialogue. A controlled comparison on MBPP reveals Multi-Token Prediction to be a degenerate special case of SFR.

t: SkillForge: Learning from Success–Failure Boundaries for Consistent Long-Horizon Agents
a: Oracle and University of Virginia, Charlottesville
ab: Long-horizon LLM agents often fail from procedural errors such as forgetting constraints, misordering tool calls, or stopping prematurely. Because these slips are unpredictable, the same agent can succeed on one run and fail on an identical task later. The resulting execution trajectories contain rich signals about which procedural choices lead to success or failure, yet existing approaches that extract reusable guidance from agent trajectories either introduce noise through imprecise distillation or depend on external retrievers for deployment. We propose SkillForge, a training-free framework that rethinks both the construction and deployment of procedural guidance: it pairs successful and failed attempts on the same task to identify critical procedural choices, consolidates and filters candidate guidance to remove low-quality entries, and loads relevant guidance on demand at inference time only when the agent’s current context signals its relevance. Across agent benchmarks including \tau^2-Bench and Terminal-Bench, SkillForge improves repeated-run consistency, reducing the consistency gap by up to 37% and lowering total token usage by up to 23.6% compared to baselines, while moderately improving single-trial performance. These results suggest a practical path toward distilling high-quality procedural guidance from past trajectories for more consistent and efficient long-horizon agents.

t: Unified-MAS: Universally Generating Domain-Specific Nodes for Empowering Automatic Multi-Agent Systems
a: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
Singapore University of Technology and Design
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
ab: Automatic Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) generation has emerged as a promising paradigm for solving complex reasoning tasks. However, existing frameworks are fundamentally bottlenecked when applied to knowledge-intensive domains (e.g., healthcare and law). They either rely on a static library of general nodes like Chain-of-Thought, which lack specialized expertise, or attempt to generate nodes on the fly. In the latter case, the orchestrator is not only bound by its internal knowledge limits but must also simultaneously generate domain-specific logic and optimize high-level topology, leading to a severe architectural coupling that degrades overall system efficacy. To bridge this gap, we propose Unified-MAS that decouples granular node implementation from topological orchestration via offline node synthesis. Unified-MAS operates in two stages: (1) Search-Based Node Generation retrieves external open-world knowledge to synthesize specialized node blueprints, overcoming the internal knowledge limits of LLMs; and (2) Reward-Based Node Optimization utilizes a perplexity-guided reward to iteratively enhance the internal logic of bottleneck nodes. Extensive experiments across four specialized domains demonstrate that integrating Unified-MAS into four Automatic-MAS baselines yields a better performance-cost trade-off, achieving up to a 14.2% gain while significantly reducing costs. Further analysis reveals its robustness across different designer LLMs and its effectiveness on conventional tasks such as mathematical reasoning.

t: Distance Is Not Enough: Forget-Retain Alignment Gap Predicts LLM Relearning Robustness
a: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
ab: Machine unlearning aims to make a model forget specific data, yet unlearned LLMs often fail to stay unlearned: brief fine-tuning can revive removed knowledge. Existing robustness predictors rely on global weight-space displacement, but distance alone can be misleading when random or destructive updates collapse performance. We argue that relearning robustness depends on update structure: robust unlearning should affect forget-critical weights while sparing retain-critical ones. We introduce the Forget-Retain Alignment Gap (FRAG), a training-free predictor that scores an update’s forget-retain alignment without running a relearning attack, and separates selective from dense updates more reliably than global distance. Building on the forget-critical, retain-sparing principle, Forget-Retain Pruning (FRP) improves relearning robustness. Our results suggest that weight selectivity better explains robustness than distance alone. Our code is available at https://github.com/Yi1-Chen/FRAG.

t: No Training, No Architecture Change: Per-Cell Warm-Up Calibration for LLM Agent Memory
ab: LLM agent memory modules universally adopt a single global retrieval depth k across all deployment scenarios; this global constraint produces an irreducible Oracle performance gap. We carry out a systematic evaluation on 19 heterogeneous deployment cells covering three LLM backbones, three multi-agent coordinators, three tasks, and two representative memory architectures (A-Mem and G-Memory). We confirm that the per-cell optimal k varies dramatically across cells, that low-capacity LLMs exhibit catastrophic accuracy collapse at larger k , and that no cross-cell feature or lookup-table shortcut reliably predicts the per-cell optimum. A theoretical analysis further shows that in the small-budget paired-binary-reward regime, every training-free bandit method we evaluate reduces to uniform-mean argmax. Motivated by this collapse, we propose per-cell warmup calibration: paired probe queries iteratively estimate the mean reward of each candidate k, the procedure commits to the empirical argmax, and a closed-form (2 σ) criterion provides earlystop. The recipe is training-free, requires no architectural modification, and introduces no hyperparameter beyond the probe budget. On all 19 deployment cells it attains 100% of the per-cell Oracle, with an average absolute improvement of +3.33 percentage points and a peak gain of +12.00 percentage points.

t: IESR: Efficient MCTS-Based Modular Reasoning for Text-to-SQL with Large Language Models
ab: Text-to-SQL is a key natural language processing task that maps natural language questions to SQL queries, enabling intuitive interaction with web-based databases. Although current methods perform well on benchmarks like BIRD and Spider, they struggle with complex reasoning, domain knowledge, and hypothetical queries, and remain costly in enterprise deployment.
