Yet existing systems can only repair errors at the failed step or simply return to the previous step and retry, and thus fail to handle two pervasive failure modes: inaccurate decomposition, where the plan is flawed before execution begins, and error propagation, where an upstream mistake surfaces downstream. We propose that addressing both requires global self-correction, the ability to identify the root cause of a failure and repair it at the right location. To this end, we propose **LoCoRAG**, a globally self-correcting agentic RAG framework. LoCoRAG maintains a persistent dual memory through a two-stage thinker-generator pipeline, separating what the corpus contains from what the system has concluded. Then, a memory-grounded failure localization module attributes each failure to specific causes and pinpoints its true origin. Together, LoCoRAG drives a self-correcting global replan that selects a matched repair, from local refinement to upstream rollback with downstream regeneration. Across existing multi-hop QA benchmarks, LoCoRAG achieves SOTA performance on all datasets and all metrics, with a 10.8 points average LLM-Acc gain over the strongest baseline on 3-hop-or-deeper scenarios.

t: WearerText: Benchmarking Wearer-Centered Scene Text Understanding in AI-Glasses Videos
a: Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
national university of singaore, National University of Singapore
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: Recent MLLMs have shown promise in scene-text-aware video understanding, yet their ability to understand scene text from the wearer’s perspective in AI-glasses videos remains underexplored. AI-glasses videos are passively captured without a camera-frame preview, limiting the wearer’s ability to adjust framing during recording. As a result, relevant text may be unstable, and the recorded view may not fully reflect the wearer’s attention. The challenge is thus not merely to read visible text, but to identify and read the right text given the wearer’s position, viewpoint trajectory, and goal. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce **WearerText**, a benchmark for **Wearer**-Centered Scene **Text** Understanding, comprising 1,101 real-world AI-glasses videos and 15,336 QA pairs spanning 13 tasks. These tasks are organized into a three-level diagnostic hierarchy: *L1 Text Perception*, *L2 Contextual Understanding*, and *L3 Wearer-Grounded Reasoning*, targeting unstable text perception, wearer-view alignment, and goal-oriented text reasoning, respectively. To ensure reliable construction and evaluation, we develop **MAH-V**, a multi-agent hybrid verification pipeline for QA construction, and propose **VerEval**, a Verified-evidence metric for open-ended Evaluation. Benchmarking 20 recent MLLMs shows that current models still struggle with wearer-centered scene text understanding, particularly on tasks requiring wearer-view alignment and goal-oriented text reasoning.

t: MultiSynt/MT: Trillion-Token Multi-Parallel Pretraining Data Translated Across 36 Languages
a: LAION and Juelich Supercomputing Center, Research Center Juelich
ab: Open web-scale pre-training corpora remain concentrated in English, limiting multilingual LLM development. We introduce MultiSynt/MT, an open synthetic parallel corpus with approximately 4.8 trillion target-language tokens across 36 European languages, produced by translating 100 billion high-quality Nemotron-CC tokens with Tower+ and OPUS-MT/HPLT-MT systems. For many medium- and lower-resource European languages, this is the largest openly available pre-training resource. On a broad multilingual benchmark suite, reference LLMs trained on MultiSynt/MT reach the final score of HPLT 2.0, a native-data baseline, using roughly 72% fewer pre-training tokens, and outperform it by approximately 15% relative at a matched 100B-token training budget. Our analyses also identify evaluation blind spots: standard multiple-choice benchmarks miss translation-quality differences that a fluency-sensitive LLM-as-judge evaluation cleanly recovers on the trained LLMs (with no fluency deficit in MultiSynt itself), and Norwegian idiomatic and culturally grounded tasks remain better served by native data. We release the corpus, including row-aligned translations from multiple systems, to support controlled research on multilingual pre-training data and evaluation.

t: Opacity Is Not Privacy: Information-Constrained Latent Communication for Multi-Agent LLM Systems
a: Southern University of Science and Technology
ab: Latent communication provides an efficient alternative to text-based exchange in multi-agent LLM systems by transmitting continuous hidden representations instead of natural-language messages. However, opacity is not privacy: latent messages may still carry private prompts, agent memory, or task-irrelevant sensitive information recoverable by downstream agents or adversaries. We study this risk through communicated latent messages, the edge-level representations that cross agent boundaries and define the privacy interface of latent multi-agent systems. We identify two coupled leakage mechanisms: instantaneous leakage from individual messages and propagation leakage accumulated across multi-round transcripts.We propose Information-Constrained Latent Communication (ICLC), a model-agnostic communication-layer framework that constrains latent information exposure without modifying backbone LLM parameters. ICLC combines a receiver-conditioned latent bottleneck, adversarial regularization over messages and transcripts, and topology-aware gates that suppress unnecessary communication edges. Across private-context question answering, collaborative reasoning, and tool-use planning, ICLC preserves the utility benefit of latent communication while reducing average leakage from 0.747 to 0.398 compared with raw latent communication. These results suggest that privacy in latent multi-agent systems should be treated as a dynamic information-flow problem over messages, edges, and interaction rounds.

t: CForce: Boosting Parallel Decoding for dLLMs via Consistency Forcing
ab: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) accelerate language generation by predicting multiple masks in a single forward pass.However, existing dLLMs can suffer from unreliable predictions in early denoising stages under aggressive parallelism strategies, leading to errors that can propagate to later stages. To tackle this issue, we present Consistency Forcing (CForce) for dLLMs, a distillation method to force the mask predictions of early stages to align with those of later stages. CForce trains the model on pre-collected self-rollout trajectories, thereby improving training-inference alignment.We introduce Confidence Adaptive KL Divergence as a distillation objective to conjoin the merits of forward and reverse KL.We further provide a theoretical analysis for the consistency objective to explain why CForce can approximately minimize the prediction error of early stages.Critically, the same formulation applies to both mask-to-token decoding and edit-capable decoding; in the edit-capable case, later token-to-token refinements provide additional supervision for earlier masked-state predictions. Experiments on non-edit and edit-capable LLaDA models show improved speed-quality trade-offs, especially under high-parallelism decoding budgets.

t: Unified Context Evolution for LLM Agents
ab: LLM-based agents can solve multi-step interactive tasks by combining reasoning with environment feedback, yet each episode starts from the same fixed context and any useful strategy discovered along the way is lost once the task ends. Existing approaches either limit learning to the current task or pool all experience into a single untyped store, without distinguishing knowledge types, tracking quality through use, or balancing what the library still lacks. We introduce Unified Context Evolution (UCE), a gradient-free framework that externalizes agent experience into an evolving library of typed Evolvable Context Units (ECUs). UCE decomposes experience into four complementary types (Memory, Strategy, Workflow, and Skill), each generated from trajectories under type-specific conditions, retrieved at decision time, scored through repeated usage outcomes, and pruned when no longer valuable. A scheduling module allocates each cycle’s generation budget toward the types where the library is weakest. Across two interactive benchmarks, UCE raises ALFWorld success from 75.4% to 96.3% and WebShop task score from 45.1% to 61.3%, and remains effective across alternative actor reasoning backbones without model retraining.

t: Exploring Collaboration between a language and a non-language agent
a: Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology, Delhi and Adobe Systems
State University of New York at Buffalo
ab: LLMs are increasingly deployed as orchestrators that coordinate specialized subagents to solve complex tasks. In many important domains (game playing, robotics, autonomous driving), the strongest available agents are not language models: their expertise is encoded in latent representations of policy, value, and learned features, not in words. Integrating such agents into LLM reasoning pipelines currently requires verbalization: compressing rich continuous representations into sparse textual summaries at each interaction step. To study whether verbalization constitutes a structural bottleneck, we introduce LLAMIA-Bench, a suite of six collaborative chess tasks spanning three facets: behavioral imitation, state assessment, and natural-language explanation. Tasks are drawn from prominent problems in chess literature and industry, each unsolvable by either component alone, and selected to vary in how much relevant signal survives verbalization.Our experiments reveal a consistent verbalization debt: the performance gap between verbalized and internalized integration widens throughout training and persists as the LLM scales from 4B to 14B parameters. The effect is sharpest on tasks whose target signal has no faithful text representation: on puzzle interest prediction, verbalized systems of all sizes remain near-chance (\leq 12/100) while internalization reaches 52/100. To close this gap, we introduce latent state internalization, which projects the subagent’s continuous representations directly into the LLM’s token stream as learned state tokens, with dynamic re-encoding as actions advance the environment state. A single 14B model, LLAMIA, trained under this paradigm matches or exceeds dedicated task specialists and frontier models including GPT-5.1 with tool access across all benchmark tasks, and generalizes out-of-distribution where task-specific finetunes collapse. In a human study with skilled chess players, LLAMIA passes as human in 61% of gameplay trials and its commentary is preferred in 72.2% of pairings.

t: Steering from Random Quotients: A Sample-Complexity Theory of Polysemantic Contrast Pairs
a: Singapore Management University and N2TP Technology Solutions JSC
Phenikaa University and N2TP Technology Solutions JSC
ab: Activation steering often averages activation differences between positive and negative prompts to construct a steering vector. This difference-in-means (DiM) estimator is simple, but a contrast pair can coactivate the intended concept together with topic, style, length, refusal, or truthfulness-related nuisance features. We model each pair as revealing the target vector through a quotient that removes its active nuisance span. The resulting polysemantic information operator determines which target components are identifiable and the number of contrast pairs needed to recover them. We establish identifiability, sample-complexity bounds, a coactivation phase diagram, and sparse-dictionary recovery guarantees. Synthetic and controlled experiments support the predicted quotient-recovery behavior. Public-data and Pythia-410M pilots instead evaluate recovery of the quotient estimand induced by chosen nuisance supports, not an externally validated semantic target. A controlled TruthfulQA counter-confounder illustrates the main NLP lesson: raw behavioral margin can reward a style-entangled DiM vector even when quotienting removes the injected style component.

t: CultureVidBench: Benchmarking Cultural Understanding in Text-to-Video Generation
ab: Text-to-video (T2V) generation models have advanced rapidly, yet their ability to represent diverse cultural contexts remains underexplored. Existing benchmarks mainly focus on perceptual quality, physical plausibility, and text-video alignment, but do not directly assess whether generated videos capture culturally specific objects, actions, rituals, visible text, or audio cues. We introduce CultureVidBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating cultural understanding in T2V generation. CultureVidBench contains 1,000 curated prompts covering 12 countries, 6 continents, 8 cultural regions, and 14 cultural aspects organized into three categories: material culture, social practice & performance, and ritual & ceremony. Designed specifically for video generation, CultureVidBench emphasizes dynamic and multimodal cultural representation, including social interactions, ritual procedure, and culturally appropriate visible text and audio. We evaluate seven representative T2V models through human user studies and MLLM-based automatic assessment across cultural faithfulness, multimodal cultural rendering, semantic adherence, and perceptual quality. Results show that although current models achieve strong semantic adherence and visual quality, they often fail to faithfully capture fine-grained cultural details, particularly for underrepresented regions, rituals, and multimodal cultural cues.

t: Can LLM-as-a-Judge Reliably Verify Rubrics in Agentic Scenarios?
a: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
ab: Rubric-based scoring has become a widely used paradigm in model evaluation, typically with LLM-as-a-Judge (LaaJ) for rubric scoring. However, the reliability of LaaJ for rubric scoring remains underexplored. This concern is especially pronounced in agentic scenarios, where long, complex outputs further challenge reliable scoring. To address this, we conduct a systematic meta-evaluation of LaaJ reliability for rubric verification. We introduce RuVerBench, the first benchmark for assessing LaaJ reliability in rubric verification for agentic scenarios. RuVerBench covers two prevalent agentic domains, deep research and agentic coding, with 2,458 instances, each containing a model-generated output, a rubric, and a human-annotated label indicating whether the output satisfies the rubric. Using RuVerBench, we evaluate numerous frontier LLMs and find that even the most advanced models achieve strong performance but still exhibit substantial noise. We further analyze the impact of key LaaJ strategies, including prompt design, batching, and majority voting, on rubric verification. We find that weaker models are more sensitive to prompt variations, batched verification presents a trade-off between accuracy and efficiency, and majority voting yields effective but diminishing returns. We have released our dataset and code to facilitate future research: https://github.com/THU-KEG/RuVerBench.

t: ABED: Assumption-Based Bidirectional Entailment Diagnosis for Open-World Logical Reasoning
ab: Open-world logical entailment requires deciding whether a set of premises entails a conclusion, entails its negation, or leaves it undecided. Many existing methods are deductive in spirit, searching for a proof and reading the label from whether that proof succeeds. When implemented through LLM-based proof search, this makes the prediction depend on a single unstable trajectory, and a failed or partial search is easily mismapped to the wrong label. We propose ABED (Assumption-Based Bidirectional Entailment Diagnosis), a training-free inference-time framework that reframes entailment classification as missing assumption diagnosis. Instead of asking only whether a conclusion can be proved, ABED asks what assumption is missing for it to hold, and classifies that gap as already closed by the premises (Null), contradicted by them (Contra), or left open (Admissible). It applies this diagnosis to both a conclusion and its negation, and determines the label from the resulting dual gap pair. Across FOLIO, ProofWriter, ProntoQA, and LogicNLI, ABED consistently outperforms prompting-based, symbolic, solver-based, and deductive baselines, improving over the strongest baseline on each dataset by 3.4, 5.3, 0.8, and 4.4 points with GPT-4.1.

t: SAFER: Spectral Correlation Prior-based Attention Signature Flow for Enhanced Robustness in Harmful Prompt Detection
a: Fujitsu Research and Development Center Co. Ltm. and Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi
Fujitsu Research and Development Center Co. Ltm.
Fujitsu Research and Development Center Co. Ltm.
ab: Most existing harmful prompt detection methods rely on surface-level semantic representations, making them vulnerable to paraphrasing, prone to false positives, and limited in their ability to generalize to novel or adversarial prompts. Recent work has explored the use of model-internal signals, such as gradients or spectral features, to train classifiers that capture latent malicious behavior beyond surface semantics. However, these approaches primarily operate on local or isolated internal features and do not model the global structure of model behavior, which limits their robustness against subtle adversarial manipulations. In this work, we focus on robust harmful prompt detection under adversarial attacks. We propose SAFER, a simple yet effective method that models cross-layer attention signature flow by learning spectral correlation priors between attention heads and constructing a cross-layer attention-head spectral graph. This facilitates explicit modeling of structured attention propagation across layers, allowing the capture of both local and global attention dynamics and leading to improved robustness. SAFER achieves superior performance across multiple benchmark datasets for harmful prompt detection, while demonstrating significantly greater resilience to diverse adversarial attacks compared to prior approaches.

t: Differentiable Geometric Alignment for LLM Spatial Reasoning: Training-Time Symbolic Constraints, Solver-Free Inference
ab: Large language models struggle with spatial and geometric reasoning. Existing remedies either fine-tune on answers, leaving geometric structure implicit, or attach a symbolic solver at inference, which is brittle under imperfect parser coverage. We propose **DGCL** (*Differentiable Geometric Constraint Layer*), a training-time objective for a typed family of spatial and geometric relations (e.g., parallelism, frame-relative left/right, vertical order) that supervises the LLM’s hidden states with a differentiable Huber residual over parser-proposed candidate constraints, a coverage regularizer, and a learned selector. Training requires a frozen constraint parser; inference does not: it is a single LLM forward pass over the text prompt plus one learned ‘[GEO]‘ token, with no parser, solver, external tool, or auxiliary head. We evaluate on three auditable datasets (planar geometry, language-grounded 3D relations, and a firewalled zero-touch counterfactual split) with 10{,}278 test instances over 5 seeds. We are explicit about attribution: a strong constraint-supervised control (A2c), which trains the selector and coverage objective on gold candidates but blocks the residual gradient from the LLM, already captures most of the improvement over plain fine-tuning (up to +26 points). Our isolated contribution is that *coupling* the differentiable residual gradient into the LLM adds a *further, stable* +4.0 to +5.2 points over this strong control across all five settings (seven pre-registered gates, Holm-corrected p{<}0.001), at 1.06\times a fine-tuned baseline’s latency. On full parser coverage a strong tool baseline marginally exceeds DGCL; DGCL’s advantage is robustness under partial or missing coverage, not superiority over oracle solvers.

t: SpeechRole: A Large-Scale Dataset and Benchmark for Evaluating Speech Role-Playing Agents
ab: Speech is essential for realistic role-playing, yet existing work on role-playing agents largely centers on text, leaving Speech Role-Playing Agents (SRPAs) underexplored and without systematic evaluation. We introduce SpeechRole, a unified framework for developing and assessing SRPAs. SpeechRole-Data contains 98 roles and 111k speech-to-speech conversations with rich timbre and prosodic variation, providing large-scale resources for training SRPAs. SpeechRole-Eval offers a multidimensional benchmark that directly evaluates generated speech, preserving paralinguistic cues and measuring interaction ability, speech expressiveness, and role-playing fidelity. Experiments show that end-to-end SRPAs such as GPT-4o Audio achieve strong fluency and naturalness, but remain limited in prosody consistency and emotion appropriateness. Current open-source end-to-end models exhibit clear performance gaps, particularly in interaction ability and role-playing fidelity, while several cascaded systems achieve relatively stable performance on these dimensions. Furthermore, role-specific training can further improve the role-playing capabilities of end-to-end SRPAs.

t: Beyond Linearization: Attributed Table Graphs for Table Reasoning
a: University of Science and Technology of China
University of Sydney and University of New South Wales
ab: Table reasoning, a task to answer questions by reasoning over data presented in tables, is an important topic due to the prevalence of knowledge stored in tabular formats. Recent solutions use Large Language Models (LLMs) for their semantic understanding and reasoning capabilities. A common paradigm of such solutions linearizes tables to form plain texts that are served as input to LLMs. This paradigm has critical issues. It requires LLMs to infer row-column-cell relations from serialized inputs, makes evidence paths harder to trace, and is subject to the "lost-in-the-middle" issue. To address these issues, we propose Table Graph Reasoner (TabGR), a model that represents tables as an Attributed Table Graph (ATG) without task-specific training. The ATG explicitly preserves row-column-cell structure while enabling graph-based reasoning over traceable evidence paths. We further propose a Question-Guided Personalized PageRank (QG-PPR) mechanism to rerank tabular data and mitigate the lost-in-the-middle issue. Extensive experiments across multiple table reasoning benchmarks show that TabGR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art models by up to 9.7% in accuracy.

t: CopyShield: A Cross-Level Benchmark of Copyright Defenses in LLMs
a: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
ab: Large language models can reproduce memorized text verbatim, yet copyright defenses are usually evaluated under incompatible protocols. We introduce CopyShield, a controlled benchmark comparing three representative defenses at distinct intervention levels: contrastive decoding (output), Direct Preference Optimization (behavioral), and activation intervention (representation). We evaluate CopyShield on two model families, LLaMA-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B-v0.3, using controlled memorization over five public-domain books and a shared protocol measuring literal leakage, calibrated non-literal leakage, utility, and degeneracy. Across these methods, intervention level is associated with distinct compliance–utility trade-offs. On LLaMA-3.1-8B, contrastive decoding remains near-degeneracy-free (0–2%) but reaches a literal-suppression floor at NV-Recall 0.192–0.203. DPO nearly eliminates literal leakage (0.263 to 0.002) but induces paraphrase-loop degeneracy in 58% of QA outputs, with no utility gain over the SFT baseline. Activation intervention attains the lowest non-literal flagging rate (1/200) by blocking 84% of non-literal queries before generation. Human evaluation confirms that DPO has low coherence, whereas activation lowers perceived copyright risk through broad refusal. On Mistral-7B-v0.3, the output- and representation-level patterns persist, while DPO degeneracy falls to 10–14%, showing that its severity is model-dependent. Together, CopyShield provides cross-level reference baselines and identifies targeted non-literal suppression as an open challenge. The code is available at https://github.com/spotai-mbzuai/CopyShield.git.

t: GRKV: Global Regression for Training-Free KV Cache Compression in Long-Context LLMs
ab: Large language models (LLMs) with extended context lengths rely on the key-value (KV) cache to support attention over prior tokens. However, maintaining the KV cache incurs substantial memory overhead, motivating KV-cache compression methods that enforce a fixed budget through eviction and merging. Modern eviction methods increasingly adopt span-based retention because preserving contiguous spans is empirically effective and better preserves semantic coherence. Yet, when combined with post-eviction merging, span-based retention concentrates merges onto a small set of span-boundary carrier tokens, producing a highly imbalanced merge pattern that exacerbates over-merging and increases information loss. To address this imbalance, we propose GRKV (Global Regression for KV Cache), a training-free KV-cache merging method that directly minimizes the discrepancy between compressed-cache and full-cache attention outputs. GRKV uses ridge-regression-based merge steps to distribute information from evicted tokens across retained tokens, while regularizing the updates to prevent over-smoothing. Across the LongBench and RULER long-context benchmarks, GRKV is the only merging method that improves overall performance with minimal overhead. Our code is available at https://github.com/pjunjie/GRKV.

t: A Universal Vibe? Finding and Controlling Language-Agnostic Informal Register with SAEs
ab: While multilingual language models successfully transfer factual and syntactic knowledge across languages, it remains unclear whether they process culture-specific pragmatic registers, such as slang, as isolated language-specific memorizations or as unified, abstract concepts. We study this by probing the internal representations of Gemma-2-9B-IT using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) across three typologically diverse source languages: English, Hebrew, and Russian. To isolate pragmatic register processing from trivial lexical sensitivity, we introduce a novel dataset in which every target term is polysemous, appearing in both literal and informal contexts. We find that while much of the informal-register signal is distributed across language-specific features, a small but highly robust cross-linguistic core consistently emerges. This shared core forms a geometrically coherent “informal register subspace”, with greater geometric concentration at the deeper layer. Crucially, these shared representations are not merely correlational: activation steering with these features causally shifts output formality across all source languages and transfers zero-shot to six held-out languages spanning diverse language families and scripts. Together, these results provide the first mechanistic evidence that multilingual LLMs internalize informal register not just as surface-level heuristics, but as a portable, language-agnostic pragmatic abstraction.

t: Code Agents Don’t Understand Root Cause:Evaluating Code Agents on Linux Kernel Fault Localization
ab: Code agents are increasingly used in debugging workflows, where fault localization (FL) is often evaluated as endpoint retrieval: whether a model names the faulty code location. This view is inadequate for Linux kernel debugging, where failure logs may expose downstream symptoms while the erroneous state is introduced earlier and propagates through various dependences. We introduce KernelPath, a 200-instance Linux 5.10 function-level FL benchmark that pairs each root cause function with a source-grounded state propagation path and a dependence layer. KernelPath evaluates both endpoint localization and ordered diagnostic process recovery. Experiments with SOTA agents show that agents often retrieve plausible candidates but remain unreliable at recovering the diagnostic process, with performance degrading sharply under complex dependence relations. Further diagnostic probes show that agents can use explicit state-transition evidence, yet fail to infer how functions affect the erroneous state, drifting toward neighboring objectives such as repair-site selection, or up stream suspicious function retrieval. These findings reveal an unstable task model for kernel FL in current code agents.

t: Training-Free Generative Retrieval
a: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Computing Technolgy, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy
ab: Large language models (LLMs) are emerging as versatile foundations for generative retrieval (GR), a paradigm that directly generates relevant document identifiers (docids) given a query. Existing ways of using LLMs for GR typically rely on heavy post-hoc training to fit a relevance data prior, often leading to overfitting and poor cross-domain generalization. Can retrieval, like other language tasks, be performed without retriever-specific training using LLMs? We conduct a preliminary study and find that constrained decoding, required to ensure valid docids, often misaligns with the model’s natural free-generation patterns. We propose FreeGR, a plug-and-play framework that adapts retrieval data to a LLM’s habitual generation behavior. FreeGR consists of three components: an LLM self-annotated docid generator, an LLM-preferred input context designer, and two decoding strategies that trade off retrieval effectiveness and efficiency. It requires no retriever-specific parameter optimization, is model-agnostic, and scales across LLM families and sizes while preserving their generative capabilities. Experiments on the NQ, MS MARCO, and BEIR datasets show that FreeGR achieves competitive retrieval effectiveness compared with several trained generative and dense retrievers, without retriever-specific parameter optimization.

t: SiMing-Bench: Evaluating Procedural Correctness from Continuous Interactions in Clinical Skill Videos
a: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
ab: Current video benchmarks for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) focus on event recognition, temporal ordering, and long-context recall, but overlook a harder capability required for expert procedural judgment: tracking how ongoing interactions update the procedural state and thereby determine the correctness of later actions. We introduce SiMing-Bench, the first benchmark for evaluating this capability from full-length clinical skill videos. It targets rubric-grounded process-level judgment of whether interaction-driven state updates preserve procedural correctness across an entire workflow. SiMing-Bench is instantiated with SiMing-Score, a physician-annotated dataset of real clinical skill examination videos spanning cardiopulmonary resuscitation, automated external defibrillator operation, and bag-mask ventilation, each paired with a standardized step-wise rubric and dual-expert labels. Across diverse open- and closed-source MLLMs, we observe consistently weak agreement with physician judgments. Moreover, weak performance on rubric-defined intermediate steps persists even when overall procedure-level correlation appears acceptable, suggesting that coarse global assessment substantially overestimates current models’ procedural judgment ability. Additional analyses with binary step judgment and step-aligned clips indicate that the bottleneck is not merely fine-grained scoring or temporal localization, but modeling how continuous interactions update procedural state over time.

t: ESSA: Evolutionary Strategies for Scalable Alignment
a: Central University and AI Research, T-Tech
ab: Online alignment of large language models (LLMs) is dominated by reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) with gradient-based optimizers such as PPO or GRPO. While effective, these pipelines require backpropagation through long rollouts, gradient synchronization across devices, and careful hyperparameter tuning, all of which become increasingly costly at scale. We present **ESSA** (Evolutionary Strategies for Scalable Alignment), a gradient-free online alignment stage that follows supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and replaces the gradient loop with inference-only black-box search. ESSA optimizes only the singular values of low-rank adaptation (LoRA) factors after a short SFT warm-start, restricting the search to a compact, task-aligned subspace where evolutionary search is practical even for 72B-parameter models. Because the loop is inference-only, ESSA is compatible with INT4/INT8 weight quantization and reduces inter-GPU communication to a few bytes per iteration. Across instruction following (IFEval), preference-based assistant tuning (HelpSteer2, HH-RLHF), and mathematical reasoning (GSM8K, MATH500), ESSA matches or exceeds LoRA-GRPO in the reported LoRA comparisons; on GSM8K it also outperforms Online DPO and PPO, while remaining competitive with both methods on IFEval. At scale, ESSA reaches a fixed MATH500 accuracy on Qwen2.5-32B/PRM800K up to 7.8× faster than LoRA-GRPO on 128 GPUs.

t: QuaNAG: LLM-driven Memory-bounded Neural Architecture Generation via Quantization-branched Exploration
ab: Human Activity Recognition (HAR) on memory-constrained edge devices demands heterogeneous, accurate, resource-adaptive architectures that are costly to design manually. Neural Architecture Search (NAS) provides an automated solution for model design, and its integration with quantization can further expose high-quality architectures under edge memory budgets. Recent NAS increasingly adopts LLM-based methods, including prompt-engineering and fine-tuning approaches. Prompt-engineering approaches suffer from 4-10 hours generation time, while fine-tuning approaches achieve minute-level generation but often sacrifice architecture quality due to the complexity of quantization. We propose QuaNAG, a Neural Architecture Generation (NAG) framework built on the insight that quantization is not an ordinary architecture attribute: it can change model feasibility, alter accuracy, and expand the feasible search space. QuaNAG therefore models quantization as branch-level search decisions and transfers quantization-aware search knowledge into an LLM through curriculum learning. Experiments on demanding HAR benchmarks over five baselines, including in-domain evaluations, out-of-domain evaluations, and on-device experiments, demonstrate that QuaNAG achieves 8.93% average accuracy improvement with several minutes generation time, satisfying all deployment requirements. Our code and model are available at https://github.com/pyq623/QuaNAG.

t: Implicit Unwatermarking in Pseudo-Reference Reranking for LLM Watermarking
a: CyberAgent, Inc. and Nara Institute of Science and Technology
Institute of Science Tokyo and Tokyo Institute of Technology, Tokyo Institute of Technology
ab: Text watermarking for large language models (LLMs) requires balancing output quality and detection reliability. We study a practically relevant reranking setting in which multiple watermarked outputs are compared against unwatermarked pseudo-references. We show that quality-only reranking can weaken watermark signals by favoring candidates closer to unwatermarked references, effectively acting as implicit unwatermarking. We propose constrained Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) selection, which treats detection as a constraint rather than a weighted objective: it filters out weakly watermarked candidates and then selects the highest-quality remaining output. Experiments across watermarking methods, datasets, and models show that constrained selection substantially improves detectability over quality-only reranking while remaining competitive in task quality. It also achieves a more favorable matched-detection tradeoff than normalized weighted MBR.

t: A Survey on Natural Language User Profiles for Recommendation: Methods, Datasets, and Metrics
ab: Natural language (NL) user interest profiles—concise, human-readable descriptions of a user’s preferences—are an emerging alternative to opaque embeddings in recommender systems, offering transparency and user control alongside predictive utility. Recent advances in large language models have made generating and consuming such profiles increasingly practical, spurring a growing but fragmented body of research. In this survey, we provide the first systematic review of NL user profiles for recommendation, organizing the literature around two coupled tasks—profile generation and profile-based recommendation—and surveying the methods, datasets, and evaluation practices currently in use. We further propose the Reference-Anchored Evaluation Taxonomy (RAET), which organizes intrinsic and extrinsic metrics around explicit (output, reference signal) pairs, and reveals where efforts have concentrated and which axes remain unexplored. Finally, we identify structural open challenges—such as the tension between transparency and task-driven optimization—establishing a clear roadmap for future research in this space.

t: Beyond Survival: Evaluating LLMs in Social Deduction Games with Human-Aligned Strategies
a: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence and University of Technology Sydney
University of Science and Technology of China and Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
ab: Social deduction games like Werewolf combine language, reasoning, and strategy, providing a testbed for studying language and social intelligence. However, most studies reduce the game to LLM-based self-play, yielding templated utterances and anecdotal cases that overlook the richness of social gameplay. Evaluation further relies on coarse metrics such as survival time or subjective scoring due to the lack of quality reference data. To address these gaps, we curate a high-quality, human-verified, multilingual, and multimodal Werewolf dataset containing over 100 hours of video, 32.4M utterance tokens, and 15 rule variants. Based on this dataset, we propose a novel strategy-alignment evaluation that leverages the winning faction’s strategies as ground truth in two stages: 1) Speech evaluation, formulated as multiple-choice-style tasks that assess whether the model can adopt appropriate stances across five dimensions of social ability. 2) Decision evaluation, which assesses the model’s voting choices and opponent-role inferences. This framework enables a fine-grained evaluation of models’ linguistic and reasoning capabilities, while capturing their ability to generate strategically coherent gameplay. Our experiments show that state-of-the-art LLMs and VLMs exhibit diverse performance, with roughly half of the models in both modalities remaining below 0.50 accuracy, revealing clear gaps in deception and counterfactual reasoning.

t: Justification of Emotional Appeal in Computational Argumentation
ab: Emotional appeals (EAs) are often treated as fallacious in computational argumentation, yet they may be justified when warranted by the context. We introduce the task of predicting EA justification and present the first human-annotated dataset for this task, covering 1,176 argument–context pairs. Grounded in philosophical literature, our framework evaluates EA justification along logical and emotional dimensions. Human annotations show that justification criteria form a shared latent judgment space, with evidential proportionality and normative acceptability most strongly associated with overall justification. We further find that EAs without logical support are not always judged fully unjustified, and stronger EAs are not necessarily judged less justified. Finally, LLM experiments show that EA justification prediction remains challenging.

t: HEAR-RAG: A Hypergraph-Based Evidence-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation Framework for Multi-Hop Question Answering
ab: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves model factuality, but multi-hop question answering still suffers from incomplete and disconnected evidence retrieval across documents or chunks. Although graph-enhanced RAG methods organize evidence with graphs or hypergraphs, existing structures still struggle to balance the completeness of higher-order factual structures with fine-grained evidence connectivity. Graph-based methods mainly rely on pairwise edges and may fail to preserve complex multi-entity facts, while hypergraph-based methods can capture higher-order contexts but may underuse low-order relations for step-by-step evidence tracing. Both types of methods may further suffer from evidence fragmentation when semantically equivalent entity mentions are not effectively organized across chunks. To address these issues, we propose HEAR-RAG, a hypergraph-based evidence-aware retrieval framework for multi-hop question answering. HEAR-RAG organizes distributed evidence into a unified factual evidence hypergraph that jointly preserves higher-order factual contexts, low-order relational clues, and source chunks. It further introduces relation-aware entity mention clustering to reduce evidence fragmentation, and uses hybrid structural retrieval to construct connected evidence paths for answer generation. Experiments on multiple multi-hop QA benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness.

t: Decouple to Forget: Semantic Mediation for Sensitive Unlearning in Large Language Models
a: Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology and The University of Melbourne
ab: Machine unlearning for large language models seeks to remove specified knowledge while preserving general capability, yet current methods often treat an entire response as the unit of forgetting. This coarse granularity causes unnecessary utility loss when the forget target is only a small set of sensitive facts embedded within otherwise benign explanations. In this paper, we introduce Decouple to Forget (D2F), a targeted unlearning method based on causal mediation that separates sensitive factual content from non-sensitive meaning and surface expression. For each example to be forgotten, D2F extracts a fact-level “mediator” representation from the answer, identifies which parts are sensitive, and removes only those parts while leaving the rest of the structure intact. We then generate counterfactual answers grounded in this mediator that preserve non-sensitive content but exclude sensitive facts, employing preference-based contrastive optimization to reduce the likelihood of information leakage while maintaining helpfulness and fluency. Experiments across various benchmark datasets show that D2F achieves a better balance between forgetting and retention than strong baseline methods. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/D2F-D596/.

t: Multi-Field Tool Retrieval
a: Quan Cheng Laboratory and Tsinghua University
ab: Integrating external tools enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to interact with real-world environments and solve complex tasks. Given the growing scale of available tools, effective tool retrieval is essential to mitigate constraints of LLMs’ context windows and ensure computational efficiency. Existing approaches typically treat tool retrieval as a traditional ad-hoc retrieval task, matching user queries against the entire raw tool documentation. In this paper, we identify three fundamental challenges that limit the effectiveness of this paradigm: (i) the incompleteness and structural inconsistency of tool documentation; (ii) the significant semantic and granular mismatch between user queries and technical tool documents; and, most importantly, (iii) the multi-aspect nature of tool utility, that involves distinct dimensions, such as functionality, input constraints, and output formats, varying in format and importance. To address these challenges, we introduce Multi-Field Tool Retrieval, a framework designed to align user intent with tool representations through fine-grained, multi-field modeling. Experimental results show that our framework achieves SOTA performance on five datasets and a mixed benchmark, exhibiting superior generalizability and robustness. We have open-sourced all the code and prompts in https://github.com/LittleDinoC/MFTR.

t: Span-Level Machine Translation Meta-Evaluation
ab: Machine Translation (MT) and automatic MT evaluation have improved dramatically in recent years, enabling numerous novel applications. Automatic evaluation techniques have evolved from producing scalar quality scores to precisely locating translation errors and assigning them error categories and severity levels. However, it remains unclear how to reliably measure the evaluation capabilities of auto-evaluators that do error detection, as no established technique exists in the literature. This work investigates different implementations of span-level precision, recall, and *F*-score, showing that seemingly similar approaches can yield substantially different rankings, and that certain widely-used techniques are unsuitable for evaluating MT error detection. We propose "match with partial overlap and partial credit" (MPP) with micro-averaging as a robust meta-evaluation strategy and release code for its use publicly. Finally, we use MPP to assess the state of the art in MT error detection.

t: Causal Abstention for Cost-Aware Language-Agent Collaboration
ab: Multi-agent language systems are often deployed under the assumption that collaboration improves reasoning quality, but this assumption breaks down once token cost, latency, and collaboration-induced errors enter the picture. We study protocol selection under a cost-aware utility objective, where the system decides on each input whether to run a collaborative protocol or fall back to solo reasoning. We propose Causal Advantage Routing for Language agents (CARL), a contextual-bandit framework that estimates the conditional collaboration advantage of each protocol over solo reasoning. CARL combines confounded execution logs with budgeted randomized probes, forms one-vs-solo doubly robust scores and shrunken DR-derived pseudo-outcomes, and at deployment uses a one-sided predictive lower bound for a future realized protocol-solo contrast, otherwise abstaining to solo execution. Across math, code, and multi-hop question-answering benchmarks with an open-weight model, CARL improves cost-aware utility and substantially reduces harmful collaboration over fixed protocols, compute-matched solo strategies, MAS routers, cascade methods, and causal routing baselines, indicating that effective multi-agent systems should estimate when collaboration is causally worth its cost rather than invoking it by default.

t: AuthorMix: Modular Authorship Style Transfer via Layer-wise Adapter Mixing
a: Saarland Informatics Campus, Max-Planck Institute and Saarland University
ab: The task of authorship style transfer involves rewriting text in the style of a target author while preserving the meaning of the original text. Existing style transfer methods train a single model on large corpora to model all target styles at once: this high-cost approach offers limited flexibility for target-specific adaptation, and often sacrifices meaning preservation for style transfer. In this paper, we propose AuthorMix: a lightweight, modular, and interpretable style transfer framework. We first train individual, style-specific LoRA adapters on a small set of high-resource authors: this allows for the rapid training of specialized adaptation models for each new target using layer-wise adapter mixing via reinforcement learning, necessitating only a handful of target- style training examples. AuthorMix ranks first on the combined style–meaning score among all baselines, including GPT-5.1, and substantially improves meaning preservation over the trained baselines; under human evaluation it is the only method best-or-tied on every dimension.

t: FineWeb-CLaR: Culture, Language, and Region Annotations for Benchmark-Aligned Corpus Auditing
a: Barcelona Supercomputing Center and German Research Center for AI
German Research Center for AI and Universität des Saarlandes
German Research Center for AI and Universität des Saarlandes
ab: Cultural evaluation coverage and robustness in language models are difficult to diagnose because pretraining corpora and cultural benchmarks are rarely indexed with comparable metadata. Benchmarks increasingly target culturally situated phenomena at the level of languages, regions, and locale-specific practices, while web-scale corpora are usually organized only by language. A shared culture–language–region layer makes these resources comparable, enabling audits of whether a target cultural phenomenon is represented in pretraining data, evaluated by benchmarks or both. To this end, we introduce FineWeb-CLaR, a large-scale annotated dataset derived from FineWeb and FineWeb-2 that places web documents on a shared culture–language–region axis for corpus auditing and benchmark alignment.FineWeb-CLaR annotates the full 30.9B-document collection from FineWeb and FineWeb-2 with URL-derived region labels and cultural-topic provenance. Our region resolver assigns a non-empty region to 25.61% of documents (7.92B). For cultural-topic analysis, we induce locale-specific topics and project them onto the 14 leaves of the Cultural Taxonomy of Liu et al. (2025), producing Locale Topic Distributions (LTDs) for corpus-side comparison. We also annotate 277 cultural NLP benchmarks with the same taxonomy, language coverage, and region coverage. Together, these resources enable direct comparison between corpus-side pretraining evidence and benchmark-side evaluation coverage.

t: Why Users Go There: World Knowledge-Augmented Generative Next POI Recommendation
ab: Generative point-of-interest (POI) recommendation models based on large language models (LLMs) have shown promising results by formulating next POI prediction as a sequence generation task. However, the knowledge encoded in these models remains fixed after training, making them unable to perceive evolving real-world conditions that shape user mobility decisions, such as local events and cultural trends. To bridge this gap, we propose **AWARE** (**A**gent-based **W**orld knowledge **A**ugmented **RE**commendation), which employs an LLM agent to generate location- and time-aware contextual narratives that capture regional cultural characteristics, seasonal trends, and ongoing events relevant to each user. Rather than introducing generic or noisy information, AWARE further anchors these narratives in each user’s behavioral context, grounding external world knowledge in personalized spatial-temporal patterns. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that AWARE consistently outperforms competitive baselines, achieving up to 12.4% relative improvement.

t: GraphRAG-Router: Learning Cost-Efficient Routing over GraphRAGs and LLMs with Reinforcement Learning
a: East China Normal University and New York University Shanghai
ab: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) has recently emerged as a powerful paradigm for knowledge-intensive question answering, especially for tasks that require structured evidence organization and multi-hop reasoning. However, existing GraphRAG systems are typically built in a one-size-fits-all manner, relying on a fixed retrieval framework and a single, often large and costly, generator LLM for all queries. This static design limits their ability to adapt to the complexity of varying questions and often incurs unnecessary computational cost. To fill in the gap, we propose GraphRAG-Router, a cost-efficient framework that adopts a hierarchical routing strategy to coordinate heterogeneous GraphRAGs and generator LLMs. Specifically, GraphRAG-Router is first warmed up through supervised fine-tuning and then optimized with a two-stage reinforcement learning procedure, whose second stage introduces a curriculum cost-aware reward to encourage difficulty-aware and economical generator allocation. Extensive experiments on six general-domain and multi-hop QA benchmarks show that GraphRAG-Router consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, reducing the overuse of large LLMs by nearly 30% while maintaining strong generalization capability.

t: Negation Without Confusion: Decomposing Bias and Recomposing Style in Text Embeddings for Negation-Aware Image Generation
a: Seoul National University, Seoul National University and Yonsei University
ab: Negation-aware image generation remains challenging for text-to-image diffusion models, which often struggle with negation due to implicit linguistic biases that are deeply entangled within text representations. As a result, bias-aligned semantics frequently dominate over intended negative constraints. To overcome this limitation, we propose a simple training-free method of Decompose and RecOmpose text embedding (DeRO), which constructs a semantic-preserving subspace and a bias subspace using auxiliary prompts and performs semantic disentanglement based on bidirectional SVD. By decomposing entangled representations and selectively recomposing disentangled semantic components, DeRO realigns text representations toward intended negation semantics while restoring residual stylistic features to preserve semantic fidelity and image quality. As a model-agnostic inference-time framework operating solely on text representations, DeRO can be seamlessly applied to diverse diffusion architectures, including both U-Net and DiT based models. Extensive experiments on both object- and concept-level negation demonstrate consistent improvements in negation-aware image generation, achieving stronger text-image alignment, better semantic fidelity, and higher human preference scores.

t: CMIE: Cross-Modal Interaction Erasure for MLLM Safety Unlearning via Counterfactual Localization and Subspace Nullification
ab: Safety unlearning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) fails when it treats danger as an object, topic, or prompt template. A useful MLLM must still recognize risky visual evidence and answer benign educational or preventive questions about the same content. The safety-critical target is narrower: the post-fusion interaction that converts risky visual evidence and unsafe textual intent into actionable harmful assistance. Existing refusal-oriented and unlearning objectives reach this mechanism only indirectly, widening refusal boundaries or leaving recoverable multimodal harmful pathways. We propose CMIE, Cross-Modal Interaction Erasure, a mechanism-level method that directly treats the harmful image-text interaction as the object of erasure. CMIE first estimates harmful interaction directions with intent-matched counterfactual contrasts that cancel unimodal main effects. It then localizes behaviorally active post-fusion layers and estimates a safe-whitened low-rank harmful subspace. A closed-form minimum-distortion weight edit erases this subspace, and projection-constrained recovery restores benign utility without rewriting erased directions. Across SafeEraser, VLGuard, and MSSBench, CMIE achieves the best overall mean rank and outperforms strong baselines on multiple safety, utility, visual selectivity, and paired-context metrics. Warning: This paper contains examples of harmful language and images, and reader discretion is recommended.

t: MemWM: Memory-Augmented Text-Based World Model
a: Huawei Technologies Ltd. and Technische Universität Berlin
Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München and Huawei Technologies Ltd.
Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München and Siemens Corporate Research
ab: World models are increasingly used to support planning in agents by predicting how environment states evolve in response to agent actions. Yet fluent next-state predictions can still omit task-critical facts, corrupt product attributes, or apply incorrect transition rules. To address such systematic prediction errors, we introduce MemWM, a memory-augmented text-based world model. MemWM uses world memory, a curated memory bank of transition rules, state caches, and hard-to-predict facts, to condition next-state imagination. We evaluate factual state preservation with Structured State Fidelity (SSF), which scores predicted states through benchmark-specific facts and fields. Compared with SFT, memory-augmented training improves SSF by up to 206.3%. In the full planning setting, we keep the policy model frozen and provide policy-side world skill: retrieved task-level skills and step-wise corrective guidance for action selection. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, memory-augmented agents improve downstream success over an SFT-trained world-model agent, with up to a 65.4% relative gain. Sensitivity analyses further show that retrieved memory improves task success and efficiency under different memory and action-budget settings.

t: Tracing Multilingual Representations in LLMs with Cross-Layer Transcoders
a: Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, Max-Planck Institute
EuroSafeAI and University of Toronto & Vector Institute
ELLIS Institute and Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, Max-Planck Institute
ab: Multilingual Large Language Models (LLMs) can process many languages, yet how they internally represent this diversity remains unclear. Do they form shared multilingual representations with language-specific decoding, and if so, why do multilingual performance gaps persist? To address this question, we train models on different multilingual mixtures and analyze their internal mechanisms using Cross-Layer Transcoders (CLTs) and Attribution Graphs. Our results reveal a consistent three-phase structure across models: early layers encode language-specific information, middle layers converge to highly shared multilingual representations, and final layers re-specialize for language-specific decoding.Training models without English produces the same shared multilingual structures, suggesting that these representations emerge independently of English dominance. We further show that decoding relies on a small set of high-frequency late-layer features that linearly encode language identity from earlier layers, and that intervening on these features allows one language to be suppressed and another substituted. Finally, through a Model-Diffing experiment, we show that non-English failures arise from weak late-layer decoding features, weak middle-layer clusters, and tokenizer fragmentation that forces early layers to specialize in word reassembly. Finetuning strengthens these features and their connections, improving token assembly and language-specific decoding, providing a mechanistic explanation for multilingual performance gaps.

t: MobQA: A Benchmark Dataset for Semantic Understanding of Human Mobility Data through Question Answering
a: The University of Tokyo, Tokyo Institute of Technology
ab: This paper presents MobQA, a benchmark dataset designed to evaluate the semantic understanding capabilities of large language models (LLMs) for human mobility data through natural language question answering. While existing models predict human movement patterns well, their ability to interpret underlying reasons or semantic meaning remains unclear. To address this gap, we annotated 14,260 trajectory points from the GeoLife dataset with 30,703 semantic labels covering points of interest, mobility modes, and visit reasons, grounding semantics-dependent questions and reference answers. Building on these annotations, MobQA provides 5,800 question–answer pairs from daily and weekly GPS trajectories, spanning factual retrieval, multiple-choice semantic inference, and free-form interpretive explanation. Our evaluation of major LLMs reveals strong performance on factual retrieval but notable limits in semantic reasoning and explanation, with trajectory length substantially impacting effectiveness. These findings demonstrate both achievements and limitations of recent LLMs for semantic mobility understanding.

t: Adaptive Reasoning for Efficient Generative Retrieval
a: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Computing Technolgy, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy
ab: Generative retrieval (GR) retrieves documents by directly generating document identifiers (DocIDs) from queries using a sequence-to-sequence model. Recent reasoning-enhanced GR methods improve retrieval effectiveness by generating intermediate reasoning before DocID decoding. However, they typically apply reasoning uniformly to all queries, even though many queries can already be handled effectively through direct DocID decoding. This introduces unnecessary token generation and retrieval latency when reasoning provides little additional benefit. In this work, we propose Generative Retrieval with Adaptive Reasoning (GEAR), a retrieval framework that dynamically allocates reasoning computation based on query-specific needs. Instead of treating reasoning as a fixed pre-retrieval procedure, GEAR learns when to reason, what retrieval-oriented context to generate, and when to transition from free-form generation to constrained DocID decoding. This adaptive behavior is implemented through a learnable retrieval transition policy optimized jointly for retrieval quality and reasoning cost. Experiments on NQ, MS MARCO, and TREC DL 2022 show that GEAR maintains retrieval effectiveness comparable to strong reasoning-enhanced GR methods while substantially reducing reasoning overhead, triggering non-trivial reasoning for only 37.1% of queries and reducing both generated tokens and retrieval latency.

t: What Matters for Aggressive Decoding-Time KV Eviction? Temporal Aggregation and Ranking Preservation
a: Language Technology, Universität Hamburg and Alibaba Group
ab: Decoding-time KV cache compression research focuses heavily on designing better token scoring functions, while the temporal rule that aggregates scores across decode steps is often treated as an implementation detail. Under aggressive KV compression, we find that exponential-moving-average (EMA) aggregation makes approximately order-preserving scorer modifications largely indistinguishable at the eviction-set level. Value-norm and entropy variants remain highly correlated with attention and produce nearly unchanged retention sets, whereas KeyDiff, key norm, recency, and a learned scorer alter the ranking and degrade substantially. We associate this stability with the evaluated aggregation, which couples layer weighting and temporal retention. Building on this observation, we introduce InertiaKV, an EMA-based decoding-time eviction method, and InertiaKV-Lazy, its periodic-refresh variant, which yields 1.34–1.46× decode throughput relative to full refresh InertiaKV. We also study Score-Free decoding as a separate empirical operating point: it scores the full context once at the first decode step, freezes that ranking, and incurs an average quality change of +0.03 while removing all subsequent scoring. Across six open-weight backbones and the LongBench, LongBench-v2, and RULER benchmarks, the results identify temporal aggregation and ranking preservation as distinct, consequential design factors; they do not imply that scoring quality is irrelevant in general.

t: Grounding LLM Agent Intent in Multi-Module Environments with Executable Action Programs
ab: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly expected to interact with external environments rather than only generate text. A key challenge in this process is to accurately and efficiently ground high-level agent intents into valid executable action sequences, especially when the environment consists of multiple interacting modules. To address this challenge, we introduce executable action programs (EAPs), a restricted Python-based intermediate representation between textual agent intents and structured environment-module action calls, which leverages the expressive power of Python to explicitly represent complex behavioral sequences, their branching relationships, and cross-module data dependencies. Based on this representation, we implement EAPRouter, which generates, validates, executes, and reuses EAPs through an agent-EAP interface and a lightweight environment module integration protocol. We evaluate EAPRouter on real agent-environment interaction traces from social simulation, a demanding application scenario with multi-agent, multi-module, and repeated interaction patterns. Experiments show that EAPRouter achieves a 60.0% grounding success rate with Kimi-K2-Instruct, outperforming the SOTA function-calling baseline by 31.6%. It also improves over the strongest baselines by 11.5%-25.4% on GLM-4.7, Claude Opus 4.5, and Gemini 2.5 Flash, with smaller gains on less code-capable models. On the cross-domain NESTFUL v2 benchmark, EAPRouter matches ReAct’s executable accuracy (83.8% vs. 84.9%) while reducing LLM calls, tokens, and execution time by about 80%. EAP pre-generation further handles over 70% of interaction requests, cache reuse covers 66.5% of the remaining ones, and safety validation blocks all tested unsafe payloads and prompt-injection attempts. The code is available at https://github.com/tsinghua-fib-lab/EAPRouter.

t: MERIT: Matching Expertise via Rubric-Informed Training for Reviewer Assignment
ab: Matching submissions with suitable reviewers at scale is a growing challenge for major venues, yet existing approaches either rely on coarse proxy signals that conflate general relatedness with true suitability, or require expensive human annotations that are difficult to scale for training. We propose MERIT, a two-stage framework that bridges this gap by converting criterion-level expertise matching into scalable suitability supervision. In the first stage, we train a reviewer assessor via reinforcement learning to identify the expertise dimensions a paper requires, match them against the reviewer’s prior work, and produce a suitability decision, with rewards provided by an LLM judge guided by paper-specific expertise rubrics. In the second stage, we distill the assessor’s predictions into an embedding-based retriever for efficient large-scale assignment. Experiments show that our 4B reviewer assessor outperforms larger general-purpose LLMs on suitability classification, and the resulting retriever achieves state-of-the-art performance across LR-Bench and the CMU Gold dataset. Our code is available at https://github.com/Luli3220/MERIT.

t: Is Memorization Context-Sensitive? Prefix-Based Extraction Beyond Isolated Prefixes
ab: Large language models (LLMs) can expose memorized training sequences under prefix-based extraction: given a prefix from a training example, the model may assign high probability to the original continuation. In deployed systems, however, prefixes are rarely evaluated in isolation. They often appear together with instructions, retrieved documents, or other task-specific context, as in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). This raises a basic question: does contextual conditioning reduce memorization, or does it change which memorized samples become exposed? We study this question through paired item-level measurements of probabilistic suffix extraction. For each prefix-suffix pair, we score the same target suffix under an empty prompt and under retrieved contexts of varying relevance, across three open-weight instruction-tuned models. We find that context does not simply erase memorization. Instead, extractable memorization consists of a context-robust core and a context-sensitive boundary. Many samples that are extractable without context remain extractable under retrieved context, especially as prefix length increases. At the same time, context mainly affects marginal samples near the extraction threshold: it suppresses some exposures, but also enables new ones that are missed by prefix-only evaluation. These findings qualify the view that RAG reduces memorization risk. Context can lower aggregate extraction by suppressing boundary cases, yet robustly extractable samples persist, and context-enabled extractability remains security-relevant.

t: ArtifactsBench: Bridging the Visual-Interactive Gap in LLM Code Generation Evaluation
a: University of Science and Technology of China
ab: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly generate executable visual artifacts, yet established code benchmarks largely overlook the visual fidelity and interaction behavior that shape user experience. We introduce ArtifactsBench, a benchmark and automated multimodal evaluation framework for visual code generation. The framework executes each artifact and records three staged screenshots—before, during, and after a scripted interaction—then scores the evidence and source code with a checklist-guided Multimodal LLM (MLLM) referee. ArtifactsBench contains 1,825 tasks across nine domains and evaluates more than 30 LLMs. On a 280-query, six-model expert study, three staged screenshots yield 90.95% referee–human Pair ACC. Across the models shared with WebDev Arena, ArtifactsBench reaches 94.4% normalized Footrule consistency with that public human-preference ranking. We release the benchmark, evaluation harness, and baseline results at https://artifactsbenchmark.github.io/.

t: MM-VeriRubric: Verifiable Evidence-Grounded Rubrics for Multimodal Reward Models
a: University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: Reward modeling is essential for multimodal alignment, yet most existing reward models only provide outcome reward, which is sparse and fails to capture human preferences. Rubrics can provide structured and fine grained evaluation signals, but building effective rubrics for multimodal tasks is challenging. In this work, we propose **MM-VeriRubric**, a framework for scalable construction of training data for multimodal rubric generation and rubric-based reward models. To better use visual evidence in images, we introduce task-aware visual clue extraction, which makes rubric generation more grounded in task-relevant visual information. MM-VeriRubric then generates evidence-grounded rubrics and constructs rubric-aligned rejected responses with controlled error dimensions, enabling the quality of each rubric to be verified through consistency checking. The verified data are used to train both a rubric generator and a rubric-based reward model. Experiments on multimodal reward model benchmarks and downstream Best of N tasks show that MM-VeriRubric improves preference judgment (+16.4% on VL-RewardBench) and provides more interpretable and diagnostic reward signals for multimodal alignment (+13.1% on MMMU-Pro using Best of 5 selection). Code is available at: https://github.com/TraceLite-AI/MM-VeriRubric.

t: Entity tracking emerges in sub-billion parameter language models and exceeds human performance in naturalistic narratives
a: University of Warsaw and IDEAS Research Institute
The Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics and University of Amsterdam
ab: Understanding language requires tracking entities across discourse - i.e., knowing where things are and how they change, even when not explicitly stated. Whether language models perform such tracking in a human-like fashion remains unclear, in part because existing evaluations rely on artificial tasks, far removed from natural language comprehension, and lack comparisons to humans. Here, we evaluate entity tracking in both language models and humans (N=48) using naturalistic narratives at multiple levels of complexity. In humans, we find that entity tracking degrades specifically with narrative complexity, not narrative length. In language models, we find that human-level entity tracking is already present at 410 million parameters - well below the multi-billion parameter, code-specialised models identified by prior work - and improves with scale, with contemporary models far exceeding human performance. Together, these results demonstrate that entity tracking, a core component of language understanding, emerges at model scales far smaller than previously thought.

t: Evaluating Time Awareness and Cross-modal Active Perception of Large Models via 4D Escape Room Task
ab: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress toward unified Omni models that integrate language, vision, and audio. However, existing environments largely focus on 2D or 3D visual context and vision-language tasks, offering limited support for temporally dependent auditory signals and selective cross-modal integration, where different modalities may provide complementary or interfering information, which are essential capabilities for realistic multimodal reasoning. As a result, whether models can actively coordinate modalities and reason under time-varying, irreversible conditions remains underexplored. To this end, we introduce EscapeCraft-4D, a customizable 4D environment for assessing selective cross-modal perception and time awareness in Omni models. It incorporates trigger-based auditory sources, temporally transient evidence, and location-dependent cues, requiring agents to perform spatio-temporal reasoning and proactive multimodal integration under time constraints. Building on this environment, we curate a benchmark to evaluate corresponding abilities across powerful models. Evaluation results suggest that models struggle with modality bias, and reveal significant gaps in current model’s ability to integrate multiple modalities under time constraints. Further in-depth analysis uncovers how multiple modalities interact and jointly influence model decisions in complex multimodal reasoning environments.

t: Athena: Vulnerability-Affected Library Identification via Knowledge Graph Completion
a: University of Sydney, University of Sydney
Hanoi University of Science and Technology
Hanoi University of Science and Technology
Singapore University of Technology and Design
ab: A single vulnerability in a widely used library can cascade through millions of dependent applications, yet more than half of vulnerability database entries contain missing or incorrect affected-library information. Existing automated approaches neglect the relational structure of vulnerability databases, treating identification as an isolated text retrieval problem. In this paper, we propose Athena, the first graph-based approach for vulnerability-affected library identification. Athena models vulnerability databases as a knowledge graph and reformulates the identification problem as knowledge graph completion (KGC). It comprises three key modules: a Modeling module that constructs a security knowledge graph integrating CVEs, libraries, CWE weakness types, CPE products, and software ecosystems; a Completion module that applies a modular KGC backbone to predict missing affected libraries for a given CVE via link prediction; and a Re-ranking module that retrieves KGC candidates and rescores them using a fine-tuned LLM augmented with knowledge graph embeddings, jointly leveraging structural and textual information. Our experiments on VulLib demonstrate that Athena significantly outperforms four state-of-the-art baselines, achieving a 32% improvement in Avg. F1 over the best baseline (i.e., VulLibGen). Notably, our KGC backbone with only 110M parameters already surpasses VulLibGen’s best configuration at 7B parameters, demonstrating the effectiveness of graph-based modeling; the re-ranking module then provides substantial further gains, consistently outperforming the best baseline across all evaluated LLM backbones.

t: Surfacing Program Structure with Auxiliary Signals for Low-Resource Code Translation
a: University of Edinburgh, University of Edinburgh
ab: LLMs are extremely good code translators, except when it matters most: translating from low-resource to high-resource programming languages. The reason may lie in the fact that code translation relies on superficial lexical cues rather than on exploiting the deeper, language-agnostic program structure. We propose BoJac (Bohm–Jacopini), a novel commenting approach that pushes LLMs to exploit program structure by verbalizing structured programming principles in a guided natural language format. By using structure, BoJac enhances the ability to translate low-resource to-high-resource code. Using equivalent code benchmarks across multiple language pairs, we compare BoJac against several forms of auxIliary guidance provided alongside the source code: synthetic free-form chain-of comments, abstract syntax tree, and I/O Traces. To disentangle structural understanding from identifier-level matching, we repeat all experiments under name mangling and extend the same comparison to LoRA Fine-tuning on signal-augmented training sets. Our results show that the strongest gains come from auxiliary signals expressed in natural language, particularly when they explicitly encode structural and computational-level properties of the source code as in BoJac. While purely structural representations appear less effective, hybrid approaches such as BoJac, which convey structural and paradigm-level information through formalised natural language, emerge as a promising direction.

t: Cross-Centaur: Modeling Individual Decision-Making Across Psychological Tasks with Language Models
a: The University of Tokyo, Tokyo Institute of Technology
ab: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as computational models of human behavior. Recent models such as Centaur have advanced this goal by fine-tuning LLMs on trial-by-trial decisions from psychological experiments. However, existing large-scale behavioral datasets do not link the same participants across different tasks, so these models learn population-level regularities but are not trained to model individual-level regularities across tasks. We introduce Cross-Psych-101, a dataset of 591 participants and 261,551 valid decisions across 12 Bandit, Tradeoff, Structure, and Social tasks. We train Cross-Centaur to predict a participant’s target-task actions from a target-task description and the source-task description paired with the same participant’s source-task behavior. Cross-Centaur outperforms off-the-shelf LLMs and Centaur on held-out participants, both within and across tasks. Probing analyses suggest that its hidden states encode participant-level behavioral tendencies that transfer across tasks. These results highlight the potential of cross-task individual-level data for predicting human decision-making with language models. Cross-Pysch-101 is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/HikaruAsano/cross-psych-101.
