Second, we construct the Latent-Chain via Induction-Supervision Masking to ensure semantic compactness and sufficiency. Third, we employ Latent-Optim with stochastic Gumbel-Softmax to guide the model toward generalizable solutions. Empirical results demonstrate that Latent-SFT consistently outperforms explicit SFT across six mathematical benchmarks (e.g., GSM8k, AIME24) while achieving a 2.7x to 5.5x reduction in reasoning length. Analysis confirms that our method effectively captures a superposition of diverse reasoning trajectories rather than merely compressing a single path.

t: Genesis: Visual Augmentation Primitives for Multimodal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
a: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Wuhan AI Research and Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: Recent multimodal large language models achieve promising results on visual reasoning tasks, approaching human-level performance on existing STEM benchmarks. However, these capabilities degrade on complex real-world scenes. We identify two intertwined causes: chain-of-thought reasoning remains largely confined to the linguistic space, and training data rarely requires each step to be anchored in visual evidence. In this work, we introduce Visual Augmentation Primitives, which leverages high-quality instruction-guided generation models to synthesize diverse photorealistic training samples and construct coherent multimodal reasoning chains throughout the generation process, requiring models to unify visual perception with logical reasoning at every step. We further introduce multimodal chain-of-thought rubric-based reinforcement learning, which extends rubric-based reward design from the text-only domain to visual reasoning, scoring intermediate reasoning steps for logical validity, completeness, and consistency, and construct the UNREAL benchmark to systematically evaluate visual reasoning on hyperrealistic scenes across controllable difficulty levels. Experiments show that a 4B model built on this framework surpasses 8B baselines, with the approach scaling consistently to 32B across visual reasoning and VQA tasks. All models, data, and code will be publicly released.

t: KV-Retriever: Aligning KV Cache Eviction with Downstream Task Loss
a: Beijing University of Post and Telecommunication
ab: The prohibitive memory footprint of the Key-Value (KV) cache imposes a critical bottleneck for efficient long-context LLM serving. Current eviction methods, ranging from attention-based heuristics to recent learnable approaches, rely on scoring criteria decoupled from the downstream task performance that ultimately matters. To address this, we introduce KV-Retriever, a layer-wise learnable importance scoring module directly optimized by the end-to-end downstream task loss. We demonstrate that aligning the scoring objective with the actual task signal—rather than intermediate proxies such as attention statistics or oracle labels—yields a fundamentally more accurate notion of token importance. Functioning as a lightweight, plug-and-play module with only \sim0.01% additional parameters on a frozen 8B backbone, KV-Retriever is compatible with diverse host eviction frameworks. Extensive experiments show that, for each backbone, one trained retriever can be reused unchanged across multiple KV cache compression architectures and delivers consistent improvements on LongBench, LongBench-v2, and RULER. KV-Retriever requires one-time supervised training with golden answers; “plug-and-play” refers to deployment into otherwise unchanged host eviction frameworks, not to training-free adaptation. Our code is available at https://github.com/Taylor-Gavel/kv_retriever.

t: Model Interruption Bench: Evaluating Real-Time Error Correction in Full-Duplex Voice Agents
ab: Full-duplex voice agents can now listen and speak at the same time, yet no benchmark asks whether they can further exploit this capability—proactively interrupting a user mid-utterance to correct a content error. We introduce the Model Interruption Bench (MIB), the first benchmark for real-time, content-aware error correction in voice agents. MIB frames the task as proactive correction of spoken chain-of-thought math: ~600 step-annotated solutions derived from GSM8K, played to the model under a streaming protocol that scores whether it interrupts in the right window with the right correction. To localize failure, we pair the full-duplex streaming evaluation with turn-based ablations that isolate error detection, and provide an automated LLM-judge pipeline with backchannel filtering and a fine-grained FP/FN sub-type taxonomy to analyze failure cases. Evaluating six voice agents, Freeze-Omni, Gemini 2.5/3.1 Flash Live, GPT-4o Realtime, Moshi, and PersonaPlex, we uncover a striking detection–interruption gap: the three most detection-capable models recognize 59–67% of errors in the turn-based condition but reach below 10% mid-speech TP% when forced to interrupt in real time. The bottleneck is not understanding errors but acting on them in time. Three behavioral archetypes emerge from the sub-type breakdown—passive, post-hoc responder, and aggressive—exposing real-time error interruption as a concrete open challenge for full-duplex voice agents.

t: What Transfers from Text to Vision? Capability Scaling Laws and Transfer Dynamics for VLMs
ab: Choosing the right large language model (LLM) backbone is the most consequential decision when building a vision-language model (VLM), yet it remains fundamentally unprincipled: compute-based scaling laws fail to generalize across model families, and no framework exists for directly predicting VLM performance before training begins. We propose the Capability-Driven Multimodal Scaling Law, the first cross-family framework that predicts VLM benchmark accuracy from directly observable textual capability. Given a low-dimensional capability score S extracted from LLM textual benchmarks via PCA, we model VLM performance as a function of S, with a per-backbone transfer rate A and an absorption rate B that quantifies data-scaling efficiency. To fit and validate the framework, we train over 150 VLMs on 34 LLMs spanning 7 model families under a strictly controlled recipe. Evaluations on more than 200 textual and 50 multimodal benchmarks show that the law accurately extrapolates transfer rate from models up to 8B parameters to 72B-scale backbones, predicts full VLM training trajectories with high fidelity, and generalizes to entirely held-out model families. Beyond the scaling law, our analysis surfaces actionable insights: certain textual benchmarks negatively correlate with multimodal performance, exposing latent benchmark-gaming behavior; base LLMs outperform instruction-tuned counterparts as VLM backbones due to higher absorption rates and lower data-scaling decay; and different model families occupy distinct positions in the transfer–absorption space. The framework turns backbone selection from costly empirical sweeps into a principled, quantitative decision.

t: INTENT-AS-A-TOOL Makes it Easy to Track Agentic Misalignment
ab: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed as autonomous agents, safety failures increasingly involve consequential actions. We study agentic misalignment, where agents take harmful actions under goal conflicts and pressures. Using chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring, we find that harmful execution is often preceded by intent signals in reasoning. However, post-hoc CoT labels are too coarse to show how intent changes during generation. We introduce INTENT-AS-A-TOOL, an approach that adds intent-targeted tools to give the model a dedicated channel for expressing commitment to a target behavior. The probability of calling an intent tool provides a judge-free, fine-grained signal of the model’s tendency to pursue that behavior. Our results show that INTENT-AS-A-TOOL complements CoT monitoring, expands post-hoc CoT labels into dense trajectories, and identifies critical steps for online intervention. These findings suggest that action preferences are useful for tracking agentic misalignment during reasoning. Our code and data are accessible: https://github.com/RebeccaZhang22/intent-as-a-tool.

t: Beyond Superficial Unlearning: Sharpness-Aware Robust Erasure of Hallucinations in Multimodal LLMs
a: Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
University of Science and Technology of China and Institute of Dataspace, Hefei Comprehensive National Science Center
Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
ab: Multimodal LLMs are powerful but prone to object hallucinations, which describe non-existent entities and harm reliability. While recent unlearning methods attempt to mitigate this, we identify a critical flaw: structural fragility. We empirically demonstrate that standard erasure achieves only superficial suppression, trapping the model in sharp minima where hallucinations catastrophically resurge after lightweight relearning. To ensure geometric stability, we propose Sharpness-Aware Robust Erasure (SARE), which casts unlearning as a targeted min-max optimization problem and leverages a targeted Sharpness-Aware Minimization (Targeted-SAM) mechanism to explicitly flatten the loss landscape around hallucinated concepts. By suppressing hallucinations under simulated worst-case parameter perturbations, our framework ensures robust removal stable against weight shifts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SARE outperforms baselines in erasure efficacy while preserving general generation quality. Crucially, it maintains persistent hallucination suppression against relearning and parameter updates, validating the effectiveness of geometric stabilization.

t: Steering Vector Fields for Context-Aware Inference-Time Control in Large Language Models
ab: Steering vectors (SVs) offer a lightweight way to control large language models (LLMs) at inference time by shifting hidden activations, providing a practical middle ground between prompting and fine-tuning. Yet SVs can be unreliable in practice. Some concepts are unsteerable, and even when steering helps on average it can backfire for a non-trivial fraction of inputs. Reliability also degrades in long-form generation and multi-attribute steering. We take a geometric view of these failures. A static SV applies the same update vector everywhere in representation space, implicitly assuming that the concept-improving direction is constant across contexts. When the locally effective direction varies with the current activation, a single global vector can become misaligned, which yields weak or reversed effects. Guided by this perspective, we propose Steering Vector Fields (SVF), which learns a differentiable concept scoring function whose local gradient defines the steering direction at each activation, making interventions explicitly context-dependent. This formulation supports coordinated multi-layer interventions in a shared, aligned concept space, and enables efficient long-form and multi-attribute control within a unified framework. Across multiple LLMs and steering tasks, SVF delivers stronger and more reliable control, improving the practicality of inference-time steering. The code is available at https://github.com/lab-flair/SVF.git.

t: TETHER: Training-Free, Elastic, ToC-Anchored Hierarchy Extraction and Recovery in Design-Driven Long Documents
a: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics
Southwestern University of Finance and Economics
Southwestern University of Finance and Economics
Southwestern University of Finance and Economics
Southwestern University of Finance and Economics
Southwestern University of Finance and Economics
ab: Converting complex documents into structured knowledge constitutes the critical infrastructure urgently required for deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) in downstream research. However, blind to the Table of Contents (ToC) as a macro-structure, existing bottom-up paradigms rely on localized visual cues, inducing heuristic fragility in high-entropy layouts where visual prominence decouples from logical depth; meanwhile, direct LLM extraction lacks spatial grounding, triggering hallucinations in long contexts. To address this, we introduce TETHER, a training-free framework that elevates the ToC from discarded noise to a vital structural prior, enabling robust adaptation across design-driven long documents. TETHER operates via a two-stage neuro-symbolic mechanism: first, it constructs a document skeleton from the raw ToC using a Large Multimodal Model (LMM) empowered by spatio-semantic constraints; second, it employs an anchor-based alignment strategy to tether content blocks to this skeleton, effectively resolving boundary ambiguities. Evaluated across a multilingual benchmark of ESG reports, product manuals, and annual reports, TETHER delivers highly precise, state-of-the-art (SOTA) zero-shot hierarchy recovery, outperforming deep hierarchical recovery models, dedicated parsers, and general-purpose LMMs. Moreover, stress tests highlight TETHER’s resilience to sparse omissions and textual noise, demonstrating that its precise semantic alignment is fundamentally anchored in topological and depth fidelity. Crucially, ablations confirm the framework’s architectural irreducibility, while achieving 90% token reduction and drastic speedups over end-to-end baselines, establishing a compelling equilibrium between structural precision and deployment scalability.

t: HOMURA: Taming the Sand-Glass for Time-Constrained LLM Translation via Reinforcement Learning
ab: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable strides in multilingual translation but are hindered by a systemic cross-lingual verbosity bias, rendering them unsuitable for strict time-constrained tasks like subtitling and dubbing. Current prompt-engineering approaches struggle to resolve this conflict between semantic fidelity and rigid temporal feasibility. To bridge this gap, we first introduce Sand-Glass, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate translation under syllable-level duration constraints. Furthermore, we propose Homura, a reinforcement learning framework that explicitly optimizes the trade-off between semantic preservation and temporal compliance. By employing a constrained reinforcement learning objective featuring a novel dynamic syllable-ratio reward, Homuraeffectively "tames" the output length. Experimental results demonstrate that Homura significantly outperforms strong baselines, achieving precise length control that respects linguistic density hierarchies without compromising semantic adequacy.

t: Discourse-Aware Policy Analysis with Argumentation: A Hybrid LLM–Symbolic Framework for Disaster Governance
ab: Policy documents shape governance outcomes, but their reasoning is often implicit, with tensions between participatory commitments and managerial control rarely stated directly. Existing computational approaches to policy discourse cannot express the frame-mediated relations that drive these tensions, where one argument narrows or instrumentalizes another, and end-to-end summarization by large language models offers little structure that domain experts can inspect or contest. To address this, we present **D-APA** (Discourse-aware Argumentative Policy Analysis), a hybrid LLM–symbolic pipeline that operationalizes critical discourse policy analysis as a quantitative argumentation graph. Given a policy text, an LLM first extracts its arguments, where each argument is classified into a *deliberative* or *managerial* frame and scanned for discourse features such as agency type and verb class. Deterministic rules over these features then connect the arguments through four frame-mediated relation subtypes, namely *agency reduction*, *agenda shift*, *instrumental support*, and *normative support*. Finally, argumentation semantics propagates linguistically grounded base scores through the resulting graph, yielding a final strength for every argument. We release a novel dataset of 100 sub-documents of disaster-risk-reduction policy from the USA, UK, Canada, and Australia, and show that our pipeline produces argument graphs that are accurate, interpretable, and consistent across jurisdictions.

t: KnowGPO: Knowledge-Grouped Policy Optimization for Search Agents
ab: Deep search agents solve knowledge-intensive tasks through long-horizon, multi-turn interactions, where assigning credit to individual search decisions is fundamentally difficult. Outcome-based reinforcement learning provides only a single terminal reward shared across an entire trajectory. Recent process-supervision methods aim to assign credit at finer granularity, but they typically anchor credit to either surface-level trajectory states or model-internal signals, both of which become unreliable in deep search where observations are heterogeneous and retrieved contexts are long and noisy. We propose KnowGPO, a reinforcement learning framework that aligns trajectories by the task-relevant knowledge they have acquired rather than by their surface observations. For each query, KnowGPO decomposes the information required to derive the answer into atomic knowledge conditions, and represents the state of a trajectory at each step by the subset of conditions it has satisfied. Trajectories sharing the same knowledge state are grouped for within-group comparison, and the incremental knowledge gain between consecutive steps serves as an environment-grounded process reward. Experiments on Xbench, BrowseComp-ZH, and GAIA show KnowGPO consistently outperforms outcome-only (GRPO) and process-supervision baselines (GiGPO, IGPO) by 3.8 to 4.2 points, with our 8B model rivaling or exceeding most 32B open-source systems. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/KnowGPO.

t: SMART: Sink-based Modality-Aware Redistribution of Transformer Attention
ab: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) often exhibit modality bias, where predictions over-rely on one modality while underutilizing others. However, the mechanism underlying modality bias remains poorly understood. In this work, we first introduce Banana-Counting, a controlled diagnostic dataset for measuring modality preference under cross-modal conflicts. Evaluations across diverse MLLMs reveal pervasive modality imbalance. Then, through attention analysis, we show that modality bias is strongly associated with imbalanced cross-modal attention allocation and modality-specific attention sinks that absorb redundant attention mass. Motivated by these findings, we propose SMART, an inference-time method that mitigates modality bias by redistributing redundant sink attention toward under-attended modalities. SMART consistently improves multimodal balance across model families. On Banana-Counting, it reduces the modality gap from 27.73 to 0.66 on LLaVA-v1.5-7B while improving balanced multimodal accuracy. Moreover, SMART generalizes effectively to downstream multimodal reasoning tasks without retraining or parameter updates.

t: KidnapRAG: A Black-Box Attack for Hijacking Reasoning in Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
ab: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are vulnerable to poisoning attacks that inject malicious documents into the retrieval process to manipulate model outputs. Recent Agentic RAG systems are more robust to such attacks because they iteratively perform retrieval and reasoning, allowing them to ignore weakly relevant poisoned documents and preserve the reasoning chain induced by the user query. However, existing attacks on Agentic RAG systems often assume white-box access to system prompts, reasoning traces, retrievers, or model parameters, limiting their applicability in realistic settings. In this paper, we study black-box poisoning attacks against Agentic RAG systems, where the attacker can only publish externally retrievable poisoned documents. We propose KidnapRAG, a sequential poisoning attack that hijacks the agent’s multi-step reasoning chain using three role-specific documents: Bait, Chain-Link, and Mal-Ins, which attract initial retrieval, induce query reformulation, and provide attacker-controlled evidence, respectively. Experiments across multiple Agentic RAG frameworks, LLM backbones, and benchmarks show that KidnapRAG consistently outperforms existing poisoning baselines under black-box conditions. Further analyses show that KidnapRAG progressively weakens the original retrieval intent, redirects retrieval behavior, and increases reliance on attacker-controlled evidence.

t: RAPA: Recursively Aligned Pathway Adaptation of Large Language Models
ab: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) adapts large language models (LLMs) by training only a small fraction of parameters. %Adapter-based approaches reduce compute per step but introduce practical overhead from the additional adapter path (e.g., extra kernel launches and activation storage). Adapter-based approaches reduce the number of trainable parameters, but introduce practical overhead from the additional adapter path (e.g., extra kernel launches and activation storage). Adapter-free approaches avoid this structural overhead by directly updating pretrained weights; however, random index selection can fragment the trainable subspace, while calibrated weight selection incurs extra cost, limiting accuracy or efficiency. We propose Recursively Aligned Pathway Adaptation (RAPA), an adapter-free PEFT method that forms index-consistent pathways through depth. RAPA follows two principles: (i) selecting balanced submatrices that maximize the number of weights alignable across layers, and (ii) recursively aligning these indices across layers and residual connections. In experiments, RAPA matches or surpasses strong PEFT baselines across most benchmarks while preserving adapter-free efficiency with minimal memory and compute overhead.

t: MemeArgs: Vision-Language Argument Mining in Persuasive Memes
ab: On today’s social media, many argumentative artifacts appear in mixed image-text format. Meanwhile, the argument mining community has seen much success in developing argument understanding technologies in text. In this work, we bridge that gap by studying vision-language argument (VLA) parsing: generating an argument graph that captures both the explicit and implicit components of a vision-language argument. To lay the groundwork for this task, we annotate MemeArgs, a corpus of argument graphs for 614 persuasive memes. We then propose an automatic evaluation protocol for VLA parsing that accommodates its generative nature and follows standard argument mining practice. Evaluating current general-purpose vision-language models, we found that they all failed to perform knowledge-grounded visual perception reliably, which distorts their understanding of the arguments. VLA parsing thus presents an exciting challenge for multimodal argument understanding.

t: Concepts Whisper: Spectral Anti-Concentration and the Dual Geometry of Transformer Representations
ab: We find that transformer concept representations systematically anti-concentrate in the spectral tail of the unembedding covariance, encoding word-level concepts in low-variance directions across a 17-model core suite and an expanded set of 22 semantic concept categories, with convergent replications from three independent extraction methods. Residual-stream difference-of-means vectors anti-concentrate in all 17 models (model-level one-sample t-test, p = 3.8e-9), and remain more tail-aligned than norm-matched random directions in 13 of 17; convergent support comes from sparse autoencoder (SAE) features (p = 4.5e-19 across concepts within a model) and linear probes on Llama and Qwen. We identify a dual geometry: activation-space concept directions anti-concentrate while static unembedding-row contrasts concentrate in high-variance directions (p < 10^-4). This investigation arose from testing whether the causal inner product of Park et al. (2024) aids cross-lingual concept transport; a matched-spectrum randomization across 17 models and four language pairs finds no evidence that Whitened Causal Alignment improves over spectral regularization alone (p = 0.95). Split-injection interventions, restricted to steering strengths at which both arms remain interpretable, show the predicted interference asymmetry in four of five models (paired Cohen’s d_z up to 1.19) with no significant reversal inside that regime, and POS-tag probing across eight models shows syntax preferentially encoded in the high-variance subspace in six of eight architectures, with a significant reversal in the Qwen 2.5 family. These results suggest transformers rotate semantic content into spectrally quiet regions during contextualized processing, where, in some architectures, interventions may reduce grammatical disruption relative to high-variance steering.

t: Seeing with You: Perception-Reasoning Co-evolution for Multimodal Reasoning
a: Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
ab: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has substantially enhanced the reasoning capabilities of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, existing RLVR approaches typically rely on outcome-driven optimization that updates both perception and reasoning using a shared reward based solely on the final answer. This shared reward blurs credit assignment, frequently improving reasoning patterns while failing to reliably enhance the accuracy of upstream visual evidence extraction. To address this perception bottleneck, we introduce PRCO (Perception-Reasoning Co-evolution), a dual-role RLVR framework with a shared policy. PRCO consists of two cooperative roles: an Observer that generates an evidence caption tailored to the question and a Solver that predicts the final answer based on this caption. Crucially, PRCO employs role-specific reward signals: the Solver is optimized using verifiable outcome rewards on the final answer, while the Observer receives a utility reward derived from the Solver’s downstream success. Extensive experiments across eight challenging multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that PRCO yields consistent improvements across model scales by over 7 points on average accuracy compared to the base model, outperforming prior open-source RL-tuned baselines.

t: Norms of Error Terms in Transformer Language Models Predict Human Reading Time Beyond Surprisal
ab: It is possible that expectation-based latency in reading time is caused by mechanistic latency in changing internal activation states to match observations; this is a primary motivation for predictive coding models (Ohams et al., 2026). This paper explores measurement of sentence processing effort that is based on the gradient signals of transformer language models during error backpropagation: the 2-norm of the gradient of surprisal w.r.t. the output of intermediate layers, i.e., the norm of the error terms at intermediate layers. Regression experiments on multiple human reading time datasets show that the norm of error terms at the output of intermediate layers of GPT-2 small add predictive power beyond baseline predictors including standard surprisal from the same model.

t: Beyond the Efficiency Paradox: Unlocking Multimodal Subspaces via Cumulative Information Span
a: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
ab: In real-world multimodal applications, different modalities often exhibit weakly aligned adaptation requirements, making it challenging for a shared adapter to effectively capture heterogeneous signals. Existing approaches typically use a unified low-rank adapter for concatenated multimodal representations, leading to competition among modality-specific adaptations and diminishing returns as the adapter rank increases. To address this limitation, we propose msLoRA, a modality-specific adaptation framework for efficient multimodal fine-tuning. msLoRA assigns independent low-rank adapters to different modalities, allowing them to capture specialized adaptation directions while maintaining efficient parameterization. Our theoretical analysis introduces the concept of cumulative information span, demonstrating that modality-specific adapters can expand the effective adaptation space and avoid the cross-modal disagreement typical of shared adapters. We evaluate msLoRA using multiple prominent open-source LLMs, including the Llama, Qwen, and Mistral families, across four multimodal tasks, showing consistent improvements in scalability and effectiveness for low-rank adaptation in multimodal LLMs. The source code is available at https://github.com/XiuzeZhou/msLoRA/.

t: GreenSwap: Verb Choice or Output Length? A Controlled Decomposition of Prompt-Level Energy Savings in LLM Inference
ab: Changing one word in a prompt can reduce large language model inference energy by up to 70%, but no prior work explains why. We introduce GreenSwap to find out. We run every prompt under three conditions: the original verb (C1), a swapped low-energy verb (C2), and the original verb with an explicit instruction to limit the response length (C3). Across three open-weight models, three task types, and 21,600 inferences, the short-answer instruction saves more energy and preserves higher quality than verb swapping in 7 of 9 settings. A token–energy correlation of r ≥ 0.998 shows that inference energy depends only on output length and not on which verb was used. Verb swapping saves energy only because it sometimes makes the model write less, and on long-form generation it backfires by producing a completely different and lower-quality response. Scoped to English instruction-tuned 7–8B models, our results show that telling the model how long to respond is simpler, more reliable, and more energy-efficient than curating verb lists.

t: Pruning Laws for Large Language Models
ab: Scaling up model parameters and training data consistently improves the performance of large language models (LLMs), but at the cost of rapidly growing memory and compute requirements, which makes deployment on resource-limited hardware infeasible. Model pruning, a widely used compression technique, reduces inference costs by removing redundant parameters. However, its impact on downstream performance remains unpredictable and is typically assessed only through costly empirical sweeps. To address this gap, we introduce pruning laws – simple and interpretable scaling relations that connect a pruned LLM’s post-pruning performance to its unpruned performance and pruning ratio. Across ten LLMs (1.3B–30B parameters), three pruning strategies (unstructured, width, and depth), and eight diverse tasks, we show that pruning laws achieve strong predictive accuracy (average extrapolation error <7%), reliably quantify performance degradation, and identify critical pruning thresholds beyond which recovery is infeasible. Moreover, we demonstrate that the same laws transfer universally across architectures, pruning methods, and even unseen models in zero-shot and one-shot setups. These results provide both researchers and practitioners with a principled framework to select pruning strategies, estimate safe pruning ratios without exhaustive tuning, and deploy LLMs efficiently under real-world compute and latency constraints.

t: Few-shot Semantic Recovery Attacks on Image Embeddings
ab: Image embeddings are an essential commodity in modern AI: stored at scale in vector databases, transferred between edge devices and cloud APIs, and traded as paid services. Image embeddings have been implicitly treated as anonymous—an assumption that has not been rigorously tested even as embedding services scale to billions of stored vectors. _We show this assumption breaks._ We propose **C**ross-modal **R**ecovery **A**ttack with **F**ew-shot **T**ransfer (**CRAFT**), a framework that recovers semantic meaning, including free-form captions and sensitive attributes. The attack focuses on the medical domain and facial features, targeting black-box image embeddings without reconstructing a single image in pixels and without any knowledge of the underlying model architecture, training data, or weights. **CRAFT** combines a public dual-encoder, a linear alignment learned from intercepted image-embedding pairs, and a fine-tuned embedding-to-text decoder; we further strengthen recovery with two augmentative techniques: cross-modal reranking against the attacker’s text encoder and chain-of-thought prompting on a diffusion-rendered low-fidelity reconstruction of the leaked embedding. Attacks succeed with as few as a single intercepted pair and transfer across five open-source and proprietary embedders. We disclose a privacy surface that current defenses cannot close. Every setting that preserves downstream utility also leaves the attack effective. Black-box image embeddings, as widely deployed in AI systems today, should not be treated as privacy-preserving artifacts.[We open source our code for reproducibility and further research: <https://github.com/siebeniris/CRAFT>.]

t: CRICO: A Certified Robustness Framework via Input-Dependent Covariance Optimization
a: Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
ab: Randomized smoothing provides certified robustness guarantees, but its direct application to text remains challenging due to the discrete, sparse, and semantically structured nature of textual inputs. We propose CRICO, an input-dependent covariance optimization framework for certified robustness in the text embedding space. CRICO estimates token-level decision influence in a black-box manner, making it readily extensible to LLMs. By adapting the certified ellipsoid to local decision structure, CRICO significantly enhances certified robustness. Experiments on multiple tasks demonstrate its effectiveness and broad applicability.

t: Beyond Consensus: Perspectivist Modeling and Evaluation of Annotator Disagreement in NLP
ab: Annotator disagreement is widespread in NLP, particularly for subjective and ambiguous tasks such as toxicity detection and stance analysis. While early approaches treated disagreement as noise to be removed, recent work increasingly models it as a meaningful signal reflecting variation in interpretation and perspective. This survey provides a unified view of disagreement-aware NLP methods. We first present a domain-agnostic taxonomy of the sources of disagreement spanning data, task, and annotator factors. We then synthesize modeling approaches using a common framework defined by prediction targets and pooling structure, highlighting a shift from consensus learning toward explicitly modeling disagreement, and toward capturing structured relationships among annotators. We review evaluation metrics for both predictive performance and annotator behavior, and noting that most fairness evaluations remain descriptive rather than normative. We conclude by identifying open challenges and future directions, including integrating multiple sources of variation, developing disagreement-aware interpretability frameworks, and grappling with the practical tradeoffs of perspectivist modeling.

t: A Gradient Perspective on RLVR Stability and Winner-Advantage Policy Optimization
a: Department of Computer Science, University of Toronto and Layer6 AI
ab: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves language-model reasoning, but GRPO-style optimization remains prone to collapse. We analyse this instability through token-level gradient dynamics, deriving a taxonomy that predicts how updates affect next-token probabilities and entropy. The taxonomy shows that stability depends jointly on the advantage sign and token distribution under the current policy. Motivated by this finding, we propose Winner Advantage Policy Optimization (WAPO), a simple online clipped policy-gradient objective that updates only on positive-advantage completions. Across mathematical reasoning and multi-hop QA benchmarks, WAPO improves training stability and matches or outperforms baselines across multiple model families. Full code can be found at https://github.com/layer6ai-labs/wapo.

t: Dreaming Up Authors: Factual Prevalence and LLM Hallucinations in Academic Authorship Attribution
ab: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used for question answering but are prone to hallucinations, yet the underlying causes, particularly the role of factual prevalence in training data, remain underexplored. In this work, we study this through academic authorship attribution, hypothesizing that hallucinations are more likely for less prevalent papers. Using citation count as a proxy for factual prevalence, we curate a dataset of 1.92 million papers across eight scientific disciplines with stratified samples by citation level. Experiments on three state-of-the-art LLMs confirm our hypothesis, revealing a robust inverse relationship between hallucination rate and citation count across all models and disciplines, with hallucination rates exceeding 98% for rarely cited papers and falling below 37% for highly cited ones. Our in-depth analysis further shows that these failures primarily reflect retrieval limitations rather than knowledge absence, and hidden-state probing of open-source models shows that factual prevalence is encoded in pre-generation representations, providing convergent mechanistic evidence for the prevalence-hallucination relationship.

t: When Facts Change: Probing LLMs on Evolving Knowledge with evolveQA
ab: LLMs often fail to handle temporal knowledge conflicts–contradictions that arise when facts evolve over time within their training data. Existing benchmarks often rely on structured sources such as Wikidata, where changes are directly exposed through versioned snapshots, and rarely account for differences in model knowledge cut-offs, limiting fair evaluation across LLMs released at different times. We introduce a novel framework for automatically constructing temporal knowledge probing benchmarks from unstructured, time-stamped corpora by discovering evolving knowledge through salient entities, concepts, and attributes; and using this structure to generate grounded questions with gold answers aligned to model cut-off dates. Using this framework, we construct **evolveQA**, spanning 3 domains: AWS service updates, Azure platform changes, and WHO Disease Outbreak News reports. Evaluating 12 open- and closed-source LLMs across 3 probing formats, we find performance drops of up to 31% on **evolveQA** compared to static knowledge questions, showing that LLMs struggle to recall temporally updated facts even when such knowledge is available in their parameters.

t: OVO-S-Bench: A Hierarchical Benchmark for Streaming Spatial Intelligence in Multimodal LLMs
a: Tsinghua University and Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory
Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
ab: Multimodal agents in robotics, AR, and autonomous driving must reason about places and layouts from continuous egocentric streams, often using evidence outside the current view. Existing benchmarks either evaluate offline over full videos or target events rather than spatial structure. We introduce OVO-S-Bench, a fully human-annotated benchmark for streaming spatial intelligence, comprising 1,680 questions over 348 source videos. Annotation involves 12 trained annotators (each also serving as a blind cross-reviewer) across roughly 804 person-hours of multi-round quality assurance. Each question carries a query timestamp and an evidence interval, and at evaluation, the model sees only the prefix preceding the query. Questions span four levels of increasing abstraction: instantaneous egocentric perception, spatiotemporal context tracking, generative spatial reasoning, and allocentric spatial mapping. Across 38 proprietary and open-source MLLMs, Gemini-3.1-Pro trails human experts evaluated under the same prefix-access protocol by 33 points (59.2 vs. 92.2), with allocentric spatial mapping as the dominant bottleneck. Notably, streaming and spatially fine-tuned MLLMs underperform their own backbones. We further find that chain-of-thought reasoning amplifies spatial errors when ungrounded in the stream. By exposing these limitations, OVO-S-Bench establishes a demanding testbed for next-generation streaming spatial MLLMs.

t: Compositional SVG Generation via VLM-Driven Hierarchical Semantic Parsing
a: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
ab: While Vision-Language Models (VLMs) excel at visual reasoning, generating structured, editable Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) remains a fundamental challenge. Existing pipelines predominantly yield flat, semantically agnostic collections of paths, where editing a single object requires manually identifying its constituent paths. To address this, we propose a VLM-driven agentic framework for semantic compositional SVG generation. Our pipeline recursively parses visual scenes into semantic and geometric hierarchies via top- down decomposition, visual grounding, and prompt-driven amodal occlusion recovery, ensuring each component is geometrically complete. Furthermore, we introduce the Semantic SVG Benchmark with human-annotated semantic groups and novel sub-component metrics (Semantic Recall/Precision, PERE) to explicitly evaluate structural compositionality and functional editability. Experiments show that our natively predicted structures surpass the upper bounds of existing flat-generation methods in both grouping quality and editability, while maintaining state-of-the-art visual fidelity.

t: The Trigger Is in the Embedding: Supervision-Free Discovery and Diagnosis of Universal Adversarial Triggers in Fact Verification
a: University of Modena and Reggio Emilia
ab: Despite their widespread adoption, the robustness of fact-checking models to adversarial perturbations remains underexplored. Existing approaches are model-specific and require gradient access or dataset-dependent optimization, with implications for generalization, efficiency, and semantic validity. We introduce FactFlip, a framework for analyzing robustness in claim verification models via universal adversarial triggers. FactFlip identifies perturbative trigger words through a lightweight, model-only procedure that ranks candidates by the alignment of their non-contextualized embeddings with class-specific decision directions, without labeled data or gradient access. Trigger discovery is decoupled from claim perturbation via an LLM-based perturb-and-verify pipeline that preserves semantic validity. Experiments show that FactFlip discriminates between strong and weak triggers, composes them constructively, and rivals fully supervised gradient-based baselines. We further show that FactFlip doubles as a diagnostic lens, surfacing socially salient model biases without any task-specific supervision.

t: HPP: Hierarchical Programmatic Probing for Long Video Understanding by Decoupling Perception and Reasoning
a: Queen Mary, University of London, BetterData Pte Ltd and Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
ab: Understanding long videos requires fine-grained perception and multi-step, higher-order reasoning over complex, long-range spatio-temporal dynamics. Vision-language models (VLMs) encode video frames into visual tokens and attempt to perform both perception and multi-step planning latently, within a single forward pass. This coupled formulation, however, is bottlenecked by the LLM’s limited capacity to discover and execute multi-step strategies in its latent representations. To address this bottleneck, we propose Hierarchical Programmatic Probing (HPP), a framework that decouples semantic perception from higher-order temporal reasoning by reformulating long video understanding as iterative, programmatic exploration of a hierarchically segmented video. Specifically, a coding-capable LLM plans and executes a multi-step strategy in an interactive coding environment, probing the video for information and invoking a VLM for localized perception on demand. To make probing tractable over long videos, we introduce three components: information-density-aware hierarchical segmentation, late-interaction semantic retrieval, and structured probing functions for coarse-to-fine temporal localization. We validate HPP on LongVideoBench, which requires both fine-grained perception and long-range relational reasoning, and show that decoupling the two via iterative programmatic probing yields substantial gains. Further results on EgoSchema, VideoMME, and MLVU demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach across diverse long-video benchmarks.

t: DiffNeCTIS: Diffusion-based Nested Compound Type Identification for Sanskrit
a: International Institute of Information Technology Hyderabad, Dhirubhai Ambani Institute Of Information and Communication Technology
Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur, Dhirubhai Ambani Institute Of Information and Communication Technology
ab: Sanskrit multi-component compounding presents a severe structured prediction challenge: the space of valid parse structures grows exponentially with compound length, implicit semantic relations are highly context-sensitive, and accurate type assignment demands simultaneous global structural coherence and local morphological precision across a fine-grained label typology. Existing systems address Nested Compound Type Identification for Sanskrit (NeCTIS) discriminatively, predicting dependency edges and semantic types in a single greedy pass. Reformulating NeCTIS as iterative generative refinement via diffusion over the full label sequence resolves this structural inconsistency but exposes a complementary bottleneck - coarse global attention that suppresses the localized morphological signals necessary for fine-grained type discrimination. We address this through a local refinement mechanism within a restricted window.We further provide the first systematic evaluation of large language models on NeCTIS, finding consistent and substantial failures under zero-shot and few-shot conditions - attributable to the absence of structural inductive biases, Sanskrit under-representation in pretraining, and morphological sensitivity requirements that broad-coverage models are fundamentally ill-equipped to satisfy.

t: SeMLI-RAG: Semantics-Guided Multimodal Late Interaction for Retrieval-Augmented Radiology Report Generation
a: University of Applied Sciences Western Switzerland, Sierre (HES-SO Valais)
ab: The consultation of reference cases in clinical radiology reporting motivates integrating multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) into automated systems. However, traditional RAG approaches employ single-vector embeddings for indexing, resulting in loss of granular information. Moreover, a semantic gap exists whereby visually similar radiographs often encode distinct pathologies. In this paper, we propose a Semantics-guided Multi-modal Late Interaction RAG (SeMLI-RAG) framework for radiology report generation. Our approach employs a weight-based late interaction strategy for retrieval to capture fine-grained radiographic features. Furthermore, we introduce an image-adaptive RAG to selectively leverage retrieved information, mitigating performance degradation caused by retrieval-induced noise. Experiments on three radiology benchmarks demonstrate that our framework yields consistent improvements over the backbone and RAG baselines across multiple evaluation dimensions. Further analysis shows that improving retrieval granularity and retrieval robustness can both benefit radiology report generation.

t: An Embarrassingly Simple Data Selection Strategy for Million-Scale Multi-Modal Instruction-Tuning
a: Tsinghua University, The University of Sheffield and University of Sheffield
ab: Recent research demonstrates that pretrained large language models (LLMs) require minimal but carefully curated data for instruction-tuning. Building on LLMs, multi-modal models further contend with far larger data volumes, heterogeneous sources, and cross-modal alignment, amplifying both the necessity and the complexity of data selection. However, existing methods rely on deeply extracted embeddings, gradients or narrow quality scores that are time-consuming to compute and limited in expressiveness, frequently failing to surpass a simple random-sampling baseline. To overcome these limitations, we step back from complex embedding spaces and target the fundamental objective of instruction tuning: how and what knowledge should be elicited from the pretrained model and exposed to users. We leverage interaction Styles as a proxy for structural diversity, and decompose data quality into capability-specific Scores, yielding an explicit yet Rich (SSR) profile for each sample. We further cast the selection as submodular coverage maximization over the capability-style grid, providing an approximation guarantee. SSR consistently delivers superior performance across two distinct architecture stacks, LLaVA-1.5 (Vicuna + CLIP) and LLaVA-OneVision (Qwen2 + SigLIP), two large-scale data pools, six data budget settings, and 14 multi-modal benchmarks. To our knowledge, SSR is the first data selection method validated at million-scale, achieving 99.1% of full-data performance using only 30% of a 2.6M pool. Furthermore, the SSR profile models and selected subsets transfer training-free across data pools and model architectures with capability extensibility.

t: Evolutionary Soups: Evolving Mixture-of-Experts for Multi-Objective LLM Alignment
a: Fraunhofer Institute for Applied Information Technology and Universität Köln
University of Stuttgart and University of Southampton

Universität Köln, Faculty of Mathematics and Natural Sciences,, Institute for Biomedical Informatics, University of Cologne, Faculty of Medicine and University Hospital and Fraunhofer Institute for Applied Information Technology
ab: Large language models are increasingly required to generate responses that satisfy multiple competing objectives. Since optimal trade-offs depend on both user preferences and input prompts, controllable multi-objective generation must dynamically adapt models at inference time without retraining. To address this, we propose Evolutionary Soups, a mixture-of-experts framework for fine-grained generation control, with gating networks trained via an evolutionary algorithm. The per-layer gating networks dynamically produce expert-merging coefficients from hidden-state representations, while the evolutionary algorithm incorporates greedy hypervolume contribution for effective evolution of these gating networks, achieving consistent improvements on large and noisy training datasets and broader coverage of the non-convex Pareto front. Experiments across three tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of Evolutionary Soups over baselines: it achieves the best hypervolume, linear utility, and Tchebyshev utility (~20% improvement) among controllable methods on all tasks.

t: Joint Constraint Aggregation for Qualifier-Sensitive Retrieval-Augmented QA
a: Carnegie Mellon University, Princeton University and University of Wisconsin - Madison
ab: Retrieval-augmented QA can fail even when the correct answer is in the retrieved evidence. This can happen when a competing answer satisfies some, but not all, of the question’s requirements and is mentioned frequently in the retrieved documents, making it look like a strong choice. To test whether this retrieval skew actually affects the decision, we manipulate it directly: increasing the prevalence of passages that favor the competing answer makes models more likely to select it. This points to a decision problem that candidate-level support alone cannot resolve. We therefore introduce Joint Constraint Aggregation (JCA), which compares candidates against the same question-derived requirements using the retrieved evidence. Across our evaluation settings, JCA improves overall accuracy, and its advantage grows when retrieval favors a competing answer. Together, these results suggest that when partial matches and retrieval prominence pull models toward a competing answer, comparing candidates against the question’s full requirements can make selection more reliable.

t: AGE-Sampler: Adaptive-granularity Graph-enhanced Event Sampling for Long-Video Understanding
a: Shenzhen International Graduate School, Tsinghua University
ab: Informative keyframe selection is critical for applying large vision-language models (LVLMs) to long-form video understanding under limited frame budgets. However, existing methods heavily rely on query-frame similarity, which can yield coarse boundaries and miss latent contextual events that are answer-relevant but not explicitly mentioned in the query. To address this issue, we propose AGE-Sampler, a training-free Adaptive-granularity Graph-enhanced Event sampling framework for long-video understanding. AGE-Sampler jointly exploits low-level visual transition cues and query-relevance signals to construct query-adaptive events, thus preserving fine-grained structures in relevant regions while merging low-relevance regions into compact intervals. To recover answer-bearing contextual evidence, we further develop a fine-grained event graph and propagate importance from high-confidence query-relevant anchors via Personalized PageRank, followed by event-level budget allocation and representative keyframe selection. Extensive experiments with different LVLM backbones show that our AGE-Sampler consistently improves long-video understanding performance, achieving average absolute gains of +6.2% on LongVideoBench, +8.8% on MLVU, and +3.8% on Video-MME, while remaining lightweight and plug-and-play.

t: RoboReason: Boosting Robotics-Relevant VLM Reasoning Through Scalable Data Generation
a: University of Pennsylvania, University of Pennsylvania
University of Pennsylvania, University of Pennsylvania
University of Pennsylvania, University of Pennsylvania
ab: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance when integrated into robot manipulation pipelines, but real-world evaluation of VLM capabilities on downstream robotics tasks is both difficult and expensive to scale. We propose that spatial and temporal ordering tasks using images from stereo and wrist cameras attached to real-world robots are particularly well-suited for evaluating visual reasoning capabilities, as they assess skills directly applicable to robots. We evaluate VLM reasoning abilities on three questions: ordering shuffled frames conditioned on a language description of the task, ordering objects depthwise based on distance from the camera, and ordering objects from left-to-right in pixel coordinates. The complexity of these tasks can also be modulated by changing the size of the set to sort. Our experiments show that several state-of-the-art vision-language models struggle on ordering tasks. To fix this, we propose a scalable autonomous training data generation pipeline, and show that both supervised finetuning and reinforcement-learning on the generated data can significantly improve VLM reasoning performance both on spatiotemporal ordering tasks as well as downstream robotics and visual reasoning tasks.

t: AnchorLens: A Shared Coordinate System for Interpreting Intermediate Representations in Large Language Models
ab: Lens methods aim to decode intermediate representations of large language models into vocabulary predictions by training independent translators for each layer. While this approach provides insights into how the final response emerges across layers, it overlooks the dominant structure shared among them. We identify that per-layer alignment problems share a dominant common structure: the first singular component of per-layer translators explains 31–64% of total spectral variance, 10–20\times above the unstructured baseline. Motivated by this evidence, we propose AnchorLens, which exploits a global-local decomposition: a shared full-rank matrix G maps layers into a common coordinate system, while per-layer low-rank adapters correct layer-specific residuals, trained in two stages. AnchorLens achieves over 90% parameter reduction relative to full-rank methods while matching TunedLens and outperforming LoRALens on next-token prediction and linear shortcut evaluations across eight benchmark tasks. These results hold across 16 models up to 120B parameters from five families: GPT-OSS, Qwen3, Qwen2.5, OLMo2, and Gemma2. Furthermore, the shared coordinate system induced by G enables geometric analyses inaccessible to independent per-layer methods, including quantification of inter-layer drift reduction and empirical validation of non-degeneracy: post-training adapter orthogonality confirms G absorbs the shared structure. Our code is publicly available on https://github.com/GiuseT/InterpretabilityLenses.git.

t: Temporal Leakage in Financial News NLP: A Multi-Architecture Audit with a Regime-Specific M&A Signal
a: Faculty of Science of Bizerte, University of Carthage
ab: Financial-news direction prediction has become a popular NLP benchmark, yet reported gains depend critically on whether the train–test split is chronological or random, i.e., on temporal leakage. We audit this dependence on a 49,799-article corpus across 16 feature–model combinations spanning TF-IDF, MiniLM, FinBERT, and fine-tuned RoBERTa-large / DeBERTa-v3-large, plus separate zero/few-shot and LoRA probes of Llama-3 and Qwen2.5 LLMs: random splits inflate MCC by 1.1× to 6.5×, tracking model capacity and feature richness, and end-to-end FinBERT fine-tuning re-amplifies rather than closes the gap (size-matched ratio 1.75×). Conditioning on event type, mergers and acquisitions (M A) is the only audited category with a positive locked-test signal under near-temporal chronological evaluation (TF-IDF MCC = 0.138 train-only, 0.068 under train∪val refit; 10,000-permutation p < 10⁻³); the signal does not transfer to FNSPID’s 2009–2020 U.S. corpus, localising the headline to our 2024–2025 European-tilted M A semantics rather than a universal predictor. Three independent role labellers converge on acquirer-tagged articles as the signal locus, a power-limited qualitative convergence rather than a hypothesis-tested asymmetry. Chronological splitting plays for financial NLP the role characteristics-purging plays for asset pricing: it strips the predictable, stale component of news and leaves a residual that is small, event-localized, and lexically shallow. We advocate leakage audits as a required disclosure for financial-NLP benchmarks.

t: AtomMem: Building Simple and Effective Memory System for LLM Agents via Atomic Facts
a: University of Science and Technology of China
Anhui University and Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of Science and Technology of China
University of Science and Technology of China
ab: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong reasoning and generation abilities, but their fixed context windows limit long-term information accumulation and reuse across multi-session interactions. Existing memory-augmented systems often construct memory in a coarse and unstable manner, relying on inefficient memory representations or unstable unconstrained updates. To address these challenges, we propose **AtomMem**, a long-term memory system designed for value-dense storage and stable memory evolution. AtomMem introduces a Fact Executor, which selectively extracts high value atomic facts from long form interactions to serve as highly efficient memory representations. Subsequently, AtomMem organizes these facts into hierarchical event structures and temporal profiles, capturing coherent episodic contexts and tracking dynamically evolving user attributes over time. During retrieval, the system activates an associative memory graph to connect fragmented memories. Experiments on the LoCoMo benchmark confirm that AtomMem achieves state-of-the-art performance across various reasoning tasks, offering a scalable and economically viable solution for deploying intelligent personalized agents. The implementation code is publicly available at [https://github.com/MINE-USTC/AtomMem](https://github.com/MINE-USTC/AtomMem).

t: Clinically Grounded Privacy Evaluation of Medical LMs
a: Stanford University and American Board of Family Medicine
ab: Medical language models (LMs) can memorize and reproduce protected health information, but privacy evaluations often focus on recovery of training text rather than disclosure under realistic threat models. We introduce a clinically grounded framework that evaluates leakage along a graded axis of adversarial access, ranging from publicly inferable demographics to leaked note fragments. At each tier, we measure verbatim memorization of patient-specific text and semantic leakage of sensitive diagnoses. Applying the framework to an LM continually pretrained on 378k clinical notes, we find that routine encounter metadata (i.e., name, date of birth, visit date, provider name, and practice location) elicits high rates of verbatim memorization across a patient’s timeline and sensitive-diagnosis recovery (AUROC 0.91 for abortion, 0.82 for HIV). At the same time, exact-match memorization can overstate disclosure: 36% of memorized tokens reflect templated documentation. Our work highlights the risks of training on longitudinal clinical data and provides a practical, reusable framework for contextual privacy evaluation of medical LMs.

t: Watch Your Norms: On Test-Time Expert Reduction in Multilingual MoEs
ab: Test-time expert reduction (top-k reduction) is a popular way to cut inference cost in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models, avoiding the expensive model retraining. Existing work, however, analyzes the effects of top-k reduction almost exclusively on English benchmarks. In this work, we provide the first systematic multilingual study of test-time top-k reduction across three contemporary MoE models, 100 languages, and 5 downstream tasks. We show that down to 75% of retained experts, the models degrade gracefully, but overall retention collapses sharply at low k and widens a structural multilingual gap: low-resource languages degrade much faster than high-resource ones. We trace the gap to a renormalization-induced norm overshoot in the MoE block, where the renormalization over the surviving expert weights inflates the MoE contribution to the residual stream. This inflation harms low-resource languages disproportionately due to their smaller residual norms. As a remedy, we propose two training-free and latency-free interventions: (i) a grid-searched global scalar to rescale the representations output by the MoE layer (global α) and (ii) a parameter-free per-token correction (token α) of expert weights derived from the routing. The proposed interventions substantially improve overall retention and reduce the multilingual gap.

t: CauTab: Counterfactual Tabular Data Synthesis with Functional and Causal-Dependency Constraints
ab: High-quality tabular data is essential for data-driven tasks, yet often limited by scarcity and privacy concerns. While synthetic data generated by recent Deep Generative Models and LLMs improves fidelity, existing methods struggle to preserve rigorous attribute dependencies. As a result, the generated data may appear statistically realistic but lack logical consistency. To address this challenge, we propose CauTab, a novel counterfactual framework for tabular data synthesis that preserves functional dependencies and causal-dependency structures. CauTab operates in a three-stage pipeline: (1) it employs an LLM-guided mining strategy to efficiently identify functional dependencies; (2) it constructs a causal-dependency graph by integrating data-driven optimization with LLM-based semantic reasoning; and (3) it executes a dependency-constrained generation process via the Abduction-Intervention-Prediction paradigm. By enforcing deterministic constraints and using the learned graph for structured propagation, CauTab improves statistical fidelity while preserving logical consistency. Experiments demonstrate that CauTab outperforms baselines in data utility and fidelity, while maintaining competitive empirical privacy and strong logical consistency.

t: An Interpretable Linguistically-Grounded Analysis of Scene Saliency in Movie Screenplays
a: Fujitsu Research and Development Center Co. Ltm.
International Institute of Information Technology Hyderabad, Dhirubhai Ambani Institute Of Information and Communication Technology
ab: We investigate the factors affecting salience in movie screenplay by posing two research questions: 1. Does Uniform Information Density (UID) predict salient scenes? 2. What other linguistic properties distinguish salient scenes from non-salient background? We answer both questions through a controlled corpus study on the MENSA corpus, paired with a Linguistically-Grounded Salience Model (LGSM), a dual-stream classifier that fuses a frozen BERT encoder with explicit linguistic features through adaptive gating. The UID picture is layered in long-form discourse. Perscene UID summaries carry no independent signal once length is controlled, but at the token level salient scenes match non-salient material in the bulk while specifically suppressing the rarest, hardest-to-predict tokens in the upper tail. UID therefore lives at the within-scene token level rather than as a per-scene aggregate. Salient scenes also show a moderate and sustained cast of central characters (following an inverted-U pattern), strong third-person usage, syntactically simpler language, and more abstract vocabulary about motivation and conflict. LGSM exploits this signature and improves recall on salient scenes over a strong semantic baseline while yielding better downstream summaries.

t: Near-Miss Context Contamination and Language-Asymmetric Evidence Arbitration in LLMs
a: Kathmandu Engineering College, Kantipur Engineering College and Dogma Group
University of Calgary and Tribhuvan University - Thapathali Campus
ab: Retrieval-augmented generation assumes that language models can use relevant context while rejecting semantically related but non-evidential context. Further, multilingual retrieval adds a second assumption that when evidence appears in different languages, models arbitrate by factual content instead of language cues. We test both these assumptions as generator-side failures to understand how models bind, compare, and trust evidence across languages. We first study near-miss contamination where we add true, relation-matched context about a nearby entity that does not answer the target question. Across Mintaka and PopQA, this context raises distractor adoption before any direct contradiction is introduced, and the effect persists across every tested model and language.We then study language evidence arbitration where English and local-language evidence disagree. We find that language preference is model-family dependent. GPT-5.4-mini leans toward English across all four languages, while DeepSeek models lean toward local-language evidence for all tested languages. We also run a label-only control where both snippets are written in English and only the source label varies and find that evidence labeled as English is over-trusted, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals excluding zero across all 16 model-language pairs. Our results thus show that context use is shaped by entity proximity, language preference, and source-language metadata.

t: PROVENA-MED: Benchmarking Provenance Faithfulness in Multimodal Clinical Reasoning
ab: Clinical language and vision-language models increasingly generate diagnostic and treatment rationales, but those claims remain difficult to audit. Existing benchmarks usually score final answers over fully revealed records, without testing whether each claim is grounded in valid patient evidence or whether models can seek missing information efficiently. We introduce Provena-Med, a benchmark for evaluating provenance-faithful multimodal clinical reasoning over linked EHR tables, clinical notes, chest radiographs, and guideline rules. Models must produce a staged artifact comprising a problem list, differential, workup, therapy, and monitoring, in which each claim cites typed evidence units and may abstain when information is insufficient. Provena-Med supports both full-information evaluation and an interactive evidence-seeking track. We further propose MM-AIS, which measures citation validity, objective support under evidence-removal tests, salient-evidence recall, and, for open-weight models, sensitivity to cited evidence. Across ten open-weight models and five cohorts, the best attribution yield is only 0.42, citation hallucination is common, and diagnostic accuracy, safety, and provenance do not reliably co-vary. Provena-Med provides an auditable testbed for evaluating grounded clinical reasoning beyond final-answer accuracy.

t: Enhancing linear attention with residual learning
ab: Linear attention offers a linear-time alternative to self-attention but often struggles to capture long-range patterns. We revisit linear attention through a prediction-correction lens and show that prevalent variants can be written as a combination of a historical prediction and a single-token correction, which creates an expressivity bottleneck. To address this bottleneck, we introduce Residual Linear Attention (RLA), a framework that equips linear attention with an explicit residual-fitting mechanism. RLA maintains an auxiliary recurrent state that learns to accumulate residual errors over time and correct the base prediction. We further instantiate a delta-rule version, Residual Delta Net (RDN), incorporating adaptive gating and residual clipping for enhanced correction control and stability. Our implementation leverages highly optimized linear attention kernels and preserves linear time and memory. Across language modeling and recall-intensive evaluations, RLA and RDN consistently outperform their respective baselines and other modern linear-attention methods, narrowing the gap to standard Transformers while retaining linear scaling.

t: AdaPath: Query-Adaptive Path-Finding via Path-Bank for Multi-Hop Implicit Biomedical KGQA
a: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology
Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology and AITRICS
ab: Path-finding over knowledge graphs has become an effective way to ground LLM reasoning on multi-hop questions. However, biomedical QA introduces two distinct challenges that general-domain methods are not designed for: (i) queries do not expose intermediate reasoning and can be answered through multiple valid pathways, and (ii) biomedical knowledge graphs are densely connected, so path-finding methods easily take wrong turns. To address these challenges, we propose AdaPath, a path-finding framework that retrieves query-adaptive meta-paths from Path-Bank, which captures both query semantics and biomedical knowledge graph structure. AdaPath provides the missing cues in biomedical queries while effectively pruning dense knowledge graph neighborhoods during multi-hop reasoning. We further release BioStrat-QA, a biomedical KGQA benchmark that stratifies multi-hop queries by how much intermediate reasoning they expose. Across biomedical KGQA benchmarks, AdaPath consistently outperforms baselines, sustaining meaningful path-finding even when multi-hop queries expose less surface information. The source code is available at https://github.com/Jun-Hyeong-Kim/AdaPath.

t: Context Compression for LLM Agents: A Survey of Methods, Failure Modes, and Evaluation
a: Institute of automation, Chinese academy of science, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of California, San Diego, University of California, San Diego
Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences
ab: As Large Language Models (LLMs) evolve into autonomous agents for long-horizon tasks, managing unbounded interaction trajectories under fixed context budgets becomes a core systems challenge. Unlike standard long-context documents, agent trajectories are heterogeneous and interleave observations, reasoning traces, and tool executions, so compression must preserve temporal dependencies, actionable state, and structural fidelity. Yet existing methods remain fragmented, making it difficult to compare design choices and reason about their reliability implications. This survey introduces a unified taxonomy of agent context compression along three dimensions: compression target (what is compressed), compression mechanism (how it is transformed and retained), and control policy (who decides when compression is triggered). We further organize recurring failures in compressed execution into F1: Pre-compression Decision Error, F2: In-compression Information Loss, and F3: Post-compression Access Failure, and examine domain-specific trade-offs in software engineering, web navigation, and deep research. By unifying the design space, failure taxonomy, and evaluation perspective, this survey provides a foundation for building scalable and recoverable LLM agents.

t: Estimating Surprisal from the Speech Signal
ab: Although language is predominantly spoken, empirical tests of surprisal theory rely almost entirely on written text. In practice, surprisal is estimated using language models (LMs) trained on text and applied to transcriptions, creating a text bottleneck that limits evaluation of the theory in the spoken modality. We remove this bottleneck by estimating surprisal directly from the speech signal using a speech LM. This raises a key question: should surprisal be defined over realization-specific acoustic inputs or over abstract linguistic units? Since a single unit can have many distinct acoustic realizations, each assigned a different probability by the model, defining surprisal over abstract units is difficult. To address this, we introduce an importance sampling estimator that approximates the probability of an abstract unit by marginalizing over realizations generated by a text-to-speech model. Using pupillometry data from a listening study, we evaluate surprisal theory in this text-free setting at multiple levels of granularity. Obtaining surprisal from several speech LMs, we consistently find that surprisal estimated via importance sampling better predicts pupil dilation than realization-specific surprisal for words. We also find that surprisal values for sub-lexical units are predictive of pupil dilation. While we find that surprisal can be estimated without recourse to text, and that marginalizing over distinct realizations of words is more predictive of lexical processing effort, surprisal as a whole is not a strong predictor of change in pupil size, regardless of its source.

t: Entropy Equilibrium Sampling: Tuning-Free Truncation for Language Model Decoding
a: National Resource Center for Chinese Materia Medica, China Academy of Chinese Medical Sciences
‌Qilu University of Technology (Shandong Academy of Sciences)‌
ab: Token sampling strategies critically influence text generation quality in large language models (LLMs). However, existing methods introduce additional hyperparameters, requiring extensive tuning and complicating deployment. We present Entropy Equilibrium Sampling (EES), a tuning-free approach grounded in information theory that dynamically determines the candidate set size using a first-crossing rule: it stops candidate-set expansion at the first index where cumulative probability mass exceeds the normalized entropy of the top-k distribution and retains the preceding prefix. We evaluate EES on reasoning, mathematical, and open-ended generation tasks across multiple model architectures and scales. Our results show that EES achieves robust performance across temperature settings without retuning truncation hyperparameters, delivering competitive accuracy with tuned baselines while maintaining diversity. Analysis reveals that the retained candidate-set size k* automatically encodes temperature effects, adapting from near-greedy behavior at low temperatures to broad candidate retention at high temperatures. By eliminating truncation-specific hyperparameter tuning, EES simplifies deployment while providing stable and competitive performance. Our code is publicly available.

t: Revisiting the Estimation of Unigram Surprisal in Computational Psycholinguistics
a: Department of Computer Science, ETHZ - ETH Zurich
ab: Contextual and unigram surprisal are standard predictors of reading time in computational psycholinguistics. While contextual surprisal is typically derived from neural language models, unigram surprisal is usually obtained from independent corpus counts. Although both quantities are deterministic functionals of a single underlying distribution—capturing conditional and marginal structure respectively—this practice breaks their probabilistic link and may introduce estimation error from the mismatch. We propose three principles for estimating unigram surprisal in psycholinguistic research, including the requirement that both quantities be derived from the same language model. We operationalize this principle by introducing a Monte Carlo estimator of unigram surprisal from a language model, along with a marginalized variant that has lower variance empirically. When unigram surprisal is re-estimated under this unified framework, we find evidence that predictors change in their predictive contribution to reading time. We also confirm prior findings that frequency can be a stronger predictor of processing effort than contextual surprisal under this unified framework.

t: AgentCollab: A Self-Evaluation-Driven Collaboration Paradigm for Efficient LLM Agents
a: Hong Kong Polytechnic University and Harbin Institute of Technology
ab: Autonomous agents powered by large language models (LLMs) perform complex tasks through long-horizon reasoning and tool interaction, where a fundamental trade-off arises between execution efficiency and reasoning robustness. Models at different capability–cost levels offer complementary advantages: lower-cost models enable fast execution but may struggle on difficult reasoning segments, while stronger models provide more robust reasoning at higher computational cost. We present AgentCollab, a self-driven collaborative inference framework that dynamically coordinates models with different reasoning capacities during agent execution. Instead of relying on external routing modules, the framework uses the agent’s own self-reflection signal to determine whether the current reasoning trajectory is making meaningful progress, and escalates control to a stronger reasoning tier only when necessary. To further stabilize long-horizon execution, we introduce a difficulty-aware cumulative escalation strategy that allocates additional reasoning budget based on recent failure signals. In our experiments, we instantiate this framework using a two-level small–large model setting. Experiments on diverse multi-step agent benchmarks show that AgentCollab consistently improves the accuracy–efficiency Pareto frontier of LLM agents.
